---

## Locality Research Guide
### Pre-1800 Arkansas (Spanish Colonial Period)
**Period:** c. 1686–1800 | **Jurisdiction:** Province of Louisiana (French, then Spanish) — Arkansas Post district

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Arkansas as a political entity did not exist before 1819 (Territory) or 1836 (State). All pre-1800 records were created and filed under the **Province of Louisiana**:

| Period | Controlling Power | Administrative Unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1762 | France | La Louisiane |
| 1763–1800 | Spain | Provincia de Luisiana |
| 1800 (Oct) | France (briefly) | Per Treaty of San Ildefonso |
| 1803 | United States | Louisiana Purchase |

The only meaningful European settlement in present-day Arkansas before 1800 was **Arkansas Post** (*Poste des Arkansas* / *Puesto de Arkansas*), established 1686 on the Arkansas River near its junction with the Mississippi. Nearly all pre-1800 records you will find concern people at or near that post. Searches filed under "Arkansas" will miss most records — you must search under **Louisiana** and specifically Arkansas Post.

---

### ⚠️ Critical Quirk: Search Under Louisiana, Not Arkansas

**Pre-1800 records are not filed under "Arkansas."** They exist under the Spanish Province of Louisiana and specifically the Arkansas Post district. When searching FamilySearch or any archive, use Louisiana as the jurisdiction and Arkansas Post as the locality.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

---

#### 1. Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
**Period covered:** French era (early 1700s) and Spanish era (1763–1800)
**Access level: Browse-only images — must be read in Spanish (and French for pre-1763 entries)**

FamilySearch has digitized **one volume** directly tied to this period and place:

- **Image Group 008814402** — *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post*, 1763–1800
  - 64 images | Language: Spanish
  - `recordSearchablePercent`: **0%** — not name-indexed
  - `fulltextSearchable`: **false**
  - Access: Browse image-by-image at FamilySearch; no keyword search possible; researcher must read 18th-century Spanish script

French-era registers (pre-1763) were maintained by Catholic missionaries and are **not digitized on FamilySearch** for this specific location. Physical and transcribed copies are held by:
- **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** — original or transcribed parish registers
- **Arkansas History Commission**, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR — transcribed copies ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))

The broader **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** collection (FamilySearch collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905), ~987,654 records) covers the same French and Spanish colonial period at the Louisiana jurisdiction level — worth checking for Arkansas Post entries that may have been registered at New Orleans or another Louisiana administrative center.

---

#### 2. Census / Population Lists (Padrones)
**Period covered:** Spanish era, 1769–1798 (several known enumerations)
**Access level: Physical/microfilm only — no indexed online version confirmed**

Spanish colonial administrators conducted periodic household censuses called **padrones** listing heads of household, family members, ages, and sometimes occupations. These are among the most genealogically rich sources for this period.

Surviving padrones for Arkansas Post are held at:
- **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain — the primary repository for all Spanish Louisiana administrative records; section *Papeles de Cuba* holds most Arkansas Post material
- **Library of Congress**, Washington, DC — holds microfilm of AGI Louisiana records ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock — holds copies and transcriptions

FamilySearch `volume_search` returned no digitized padron volumes for Arkansas. These must be consulted on microfilm or in person.

---

#### 3. Land Records (Concessions / Grants)
**Period covered:** French and Spanish eras
**Access level: Physical/microfilm only for most; partial digitization through Louisiana collections**

Spanish governors issued land concessions (*mercedes de tierras*) to settlers at Arkansas Post. These documents name the grantee, describe tract boundaries, and often name adjacent landowners (useful for cluster research).

- **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville — original concession files
- **Arkansas History Commission** — transcriptions and microfilm
- **Bureau of Land Management, General Land Office (GLO)** — post-1803 U.S. land patents that sometimes reference prior Spanish grants; searchable at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)
- The **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** collection ([1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — actually collection 2078341) may contain related property inventories from the colonial-era Louisiana jurisdiction

---

#### 4. Military Records
**Period covered:** Spanish era, 1763–1800
**Access level: Physical/archival — no digitized FamilySearch collection confirmed for this period**

Arkansas Post was a garrisoned military post throughout the Spanish period. Military records include:
- Muster rolls (*listas de revista*) — name soldiers, rank, pay, birthplace
- Officer service records (*hojas de servicio*)
- Post correspondence

These are held primarily at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Papeles de Cuba section) and the **Archivo General Militar de Segovia**, Spain. The Library of Congress microfilm series covers portions. Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) holds some Spanish colonial military records but coverage for Arkansas specifically is not confirmed in tool results.

---

#### 5. Civil/Administrative Records (Notarial Acts, Correspondence)
**Period covered:** Spanish era, 1763–1800
**Access level: Physical/archival**

The Arkansas Post commandant kept civil records including contracts, depositions, wills, and correspondence. These form part of the **Papeles de Cuba** series at the AGI and are partially microfilmed at the Library of Congress. No digitized FamilySearch collection was returned for this record class.

---

#### 6. Post-1803 Records That Reflect Pre-1800 Ancestry

Although outside your target window, several early American-era sources document families who lived in Arkansas under Spanish rule:

- **Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870** (FamilySearch collection [2085124](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2085124), ~178,345 records) — the 1819–1820 territorial census often captures people who were present before 1803
- U.S. public land claim proceedings (post-1803) required settlers to prove prior French or Spanish grants — these claim files name families and their colonial-era land histories, and are at **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov))

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Archivo General de Indias (AGI)**, Seville, Spain | Original padrones, land concessions, military records, civil correspondence for Spanish Louisiana | In person or via microfilm at Library of Congress; online portal at [pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es) |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, DC | Microfilm of AGI Papeles de Cuba series (Louisiana records) | On-site reading room; some finding aids online |
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR | Transcriptions and microfilm of colonial records; state archives for post-1819 records | On-site; [history.arkansas.gov](https://www.history.arkansas.gov) |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | French and Spanish sacramental registers | Contact diocese archives directly |
| **FamilySearch** (online) | 1 browse-only volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers (1763–1800); Louisiana church records 1718–1925; post-1819 Arkansas collections | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **NARA** (National Archives) | Post-1803 U.S. federal land claim files reflecting Spanish grants | In person or via Ancestry/Fold3 for some series |
| **Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records pre-1763 | In person or via [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr) |

---

### Digitization Level Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Digitization | Searchability |
|---|---|---|
| Sacramental Registers, Arkansas Post 1763–1800 | ✅ Images online (64 pp.) | ❌ Browse-only; 0% indexed; Spanish |
| Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925 | ✅ ~493,000 images | Partially indexed |
| Padrones (censuses) | ❌ Not digitized on FS | Physical/microfilm only |
| Land concessions | ❌ Not digitized on FS | Physical/microfilm only |
| Military records | ❌ Not digitized on FS | Physical/archival |
| Notarial/civil records | ❌ Not digitized on FS | Physical/archival |
| Post-1803 land claims (reflect colonial grants) | Partial (NARA/Ancestry) | Some indexed |

---

### Key Research Warnings

1. **Search Louisiana, not Arkansas.** No pre-1800 Arkansas jurisdiction exists in record systems — use "Province of Louisiana" or "Arkansas Post" as your locality.
2. **The one digitized FamilySearch volume (008814402) must be browsed page-by-page in 18th-century Spanish.** There is no name index and no full-text search. A researcher unable to read colonial Spanish script will need a translator or transcriptionist.
3. **The AGI (Seville) is irreplaceable.** Most original administrative records never left Spain. The Library of Congress microfilm series is the best U.S. access point before planning an overseas trip.
4. **Population was tiny.** Arkansas Post had only a few dozen to a few hundred residents throughout this period. If your ancestor is not found in the sacramental registers, the padrones are the next best source — and both are held primarily in archival rather than online form.
5. **French-era records (pre-1763) require French-language skills** and may be held in ANOM (France) as well as the Diocese of Little Rock.
6. **Post-1803 U.S. land claim files** are a powerful substitute: settlers who held Spanish grants had to file documentation proving their prior title, often generating detailed family narratives in early American court records.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (Pre-Statehood, ~1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Status in 1790:** Not yet a state. The area that would become Ohio was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The Northwest Territory also encompassed present-day Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota.
- **First county organized:** Washington County (1788) — the first governmental unit created within the future state of Ohio
- **Second county organized:** Hamilton County (1790) — in the southwestern region
- **Ohio statehood:** March 1, 1803 — the first state carved from the Northwest Territory
- **Territorial capital:** Marietta (seat of Washington County and territorial administration)
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, early land speculation; dominated by the need to survey and distribute public lands
- **Ethnic composition:** Early Anglo-American settlers (largely from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England), with distinct colonial sub-populations tied to the land districts below; Indigenous nations (Shawnee, Delaware/Lenape, Wyandot, Miami) still occupying large portions of the territory in 1790
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuit riders, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker (especially in the Virginia Military District migration corridor), and scattered Catholic missionaries; formal institutional church records are sparse before ~1800
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787); Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794); Treaty of Greenville (1795) — which opened much of what is now central and northern Ohio to American settlement; Ohio statehood (1803)

---

## Boundary Changes

This is the most important factor for pre-statehood Ohio research. Boundary changes were **frequent and dramatic**, and the correct jurisdiction must be identified for every event date.

**Territorial layer (before 1803):**
All of present-day Ohio was governed as the **Northwest Territory** from 1787 to 1803. Records generated before any county was organized technically belong to the territorial government. Early court, land, and probate records created under territorial authority are held at the **Ohio History Connection** in Columbus ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)).

**County formation sequence (relevant to 1785–1803):**
- **Washington County (1788):** Created from the whole unorganized territory — in 1788 it covered essentially all of future Ohio. If an ancestor's event pre-dates any other county's formation and their location cannot be pinned, Washington County is the default territorial jurisdiction.
- **Hamilton County (1790):** Carved from Washington County; covered the southwestern corner of future Ohio (Cincinnati area).
- Additional counties were carved rapidly in subsequent years. Because boundaries shifted so frequently, researchers **must determine which county held jurisdiction at the exact date of the event**, not today's county boundary.

**Two distinct land-grant districts create a geographic split within Ohio itself:**
- **Virginia Military District** (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers, south-central Ohio): Reserved by Congress for Virginia's Revolutionary War veterans. Uses a **metes-and-bounds survey system** rather than the federal township grid. Land warrant records are held at the **Virginia State Library** (Richmond), not in Ohio repositories. ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): Set aside for Connecticut's "fire lands" claimants. Surveyed on a different grid system. Records are held at the **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland. ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))

**Quirk:** Which land-record repository holds a document for your ancestor depends entirely on *where within Ohio* they settled — the Virginia Military District, the Connecticut Western Reserve, or neither (federal land). An Ohio ancestor in 1790 could have records split across Columbus, Richmond (Virginia), and Cleveland. Establish their specific location before searching land records.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Civil registration:** Ohio did **not** require statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths in 1790 or at statehood (1803). Statewide registration came much later. The collection **"Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001"** (FamilySearch collection 1417891) — whose earliest date is 1840 — confirms that county-level death recording did not begin until after our 1790 target window.
- **What exists for the 1789–1803 window:** Marriage records only, at the county level. FamilySearch collection **"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (id: 1803785; 1,523,678 records; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785)) — **indexed + images**, starting 1789. This is the single most accessible vital record for the territorial period.
- **Births and deaths:** No civil registration of births or deaths existed in 1790. Church records (below) are the only substitute source for baptisms and burials.
- **Digitization level:** County marriages → **indexed + images** (FamilySearch). Birth and death records for 1790 → **do not exist** as civil records; use church registers.

### Church Records

- **What FamilySearch holds:** Collection **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (id: 2246917; 678,234 records; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917)) — **indexed + images**, dating from territorial founding. This is a primary source for baptisms and burials in the pre-statehood period.
- **Denominations present:** Methodist circuit riders reached Ohio settlements quickly after Marietta's founding in 1788. Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker congregations followed migration routes from Pennsylvania and Virginia. Catholic records exist near French-era settlements. Early records are sparse and uneven — many congregations did not form formally until after 1800.
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Physical holdings:** The **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) holds original church registers not yet digitized. Denominational archives (Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia; Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore) may hold registers for congregations with pre-statehood origins.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch collection → **indexed + images** for what is digitized; many early registers are physical only.

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** The first U.S. Federal Census was taken in **1790**, but the Northwest Territory was only partially enumerated. Coverage of the Ohio settlements in 1790 is fragmentary — many early settlers in Washington County (Marietta) and Hamilton County (Cincinnati) appear, but large portions of the territory were not reached. The 1800 federal census includes Ohio as a territory and is more complete.
- **No territorial or state census** existed for the 1790 period.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** The earliest digitized volume covering the pre-statehood period found in the survey is **Washington County, Ohio Tax Records, 1799–1803** (imageGroupNumber 005112240; 73 images; 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — meaning it must be **browsed image-by-image** for nearly all names. This volume is the best extant substitute for a missing 1790–1800 population enumeration for Washington County.
- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (id: 1987542; 345,890 records; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542)) begins in 1800, just outside the 1790 window but capturing early statehood and late-territorial settlers.
- **Digitization level:** 1800 tax records → **indexed + images**. 1799–1803 Washington County tax volume → **browse-only images** (12% indexed).

### Land Records

This is the **richest record category** for the 1785–1803 period.

- **Federal land patents (Ohio as a public land state):** Ohio is a federal-land state. Land entered directly from the federal government was recorded at the **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO)** — searchable free at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). This is the best source for initial land entries in the 1787–1803 window.
- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"** (id: 1542187; 234,567 records; [search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187)) — **indexed + images**, spanning from the very first year of the Northwest Territory through early statehood.
- **Territorial Land Records volume (browse-only):** Volume **005112233** (51 images; 0% indexed; not full-text searchable) covers **Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799** — filed under the territorial jurisdiction, not an Ohio county. This volume must be browsed **image-by-image** with no name index. It is the earliest digitized land record set for the Ohio settlements and is a critical but labor-intensive source.
- **Virginia Military District:** Metes-and-bounds grants; warrant records held at the **Virginia State Library**, Richmond. Not in Ohio repositories. Researchers with ancestors in south-central Ohio (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) must look to Virginia for the initial grant documentation.
- **Connecticut Western Reserve:** Records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland.
- **Survey system note:** Most of Ohio (outside the Virginia Military District and Connecticut Western Reserve) uses the U.S. Public Land Survey System (township and range grid), making location from a land description straightforward.
- **Digitization level:** FamilySearch Ohio Land Records, 1787–1840 → **indexed + images**. Territorial Land Records volume → **browse-only images**. Virginia Military District warrants → **physical only** (Virginia State Library).

### Probate and Court Records

- **Where created:** Under the Northwest Territory's court system, probate and court records were filed in the territorial courts (Washington County, then Hamilton County as it was formed). After counties were established, the county Court of Common Pleas held probate jurisdiction.
- **Where held:** Early court and land records are held at the **Ohio History Connection** (formerly Ohio Historical Society), Columbus ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)). County courthouse records date from each county's formation.
- **Online access:** No specific probate or court record collection for 1780–1803 was returned by `collections_search` or `volume_search`. These records are likely physical only at the Ohio History Connection and individual county probate courts.
- **Digitization level:** **Physical only** or microfilm for this period; check Ohio History Connection finding aids.

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Northwest Indian War (1785–1795), culminating in the Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794) and Treaty of Greenville (1795), directly involved settlers in and around Washington and Hamilton Counties. Service in territorial militia and U.S. Army units generated records.
- **Revolutionary War veterans:** Many early Ohio settlers were Revolutionary War veterans who received land bounties in the Virginia Military District or elsewhere. Their pension and bounty land warrant files are at **NARA** (Washington, D.C.) and searchable via **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) and **Ancestry** ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)).
- **Records held:** NARA holds compiled military service records and pension files. The **Ohio History Connection** holds state adjutant general records.
- **Digitization level:** Revolutionary War pension files → **indexed + images** (Fold3, Ancestry, FamilySearch). Northwest Indian War militia service → mostly **physical or microfilm** at NARA.

### Tax Records

- **Earliest available for Ohio:** Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803 (volume 005112240 — browse-only, 73 images, 12% indexed). This is a direct substitute for the missing population enumeration between the 1790 and 1800 censuses.
- **FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (id: 1987542) — **indexed + images**, starting 1800.
- **Value for 1790 research:** Tax lists name adult male property-holders annually, making them the best annual population substitute before reliable census coverage. An ancestor absent from the partial 1790 census may appear in territorial tax lists.
- **Digitization level:** 1800–1850 collection → **indexed + images**. 1799–1803 Washington County volume → **browse-only images**.

### Cemetery Records

- **Online databases:** **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) is the principal online cemetery index for Ohio. Pre-1803 burials are rare in Find A Grave given the sparse early settlement; most pre-statehood burials were in small family or congregation plots.
- **Sexton records:** Formal cemetery sexton records rarely exist before county organization. Family burial plots on original land grants, churchyard burials, and early public burying grounds are the norm for 1790.
- **Digitization level:** Find A Grave → free online index with images where uploaded. Sexton records for 1790 → generally do not exist or are **physical only** at local historical societies.

### Newspaper Records

- **Earliest Ohio newspapers:** The *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* (Cincinnati, 1793) is among the earliest territorial papers; the *Ohio Gazette* (Marietta) also dates to the territorial period. These predate most rural Ohio settlements by several years.
- **Online access:** **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) holds some early Ohio papers. The **Ohio History Connection** digital newspaper archive and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) are the primary free repositories for early territorial newspapers.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, land sale notices, runaway notices, and legal publications (estate settlements) appear from 1793 onward. Before 1793, no local Ohio newspaper existed.
- **Digitization level:** Partial **online** coverage; significant holdings still on **microfilm** at Ohio History Connection and public libraries.

### Immigration and Emigration Records

- **Migration routes:** Early Ohio settlers arrived overland via the Wilderness Road and then northward from Kentucky, or by boat down the Ohio River (Pittsburgh to Marietta or Cincinnati). No formal immigration records exist for these internal migrations.
- **Naturalization:** Foreign-born settlers (primarily German and Scots-Irish via Pennsylvania) filed declarations of intention and petitions in any court of record. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in county courts. Ohio History Connection and county courthouse holdings.
- **Relevant ports for international arrivals:** Philadelphia and Baltimore were the primary entry ports for immigrants who later moved to Ohio. Passenger lists for arrivals at those ports are at **NARA** and searchable via Ancestry and Fold3.
- **Digitization level:** Passenger lists at ports of entry → **indexed + images** (Ancestry, FamilySearch). Ohio naturalization records, 1790–1803 → **physical only** at Ohio History Connection and county courthouses.

---

### Physical Repositories

| Ohio History Connection, Columbus | Early territorial court records; probate; state adjutant general military records; microfilm of county records | In-person; online finding aids at ohiohistory.org |

| Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve land records; NE Ohio family papers | In-person; some finding aids online |

| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Military service, pension, naturalization, federal land entry records | In-person; digitized via Ancestry/Fold3/FamilySearch |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist but are **not available in any online database** for the 1785–1803 period:
- **Territorial court proceedings** (Washington County and Hamilton County courts of general quarter sessions) — physical only at Ohio History Connection
- **Probate records** from the territorial period — physical at county probate courts and Ohio History Connection
- **Virginia Military District warrant surveys** — largely physical at Virginia State Library (some digitized through Library of Virginia)
- **Early church registers** for many individual congregations — physical at local churches, Ohio History Connection, and denominational archives
- **Quaker removal certificates** (critical for tracing Quaker migrants into Ohio) — at monthly meeting archives

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **No civil birth or death registration** existed in Ohio in 1790. The county death records collection starts in 1840; birth registration came even later. There are no substitutes that cover all individuals — church baptism and burial records are the closest alternative, but they cover only church members.
- **Sparse 1790 federal census coverage** in the Northwest Territory: the enumeration of the future Ohio settlements was incomplete. The 1800 census (Ohio Territory) is more comprehensive.
- **No county-level records before county formation:** Washington County was not organized until 1788, Hamilton County until 1790. Events before those dates have no county-level paper trail. The territorial government's own records are the only administrative documentation.
- **Two volume-search results only** were returned for the 1780–1810 window — indicating that very little of the pre-statehood Ohio record corpus has been digitized and indexed. This is a significant **digitization gap**, not an absence of original records.
- **Native American displacement:** The Treaty of Greenville (1795) opened central Ohio to settlement, meaning many parts of the state had no European-American settlers at all in 1790 — records simply do not exist for those areas until after 1795.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Identify the county that existed at the event date** before searching anything. In 1790, only Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790) existed. An event anywhere else in future Ohio belongs under Washington County jurisdiction ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)).

2. **Determine which land district your ancestor settled in.** Settlers in the Virginia Military District (Scioto to Little Miami) → Virginia State Library for initial warrant. Settlers in the Connecticut Western Reserve (NE Ohio) → Western Reserve Historical Society. Everywhere else → BLM GLO and FamilySearch Ohio Land Records, 1787–1840 ([Ohio Genealogy — Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)).

3. **The territorial land records volume (005112233) must be browsed image-by-image** — it is 0% indexed and not full-text searchable. Plan for a manual page-by-page review of all 51 images if you need the 1788–1799 territorial land records.

4. **Use tax records as a census substitute.** Washington County Tax Records (1799–1803) and the FamilySearch Ohio Tax Records, 1800–1850 collection are the best annual population substitutes for the gap between the 1790 and 1800 censuses and the absence of birth/death registration.

5. **Search the origin state before searching Ohio.** Most 1790 Ohio settlers came from Virginia, Pennsylvania, Maryland, New Jersey, or New England. Their birth, marriage, church, and even early land records are in those origin states. A FAN (family, associates, and neighbors) search in those origin communities often unlocks the Ohio generation.

6. **Revolutionary War pension files at NARA** are among the most informative pre-statehood records: they contain depositions naming spouses, children, ages, and migration history — effectively a biographical summary for veterans who settled in Ohio by 1790.

7. **The Ohio History Connection's online catalog** (ohiohistory.org) is the finding aid for territorial-period records not yet digitized. Many Washington County and Hamilton County original records are findable there before a physical visit.

8. **Check both sides of the Ohio River.** Families in the Cincinnati/Hamilton County area (1790) had near-constant cross-river activity with Kentucky (also only established 1792 as a state). Kentucky court, land, and church records may document the same individuals and families — especially before 1792 when Kentucky was still Virginia's Kentucky County and District.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (Gold Rush Era, c. 1848–1865)

## Jurisdiction Overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Formed as state** | September 9, 1850 — bypassing territorial status entirely |
| **Pre-statehood** | Alta California under Mexico (until Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Feb. 2, 1848); then brief U.S. military administration 1848–1850 |
| **Capital** | Sacramento (from 1854) |
| **Economy** | Gold mining (placer and hard-rock), maritime trade, merchant and supply services, emerging agriculture |
| **Population influx** | ~300,000 migrants 1848–1855, drawn from across the U.S. and abroad — predominantly transient and male |
| **Ethnic diversity** | Americans from eastern states, Mexicans, Chileans, Chinese (from ~1850), Australians, British, French, German, Irish, African Americans, Native Californians |
| **Religions** | Catholic (dominant pre-Rush; Franciscan Mission system); Protestant denominations (Methodist, Baptist, Congregationalist, Episcopal) established from 1849 |

---

## Boundary Changes — Critical for Record Location

California had **27 counties at statehood in 1850**; county lines were redrawn frequently as population surged through the 1850s. This directly affects where records are held:

- A record created in a given county in 1852 may have been transferred to a successor county as boundaries shifted. **Always verify the formation date and boundary history of the specific county** before limiting a search.
- The principal Gold Rush mining counties were in the **Mother Lode / Sierra Nevada foothills**: El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne, and Mariposa. Records were generated at the **county** level.
- Before 1848, civil authority rested with **Mexican alcalde courts** and **Franciscan missions** — records from that era are in the California State Archives and individual mission archives, not county courthouses.

---

## Available Record Types

### 1. Census Records

**This is your starting point for Gold Rush research — and the order matters:**

| Census | Years | Coverage | Access Level | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **California State Census** | 1850–1852 | Statewide | **Indexed + images** (88% indexed; full-text searchable) — FamilySearch vol. 006601001, 522 images | ⭐ Search *before* the 1850 federal census — more complete for California |
| **1850 Federal Census** | 1850 | Statewide | Indexed + images via Ancestry.com | ⚠️ **Partially destroyed — some county returns are missing** and unrecoverable ([California Genealogy – Pre-Statehood Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records)) |
| **1860 Federal Census** | 1860 | Statewide | Indexed + images via Ancestry.com | Complete; essential for who stayed after the Rush |
| **Mortality Schedules** | 1850, 1860 | Statewide | Indexed via Ancestry.com | Record deaths in the year preceding each census — valuable given sparse death registers |

---

### 2. Vital Records (Civil Registration)

**California had no statewide civil registration until 1905.** County-level registration began at statehood in 1850 but was very inconsistent — transient miners who moved camp frequently and died far from settled communities often left **no county vital record at all.** ([California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

| Record Type | FamilySearch Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **County Births** | [2017276](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) — *California, County Births, 1850–1919* | 1850–1919 | 789,456 | **Indexed + images** |
| **County Marriages** | [1452832](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) — *California, County Marriages, 1850–1952* | 1850–1952 | 567,890 persons | **Indexed + images** |
| **County Deaths** | Not found in FamilySearch collections for this period | 1850+ | Unknown | Likely **physical only** at county courthouses |

**Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (see below); mortality schedules; newspaper death notices.

---

### 3. Mining Claim Registers ⭐ (Gold Rush-specific)

| Volume | Place | Dates | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch vol. **006601002** | San Francisco, CA | 1849–1855 | 340 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable; must be examined image by image |

- County recorders' offices hold mining claim records for their respective counties. Digitization and availability vary widely — assume **physical only** unless confirmed otherwise. ([California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

---

### 4. Immigration & Passenger Records

| Record Type | Dates | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ship passenger manifests (San Francisco)** | 1848–1865 | NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA; partial index on FamilySearch and Ancestry | Partially indexed; some browse-only |
| **Sacramento Port Arrival Registers** | 1849–1858 | FamilySearch vol. **006601003** — 298 images | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable |
| **Overland trail rosters** | 1848–1855 | California State Library; Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) — manuscript collections | **Physical only**; not centrally indexed |

Most forty-niners arriving by sea entered at **San Francisco**. Manifests record every person aboard — examine the full page for traveling families, including infants. ([California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

---

### 5. Voter Registration — Great Registers

- FamilySearch collection **[1923340](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)** — *California, Great Registers, 1866–1910* — **1,345,678 indexed records with images. Indexed + images.**
- ⚠️ Starts **1866**, outside the strict 1850s window — but essential for men who settled after the Rush. Each entry records **name, age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description**, making Great Registers one of the best tools for identifying geographic origins.

---

### 6. Land Records

| Source | Content | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from 1850 | Free online |
| **County deed books** | Post-patent land transfers | In-person at county recorders' offices |
| **Spanish/Mexican land grants (Ranchos)** | Pre-statehood land grants; relevant for Mexican-era families | California State Archives; NARA Pacific Region — physical |

California is a **federal land state** (rectangular survey). Miners who transitioned to farming after the Rush often appear in BLM patent records.

---

### 7. Probate & Court Records

- Probate files (wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship) are held at **county superior courts and county archives** from 1850.
- **Mining disputes** were extraordinarily common in the 1850s — court case files may document a miner's origins and connections even when no vital record survives.
- **Naturalization records (pre-1906)**: any court of record could naturalize — check federal district courts (NARA San Bruno), state courts, and county courts. No single index covers all pre-1906 California naturalizations.
- Federal court records at **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** — https://www.archives.gov/

---

### 8. Military Records

| Conflict | Record Types | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mexican-American War (1846–1848) | Service records, pension files | NARA; [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) | Online (subscription) |
| California Indian Wars (1850s) | State militia muster rolls | California State Archives | In-person |
| Civil War (1861–1865) | California Union volunteers; service, pension records | NARA; [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) | Online (subscription) |

---

### 9. Church Records

| Denomination | Record Types | Where Held | Language |
|---|---|---|---|
| Catholic (Mission era) | Baptisms, marriages, burials, 1769–1850 | FamilySearch collection **[1804372](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372)** — *California, Mission Records, 1769–1850* — 98,765 indexed records | Spanish/Latin |
| Catholic (Diocese of SF, Sacramento, from 1850s) | Parish registers | Archdiocesan archives; some FamilySearch microfilm | English/Spanish |
| Protestant (Methodist, Baptist, etc.) | Membership, baptism, marriage, burial | Individual denominational archives; Bancroft Library; California State Library | English |

---

### 10. Newspapers

| Resource | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu) — *Alta California*, *Sacramento Union*, and others | From 1846 | **Free online** |
| [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) | From 1840s | Subscription |
| California State Library microfilm | 1840s onward | In-person |

Newspapers published **ship arrival passenger lists, mining claim notices, probate legal notices, death announcements, and community news** — rich sources for tracking transient Gold Rush populations.

---

### 11. Cemetery Records

- [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) — free; covers many California burial sites
- ⚠️ Gold Rush-era graves are often unmarked, in remote mining camps, or in pioneer cemeteries not yet surveyed; physical sexton records (where they survive) are held by county parks or local historical societies.

---

### 12. Tax Records

- County property and personal property tax records from 1850; held at county assessors' offices and county archives.
- **No digitized California tax record collection appeared in FamilySearch results** for this period — treat as **physical only**.
- Annual tax lists provide year-by-year snapshots between census enumerations — valuable for tracking where a miner was each year.

---

### 13. City Directories & Biographical Compendiums

- San Francisco and Sacramento city directories from the early 1850s list residents and businesses; some are digitized on Google Books / HathiTrust.
- Illustrated history county atlases and biographical compendiums from the 1870s–1880s often include retrospective sketches of Gold Rush pioneers that name origins and earlier movements.
- **California State Library** and **Bancroft Library** hold the fullest runs.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | What's Available | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789K); County Marriages 1850–1952 (568K); Mission Records 1769–1850 (99K); 1852 State Census (88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (browse-only); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1.3M) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | 1850 & 1860 federal censuses; passenger lists; various California collections | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from 1850 | Free |
| California Digital Newspaper Collection (cdnc.ucr.edu) | California newspapers from 1846 | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers | Subscription |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** | Ship passenger manifests; federal court records (naturalizations); federal land records | In-person; some via NARA online catalog |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State government records; militia muster rolls; Spanish/Mexican land grant files; vital records (post-1905) | In-person; online catalog |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Manuscript collections; newspapers; city directories; overland trail journals | In-person; some digitized |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush manuscripts, diaries, journals; personal papers; biographical material; church records | In-person by appointment |
| County Superior Courts / Recorders | Deeds; probate files; court records; county vital records; mining claims | In-person; varies by county |
| Catholic Archdiocesan Archives (SF, Sacramento) | Parish registers of baptisms, marriages, burials | Contact diocese directly |

---

## Records NOT Online

- County **death records** for 1848–1865 — no FamilySearch digitized collection found; held at county courthouses
- County **tax records** (property and personal property) — physical only
- **Overland trail rosters** — no centralized database; manuscript collections at California State Library and Bancroft Library
- Most **county mining claim records** beyond the San Francisco register
- **State militia muster rolls** — California State Archives in-person
- Most early **Protestant church registers**
- Many **1850s city directories** — some on HathiTrust/Google Books; many require in-person visits

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1850 federal census partially destroyed**: several California county returns did not survive — substitute with the 1852 state census ([California Genealogy – Pre-Statehood Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records))
- Gold Rush mining camps were informal; **many miner deaths were never recorded anywhere**
- Various county courthouse losses from fires and floods occurred in the 19th century — check specific county histories before concluding a record type is missing

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search the 1852 California state census first** (FamilySearch vol. 006601001, 88% indexed) — it is more complete for California than the partially-destroyed 1850 federal census. ([California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))
2. **Mining Claim Registers and Sacramento Port Arrival Registers on FamilySearch are browse-only** (0% indexed) — budget time to examine them image by image, organized by the county or district where your ancestor mined.
3. **Great Registers (1866+) are the best comprehensive population list** for men who stayed — birthplace, occupation, and physical description recorded.
4. **Ship manifests are rich for sea arrivals** — California newspapers (*Alta California*) also published passenger lists by ship name; cross-reference NARA San Bruno manifests with newspaper arrivals. ([California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))
5. **County boundaries changed rapidly in the 1850s** — always verify county formation and boundary-change dates before limiting a search to one county.
6. **Mining disputes in county court files** can document a miner's origins and connections even when no vital record exists.
7. **BLM GLO patents** (free at glorecords.blm.gov) reveal when and where a miner acquired land — marks the transition from transient miner to settler.
8. **FamilySearch has 14 total digitized volumes** for California 1848–1865, but full pagination was not returned — search FamilySearch directly for the complete set.
9. **Consult the Bancroft Library**: it holds extraordinary Gold Rush-era manuscript collections — personal papers, diaries, and oral history transcripts — that name individuals and their origins. Essential for well-documented miners. ([California Genealogy – Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))
10. **For the 1848–1850 gap** (pre-statehood): the U.S. military administered California; very few civil records exist. Ship manifests and Mexican-era alcalde records (California State Archives) are the primary sources.

---

# 🗽 Locality Research Guide: New York City — Colonial Period, 1700s

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**New York City in the 1700s was essentially Manhattan (New York County)**, a thriving British colonial port under the Province of New York. The city's record-keeping history spans two colonial powers:

- **Dutch period (1626–1664):** Founded as *New Amsterdam*. Dutch Reformed Church kept the earliest vital registers.
- **British period (1664–1783):** Renamed New York; Anglican, Presbyterian, and other denominations added their record streams. The city served as the provincial capital throughout.
- **Post-Revolution (1783–1800):** New York State formed in 1788; briefly served as the first U.S. capital (1789–1790).

> **Critical boundary note:** In the 1700s, today's five NYC boroughs were *separate jurisdictions*. If your ancestors lived outside Manhattan, their records fall under different counties and record series:
> | Modern Borough | 1700s Jurisdiction |
> |---|---|
> | Manhattan | New York County |
> | Brooklyn | Kings County |
> | Queens | Queens County |
> | Staten Island | Richmond County |
> | The Bronx | Westchester County (partly) |
>
> The five boroughs did not consolidate into one City of New York until **1898**. Search the appropriate county for each area.

---

## Record Types, Availability & Access

### 🙏 Church Records — **PRIMARY SOURCE for vital events**
*There was no civil vital registration in New York City during the 1700s.* New York City did not begin local birth/death registration until 1853, and statewide registration did not begin until 1880. **Church registers are your only systematic source for baptisms, marriages, and burials in this period.**

| Denomination | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Dutch Reformed | Registers from 1639, continuous through the 1700s | **FamilySearch volume 007733180** (1700–1776, 211 images) — **browse-only, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable**; must be browsed image-by-image. **Written in Dutch** — requires Dutch-language reading ability. Also: Reformed Church in America Archives. |
| Anglican / Episcopal | Trinity Church (founded 1697) — extensive baptism, marriage, burial registers | Trinity Church Archives (NYC); partially on FamilySearch collection [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) |
| Presbyterian | Wall Street (First) Presbyterian, founded 1716 | Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia); some on FamilySearch |
| Lutheran | Evangelical Lutheran congregation | FamilySearch collection 1469062 |
| Jewish | Shearith Israel (oldest U.S. Jewish congregation, est. 1654) | American Jewish Historical Society |
| French Huguenot | Active community in NYC colonial period | Huguenot Society of America |

**FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Church Records, 1640–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) (2.3M records, 1.1M images) — **indexed + images**; search this first for non-Dutch Reformed congregations.

> ⚠️ The Dutch Reformed volume is **entirely browse-only and in Dutch**. Do not assume a failed keyword search means no record exists — you must page through the images manually, or seek a transcribed/translated edition.

---

### 📜 Probate Records — **STRONG coverage**
Wills and estate administrations are among the best-surviving colonial NYC record classes.

- **Colonial era:** Probates went through the **Prerogative Court of the Province of New York** (not the county court). These are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills on File in the Surrogate's Office, City of New York* — a multi-volume series published by the **New-York Historical Society**, covering 1665–1801. Check their library collection.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) (987K records, 493K images) — **indexed + images**.
- **Physical repository:** New York County Surrogate Court (Manhattan).

---

### 🌍 Land Records — **STRONG coverage**
Land transactions are another well-preserved colonial record class and often name family relationships.

- Colonial land **patents** were granted by the royal Provincial government (records at **New York State Archives**, Albany).
- Deed books (post-conveyance) are at the **New York County Clerk's office** and the State Archives.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Land Records, 1630–1975](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) (1.5M records, 783K images) — **indexed + images**.

---

### 🏛️ Colonial Government & Court Records
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** — the Province of New York's administrative records — are held at the **New York State Archives** (Albany). These include council minutes, court orders, and correspondence that frequently name residents.
- **Mayor's Court of New York City** — heard civil and minor criminal matters. Records survive and are held at the **New-York Historical Society** and the NYC Municipal Archives.
- **Court of Chancery** and **Supreme Court of Judicature** records are at the New York State Archives.
- The **wiki** notes these collections directly: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

### 💰 Tax Records
- **Colonial ward tax lists** survive for some years — lists of taxable property by ward. Held at the NYC Municipal Archives and New-York Historical Society.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) (123K records) — covers only the *very end* of the colonial century (1799 onward). Useful for the period's close but not for most of the 1700s.

---

### ⚔️ Military & Militia Records
- **Colonial militia rolls** list men of military age by ward — a useful population surrogate when other records are missing. Source: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)
- **French and Indian War (1754–1763):** Provincial muster rolls at the New York State Archives.
- **Revolutionary War:** Both **Patriot** (Continental/state forces) and **Loyalist** records exist. NARA holds federal pension files. Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) is the primary online access point.
- **British Loyalist claims:** If ancestors remained loyal to the Crown, British government compensation claims (held at The National Archives, Kew, UK) may survive.

---

### 🧾 Colonial Censuses & Population Lists
New York Province conducted several colonial enumerations — these predate the first federal census (1790) and are invaluable for the 1700s:

| Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1698 | Provincial census, survives |
| 1703, 1712, 1723 | Provincial censuses |
| 1731, 1737, 1746 | Provincial censuses |
| 1749, 1756 | Provincial censuses |

These are typically published/transcribed and available through the **New-York Historical Society** and the **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)**.

The first **federal census** is 1790 — useful to anchor families just after the colonial period.

---

### ⛵ Immigration & Passenger Records
New York was already a major entry port in the 1700s. Pre-federal passenger lists are sparse compared to later periods, but some survive:
- **Port of New York arrivals** — scattered lists; NARA holds what survives federally.
- **Dutch colonial passenger lists** (pre-1664 era) are published in genealogical compilations.
- No systematic passenger list series exists for 1700–1820; search published indexes and the **New-York Historical Society** manuscript collections.

---

### 📰 Newspapers
- **New York Gazette** (founded 1725) — the colony's first newspaper. Carried vital notices, runaway servant ads, estate notices, and ship arrivals.
- Available through [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) and the **New-York Historical Society**.

---

### ⚰️ Cemetery & Burial Records
- **Trinity Churchyard** (Manhattan) — one of the oldest surviving burial grounds, with interments from the 1680s onward.
- **Dutch Reformed burial grounds** — records partially in church registers.
- [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes many colonial NYC gravestones.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts, land patents, court records, militia rolls | In-person; some digitized |
| **New-York Historical Society** (NYC) | Abstracts of Wills, Mayor's Court records, colonial manuscripts, church records | In-person; some digitized online |
| **NY Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)** | Extensive NYC colonial genealogy collections, published indexes | Membership/subscription; [newyorkfamilyhistory.org](https://newyorkfamilyhistory.org) |
| **NYC Municipal Archives** | City administrative records, some colonial-era ward records | In-person; online finding aids |
| **Reformed Church in America Archives** (New Brunswick, NJ) | Dutch Reformed registers, classis records | In-person |
| **Trinity Church Archives** (NYC) | Anglican/Episcopal registers from 1697 | In-person; some published |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society** (Philadelphia) | Presbyterian records | In-person; some online |
| **FamilySearch** | Church (1469062), Land (2078654), Probate (1542780) collections | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Additional digitized NY collections | Subscription |
| **NARA** | Military pensions, federal records | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription; [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Church Records | ✅ Indexed + images (collection 1469062) | Dutch Reformed volume browse-only & in Dutch |
| Land Records | ✅ Indexed + images (collection 2078654) | |
| Probate Records | ✅ Indexed + images (collection 1542780) | Colonial wills also in published NY-HS Abstracts |
| Dutch Reformed Registers 1700–1776 | 🔍 Browse-only images only (vol. 007733180, 211 images, in Dutch) | Must page image-by-image; no keyword search |
| Tax Rolls | ✅ Indexed (collection 1678432) | **1799–1804 only** — post-period for most of the 1700s |
| Colonial Government Records | 📦 Physical (NY State Archives) | Limited digitization |
| Colonial Censuses | 📦 Physical / published transcriptions | NY-HS and NYG&B hold these |
| Military / Militia | 📦 Physical + Fold3 | NARA for federal; State Archives for provincial |
| Newspapers | 🌐 Newspapers.com, NY-HS | Partial coverage |
| Cemetery Records | 🌐 Find A Grave | Partial |

---

## Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **"New York City" in the 1700s = Manhattan only.** Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, and the Bronx were separate counties — search Kings, Queens, Richmond, and Westchester Counties respectively for families in those areas.
2. **No civil vital registration before 1853 (city) / 1880 (state).** Church records are the *only* systematic vital source for the entire 1700s. If your ancestor wasn't baptized in a church, there may be no birth record at all.
3. **Dutch Reformed registers are browse-only and in Dutch.** The FamilySearch volume (007733180, 1700–1776) is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — a failed search does not mean no record exists. Budget time for image-by-image browsing, or seek a published Dutch-language transcription.
4. **Colonial wills went through the Prerogative Court** (provincial level), not the county surrogate. The New-York Historical Society's published *Abstracts of Wills* series (1665–1801) is the primary finding aid.
5. **Dutch-heritage families may use patronymic surnames** (e.g., Pieter Jansen = Pieter, son of Jan) especially in early records — surnames were not fully fixed in NYC's Dutch community until the mid-1700s.
6. **Loyalist families** left NYC at the Revolution's end (1783); their records may continue in Canada (Nova Scotia, Ontario) or Britain. British Loyalist compensation claims survive at The National Archives, Kew.
7. **Colonial censuses** are published transcriptions, not indexed on FamilySearch — search through NYG&B and NY-HS finding aids.

---

**Starting point recommendation:** Begin with the FamilySearch church records collection ([1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)) and probate collection ([1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)), then contact the **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** for colonial-specialist guidance and access to their published indexes. For Dutch Reformed families, plan to browse volume 007733180 image-by-image on FamilySearch.

# Virginia Revolutionary War Locality Research Guide
## Place: Virginia, United States | Period: 1775–1783 | Focus: Military & Wartime Family Research

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and operated as a **colony through July 1776**, then as a state under the Virginia Declaration of Rights and Constitution. It contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony, and the war's decisive engagement — Yorktown — was fought on Virginia soil in 1781. (Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia)

**Critical administrative facts for this period:**
- All record-keeping was at the **county level** — no statewide vital registration existed during 1775–1783.
- Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded at the **Anglican/Episcopal parish level** until independence disrupted the established church; some parishes stopped keeping registers in the late 1770s–1780s.
- Virginia's **1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. County tax lists starting in **1782** are the primary household substitute.
- County boundaries shifted **frequently** in late 18th-century Virginia — new counties were carved from old ones throughout this period.
- Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to Revolution veterans, meaning records for some veterans extend beyond Virginia itself.

---

## 🪖 Military Records — Primary Sources

### 1. FamilySearch: Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783
**Collection ID:** 1945678
**Link:** https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678
**Reported records:** 345,678 | Images: 172,839
**Digitization level:** Indexed (surfaces in FamilySearch name search)

This is the most directly targeted collection on FamilySearch for this period and research focus. Search it first.

---

### 2. Continental Line Service Records & Muster Rolls
**Repository:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), **Record Group 93**
**Online access:** Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com/ (subscription)

Compiled Military Service Records (CMSRs) document individual service: enlistment dates, unit, rank, pay, and presence on muster rolls. Virginia units in the Continental Line are among the best-documented in the Revolution.
*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*

---

### 3. Virginia Militia Records
**Repository:** Library of Virginia, Richmond
**Online access:** Partial — some volumes digitized via FamilySearch and Fold3; many remain physical/microfilm only at the Library of Virginia.

Militia muster rolls, pay vouchers, and wartime documents separate from Continental service. Especially important for men who served locally rather than in the Continental Army.
*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*

---

### 4. Pension & Bounty-Land Warrant Application Files
**Repository:** NARA, **Record Group 15**
**Online access:** Fold3 — https://www.fold3.com/; Ancestry.com — https://www.ancestry.com/

**These are the richest genealogical sources for this period.** A pension application can include:
- The veteran's narrative of his service
- Birth date, birthplace, and marriage information
- Names of spouse and children
- Depositions from witnesses (neighbors, fellow soldiers)
- Marriage certificates sometimes transcribed into the file

Applications were filed in the veteran's **county of residence at time of application** (often 1818–1833 under the Pension Act of 1832), not necessarily a Virginia county — search NARA files even if your ancestor later moved to Kentucky, Tennessee, or Ohio.
*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*

---

### 5. Virginia State Navy Records (Published)
**Access:** Published transcriptions available at the Library of Virginia and major genealogical libraries.

Documents service in Virginia's own state navy, entirely separate from the Continental Navy. Published indexes make these accessible without a repository visit.
*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)*

---

### 6. Virginia Military District of Ohio — Bounty Land Records
**Repositories:** Library of Virginia (Richmond) **and** Ohio State Archives
**Access:** Physical/microfilm; some digitized

Veterans who received land grants in the Virginia Military District (a tract reserved in present-day Ohio) appear in Virginia's **warrant and survey records** even if they later settled in Ohio. Search **both** the Library of Virginia and Ohio State Archives for these records.
*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)*

---

## 📋 Census Substitutes (the 1790 census is gone)

### 7. Personal Property & Land Tax Lists, 1782–1850
**FamilySearch Collection ID:** 1456723
**Link:** https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723
**Reported records:** 456,789 | Images: 228,394
**Digitization level:** Indexed

Annual county tax lists beginning in **1782** are the primary substitute for the destroyed 1790 census. They list heads of household, taxable property (horses, cattle, enslaved persons), and sometimes additional family members. Tracking a family year-by-year through these lists can reveal:
- Residence continuity during wartime
- Sudden absences (military service, death, or relocation)
- Household composition changes (sons coming of age, widows listed)

*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)*

---

## ⛪ Church Records

### 8. Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929
**FamilySearch Collection ID:** 1598230
**Link:** https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230
**Reported records:** 1,234,567 | Images: 617,283
**Digitization level:** Indexed

Anglican/Episcopal **parish vestry books and registers** are the primary vital records source for this era. They document baptisms, marriages, and burials. After independence (1776) dissolved the church-state relationship, some parishes collapsed or stopped recording — this creates gaps in the late 1770s–1780s. Check:
- **Episcopal/Anglican registers** (dominant in Tidewater and Piedmont Virginia)
- **Presbyterian registers** (Shenandoah Valley, southwestern Virginia)
- **Baptist and Quaker records** (Piedmont and western counties; Quakers especially documented military exemptions)
- **Methodist records** (growing rapidly in this period, especially in rural areas)

Denominational archives hold originals; FamilySearch has microfilm/digital copies of many registers.

---

## 🏡 Land, Marriage & Will Records

### 9. Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900
**FamilySearch Collection ID:** 1734285
**Link:** https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285
**Reported records:** 2,567,890 | Images: 1,283,945
**Digitization level:** Indexed

All filed at the county level. Key record types within this collection for the Revolutionary period:
- **Marriage bonds and licenses** (county clerk — often the only marriage record when parish registers are missing)
- **Deeds** (property transfers; witness lists name neighbors and relatives)
- **Wills and estate inventories** (especially important for families who lost a soldier — identify widows, minor children, and heirs)
- **Land grants** from Virginia's western territories (document post-war settlement patterns)

---

## ⚖️ County Court Records

### 10. Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920
**FamilySearch Collection ID:** 2134567
**Link:** https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567
**Reported records:** 1,789,012 | Images: 894,506
**Digitization level:** Indexed

County court order books recorded civil and legal transactions that are invaluable for wartime family research:
- **Orphan court / guardian bonds** — appointed guardians for soldiers' minor children
- **Estate administrations** — document families who lost a soldier/father
- **Apprenticeships** — children of deceased soldiers sometimes apprenticed
- **Road and jury orders** — confirm a man was present (or absent) in a county in a specific year
- **Criminal cases** — desertion, treason, or Loyalist-related proceedings

---

## 📰 Newspapers & Published Sources

### 11. Virginia Newspapers (Wartime Issues)
**Online access:** Newspapers.com — https://www.newspapers.com/ (subscription)

The *Virginia Gazette* (Williamsburg, multiple competing editions during the war) published:
- Troop musters and call-ups
- Lists of deserters
- Death and casualty notices
- Loyalist property confiscation announcements
- Official proclamations naming individuals

Search by name for wartime mentions of your ancestors.

---

## 🏛️ Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia** (Richmond) | Militia records, land grants, county court records, tax lists | In-person; [lva.virginia.gov](https://www.lva.virginia.gov) for some digitized material |
| **NARA** (DC / College Park) | Continental CMSRs (RG 93), pension files (RG 15), bounty-land warrants | In-person; Fold3 online |
| **FamilySearch.org** | 5 indexed Virginia collections overlapping 1775–1783 (see above) | Free online |
| **Fold3.com** | Compiled Military Service Records, pension files, muster rolls | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | DAR lineage records, pension abstracts, census substitutes | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Virginia Gazette and other colonial/wartime papers | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records for veterans and family members | Free — https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| **NARA (UK/Loyalist)** | Loyalist claim files (Audit Office records) for Virginia Loyalists | The National Archives, Kew, England |

---

## ⚠️ Critical Research Quirks

1. **The 1790 census is gone.** Virginia's copy was destroyed in 1814. Use the 1782+ personal property tax lists (FamilySearch collection 1456723) as your household substitute — they're annual and nearly as informative.

2. **Parish records have a late-1770s gap.** Independence disrupted the Anglican church; some parishes stopped keeping registers between ~1776–1785. Always check **both** parish registers **and** county court marriage bonds as parallel vital-records sources.

3. **County boundaries shifted constantly.** A family in "Augusta County" in 1775 might be in "Rockingham County" by 1778 or "Pendleton County" by 1788. Verify the exact county at the date of the event before assuming a record is missing.

4. **Pension applications were filed late and elsewhere.** Veterans filed under the Pension Act of 1818 and especially the Act of 1832 — often 40–55 years after the war, and in the county of residence at that time, which could be Kentucky, Tennessee, Indiana, or Ohio. Always search NARA RG 15 regardless of where a veteran died.

5. **Bounty-land records span two archives.** Virginia's Military District of Ohio records are split between the Library of Virginia and Ohio State Archives — search both.

6. **Loyalist families left Virginia.** Those who fled may have records in Nova Scotia, Ontario, or British Audit Office loyalist claims files (held at The National Archives, Kew, England). NARA also holds some U.S.-side loyalist documentation.

7. **FamilySearch Wiki Virginia-specific pages** did not return Virginia-specific content during this survey (all four wiki-place-page sections returned a generic fallback guide). Consult the wiki directly for current guidance:
   - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia
   - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War

---

## Where to Start

For a Virginia ancestor with suspected Revolutionary War service, work this sequence:

1. **FamilySearch collection 1945678** (Virginia Military Records, 1775–1783) — name search first
2. **NARA RG 15 pension files** via Fold3 — even if your ancestor moved out of Virginia
3. **1782–1784 personal property tax lists** (collection 1456723) — establish county of residence
4. **County court order books** (collection 2134567) — look for orphan court, estate, or guardian entries if a soldier died
5. **Parish/church records** (collection 1598230) — baptisms, marriages, burials around the war years
6. **Marriage bonds and wills** (collection 1734285) — especially if you need to prove family relationships
7. **Virginia Gazette** on Newspapers.com — search the soldier's name for wartime notices
