# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (Early 1800s — c. 1800–1850)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **City founded** | 1718 by France |
| **Under Spanish rule** | 1763–1800 |
| **Louisiana Purchase** | 1803 — New Orleans passed to the United States |
| **Territory of Orleans** | 1804–1812 |
| **State of Louisiana admitted** | 1812 |
| **Administrative unit** | Orleans Parish (Louisiana uses *parishes*, not counties; civil law/Napoleonic Code applies) |
| **Administrative center** | New Orleans |
| **Economy** | River trade, cotton, sugar, port commerce — one of the busiest ports in North America |
| **Ethnic/racial composition** | French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, free people of color (*gens de couleur libres*), enslaved African Americans, Anglo-Americans (post-1803), Irish and German immigrants (1820s–1840s), Haitian refugees (post-1809) |
| **Dominant religion** | Roman Catholic, with small Protestant communities growing after 1803 |
| **Languages of records** | French (predominant through the 1820s), Spanish (colonial-era), English (growing from 1803 onward); many records are bilingual or trilingual |

> **Important legal context:** Louisiana is the only U.S. state operating under a civil law tradition derived from French and Spanish colonial codes (the Napoleonic Code). This means probate records are called *successions*, guardianship records are called *tutorships*, and the central legal instrument for nearly every transaction — property sales, wills, marriage contracts, manumissions, estate inventories — is the **notarial act**, not the deed or common-law will. Notarial records are the single most important record class for New Orleans research in this period.

---

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes during the period

| Period | Jurisdiction | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| pre-1803 | Colony of Louisiana (French/Spanish) | Records created under colonial authority; Spanish Cabildo governed 1769–1803 |
| 1804–1812 | Territory of Orleans | U.S. territorial government; records begin transitioning to English |
| 1812 onward | State of Louisiana, Orleans Parish | State government, parish civil law courts |

**Quirk:** Records created before 1803 are colonial records, not state records. Spanish and French colonial records are held at different repositories than post-1803 Louisiana state records — treat them as two separate research trails that connect at 1803.

---

## Disasters and record survival — the core research problem

### What happened
New Orleans was struck by a cascade of disasters in the late colonial and early American periods:

| Event | Year | What was lost |
|---|---|---|
| Good Friday Fire | 1788 | ~815 structures in the French Quarter burned; many colonial civil records destroyed |
| Second Great Fire | 1794 | ~212 structures burned; further record losses |
| Yellow fever epidemics | Recurring (1817, 1819, 1822, 1829, 1832, 1839, 1847–1848 were especially severe) | Death tolls in the tens of thousands; some burial and death records are fragmentary for epidemic years |
| Hurricanes and river floods | Periodic throughout 1800–1850 | Localized archival damage at various times |

*(Source: [New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*

### What survived and why
Despite the fires, **more survives than researchers expect**, for two structural reasons:

1. **The Catholic Church kept duplicate registers.** Sacramental registers were maintained at both the local parish level and at the diocesan level. When a parish copy burned, the diocesan copy often survived, and vice versa.
2. **The Spanish colonial notarial system required redundant copies.** Notarial acts were recorded in bound volumes (*protocoles*) that the notary held — and because notaries were required to deposit copies with the colonial government, many records exist in two places. This is why the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center today holds **over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734**, the largest such collection in the United States, despite the fires. *(Source: [New Orleans Genealogy — Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Birth registration:** Louisiana did **not** have comprehensive statewide civil birth registration in the early 1800s. No statewide birth registration system is documented for this period in the tool results. **Church sacramental registers (baptisms) are the primary substitute.**
- **Death registration:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964" (collection [1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892)) begins in 1819, suggesting some level of death registration existed in New Orleans from that date — likely city/parish records, not truly statewide. This collection is **index-only** (0 images returned by tools); the underlying registers must be consulted separately.
- **Marriage registration:** The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957" (collection [1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)) begins in 1837 — covering only the tail of the early 1800s. For marriages before 1837, **church registers and notarial marriage contracts** are the primary sources.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans) sacramental registers record baptisms, marriages, and burials **from 1731**, though with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires. Where the parish register was destroyed, the diocesan copy at the Archdiocese of New Orleans often survived. *(Source: [New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*

### Church records ⭐ *Primary substitute for missing civil vital records*
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral from 1718), with Protestant congregations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist) appearing from the 1820s–1830s after Anglo-American settlement grew.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — and also **confirmations** (a separate dated event, often years after baptism, naming the child at a later age). Catholic registers also recorded the free Black and enslaved populations, making them critical for African American research.
- **Where held:**
  - **FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — digitized and indexed; covers the full target period. This is your first-stop search.
  - **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** (1000 Howard Ave., New Orleans) — holds diocesan-level duplicate registers; critical when the parish copy was lost in a fire.
  - **Local parishes** — some still hold original registers.
- **Access level:** FamilySearch collection 1612905 — **Indexed + images** online (free).
- **Language:** French and Spanish through the 1820s; English increasingly from the 1830s. Researchers must be able to read Latin abbreviations in Catholic registers.

### Notarial records ⭐⭐ *The most distinctive and voluminous source for New Orleans*
- **What they are:** Under Louisiana civil law, a licensed notary recorded nearly every significant legal act: property sales, successions (wills and intestate estates), marriage contracts, acts of manumission (freeing enslaved persons), business partnerships, loans, and more. These are not equivalent to "notary public" stamps in common-law states — they are full legal records with detailed information about family relationships.
- **Survival:** The notarial system's redundancy helped much survive the 1788 and 1794 fires. The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (400 Royal St., New Orleans) holds **over 30 million pages of notarial acts from 1734 onward** — the largest such collection in the United States. *(Source: [New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*
- **FamilySearch volume:** One digitized volume is confirmed: **Image Group 004990115** — "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)," Orleans Parish, 1803–1820, 167 images, French and English.
  - **Access level: Browse-only images.** This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image, and researchers must read French and English handwriting. It is the surviving microfilm copy of records from that window.
- **Physical access:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (in person or by correspondence) holds the bulk of this collection. No comprehensive online digitization of the full archive has been confirmed by tools.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Federal enumerations for New Orleans/Orleans Parish exist from **1810** onward (1800 census did not include this territory at statehood). Key censuses in the target period: 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840.
- **1810 and 1820 censuses** are name-only (head of household) with tick-mark age/sex columns; they do not name everyone in the household.
- **Territorial/colonial censuses:** Spanish colonial censuses (*padrones*) were conducted periodically in the late 1700s and survive at the Louisiana State Archives and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain). These can fill the pre-1803 gap.
- **Access:** Federal censuses for Louisiana are indexed and imaged on both Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). Colonial *padrones* are physical or microfilm only at the Louisiana State Archives or Spanish archives.

### Probate records (successions, tutorships)
- **What they are:** In Louisiana civil law, probate is called a *succession*. Succession records are rich: they name heirs, list property (including enslaved persons), name creditors, and may reveal family structure across generations. Guardianship records are called *tutorships*.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — covers the full target period from pre-statehood through 1850. **Indexed + images** online (free).
- **Physical repository:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (New Orleans) holds original succession files; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) holds some transferred records.

### Land records
- **System:** Louisiana used a French/Spanish system of long-lot grants (*arpents* measured from a river or bayou), not the rectangular survey used in most of the US. Land grants, sales, and mortgages were recorded as **notarial acts** (see above) — not in separate deed books as in common-law states.
- **Federal land patents:** After 1803, the U.S. General Land Office issued patents for confirmed grants and new entries. These are searchable at the **BLM General Land Office Records** website (glorecords.blm.gov — free).
- **Where held:** Notarial Archives for private transactions; BLM GLO for federal patents; Louisiana State Land Office for state grants.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** War of 1812 (Battle of New Orleans, January 1815); various militia musters.
- **Record types:** War of 1812 service records and pension files at **NARA** (Ancestry/Fold3, subscription); Louisiana militia records may be at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Access:** NARA holdings are indexed and searchable on [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) and Ancestry. Pension files are particularly rich, containing biographical information.

### Immigration records
- **New Orleans was a major port of entry** — the second-busiest in the U.S. after New York for much of the early-to-mid 1800s. Thousands of Irish, German, and other European immigrants arrived through the Port of New Orleans.
- **Passenger lists:** Federal passenger list requirements began in 1820. Pre-1820 lists are spotty. NARA holds the original lists; Ancestry and FamilySearch have indexed them.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — federal, state, or local. In New Orleans, check the U.S. District Court records at NARA's Southeast Region (Atlanta) as well as Orleans Parish court records.

### Newspapers
- **New Orleans newspapers from the early 1800s** include *Le Moniteur de la Louisiane* (French, 1794–1814), *Louisiana Gazette* / *New Orleans Gazette* (English, 1804+), and *L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans* (French, 1827–1923). These published marriage notices, death notices, legal advertisements (estate sales, sheriff's sales, manumission notices), and immigration arrivals.
- **Where held:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription); Louisiana State University's Louisiana Digital Library; New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division.
- **Content value:** Obituaries and death notices may be the only record of a death in an epidemic year when burial registers are fragmentary.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), Lafayette Cemetery No. 1 (1833). New Orleans famously uses above-ground tombs due to the high water table.
- **Online:** [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage. Sacramental burial registers (see Church Records) are more comprehensive for the early 1800s.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's records at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives.

### Tax records
- **Orleans Parish tax assessment rolls** survive for parts of the period and can substitute for missing census years. Held at the Louisiana State Archives.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | What's available for New Orleans 1800–1850 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1718–1925 ([1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)); Probate Records 1756–1984 ([2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)); Statewide Death Index 1819–1964 ([1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892)); Parish Marriages 1837–1957 ([1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)); Notarial Acts browse volume 1803–1820 (image group 004990115) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. Federal Census collection; War of 1812 service records; passenger lists | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records (War of 1812, pension files) | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions (partial) | Free |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |
| **NARA Online** (archives.gov) | Some passenger lists, naturalization records | Free / subscription via partners |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** (400 Royal St., New Orleans) | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734; marriage contracts, successions, manumissions, property acts | In-person; some microfilm via interlibrary loan |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** (1000 Howard Ave.) | Diocesan duplicate sacramental registers; fills gaps left by parish copy losses | In-person or correspondence |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | Territorial records (1804–1812); colonial Spanish *padrones*; some transferred court records; tax rolls | In-person; some digitized |
| **NARA Southeast Region** (Morrow, GA) | Federal court records for Louisiana including naturalizations; census originals | In-person; some digitized |
| **Louisiana State Museum — The Cabildo** (New Orleans) | Spanish colonial Cabildo records and artifacts | In-person research by appointment |
| **New Orleans Public Library — Louisiana Division** | City directories (from 1805); early newspapers; local history collections | In-person; some digitized |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial records including Louisiana *padrones* and correspondence | In-person or via digital portal (PARES) |

---

## Known record losses

| Loss | Date | What was destroyed | Substitute |
|---|---|---|---|
| Good Friday Fire | 1788 | Most of the French Quarter; colonial civil records | Spanish-era notarial copies; diocesan church register duplicates |
| Second Great Fire | 1794 | Further French Quarter destruction | Same as above; many notarial acts survived in duplicate |
| Yellow fever epidemic years | Recurring | Burial registers may be fragmentary in worst epidemic years | Newspapers (death notices); notarial succession records filed shortly after death |
| Pre-1803 civil vital registration | — | No civil birth/death registration existed under colonial rule | Church sacramental registers at St. Louis Cathedral from 1731 |

**Key insight:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 destroyed a great deal, but the **notarial system's built-in redundancy** and the **Catholic Church's dual-register practice** mean that many records researchers assume are gone actually survive in duplicate form — just at a different repository than expected. Before concluding a record is lost, check both the Notarial Archives and the Archdiocesan Archives.

---

## Records NOT online (must be accessed in person or by correspondence)

- **The bulk of the New Orleans Notarial Archives** — only one microfilm browse-only volume (1803–1820, image group 004990115) has been confirmed digitized by tools; the 30-million-page main collection requires an in-person or correspondence visit to 400 Royal St., New Orleans.
- **Full St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** beyond what FamilySearch collection 1612905 covers — the Archdiocesan Archives holds additional material.
- **Spanish colonial *padrones*** and Cabildo records — Louisiana State Archives and the Cabildo; some accessible through the Archivo General de Indias (Seville).
- **Orleans Parish tax assessment rolls** — Louisiana State Archives.
- **City directories** (New Orleans directories exist from 1805) — New Orleans Public Library Louisiana Division; partially digitized.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with notarial acts, not vital records.** Because civil birth/death registration barely existed before the 1840s–1850s, and the 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed what colonial civil records existed, notarial acts are the backbone of New Orleans research. A succession (probate) record filed within weeks of a death names heirs, relationships, property, and often place of origin. Search FamilySearch collection 2078341 first, then contact the Notarial Archives Research Center for deeper digs. *(Source: [New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*

2. **Check both the parish and diocesan copy of every church register.** The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed parish-level records at St. Louis Cathedral — but diocesan-level duplicate registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives survived for many of those same years. Do not stop at "the parish register was lost" without also checking the diocesan copy. *(Source: [New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*

3. **Records are in French and Spanish — plan accordingly.** Through the 1820s, most church and notarial records are in French, with Spanish appearing in the colonial-era records. Catholic sacramental records use Latin abbreviations. Budget time for translation or use a specialist; do not rely on automated translation for legal documents.

4. **The notarial acts volume on FamilySearch (image group 004990115, 1803–1820) must be browsed image by image** — it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Read French handwriting is required. Use the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center's in-house finding aids to target specific notaries and date ranges before browsing.

5. **"Free people of color" (*gens de couleur libres*) had legal standing and appear extensively in notarial and church records.** New Orleans had the largest free Black population of any U.S. city in this period. Catholic registers recorded baptisms and marriages for this community from the colonial era onward. Manumission acts in the Notarial Archives are the primary source for tracing enslaved ancestors who were freed.

6. **For epidemic death years, turn to newspapers.** In severe yellow fever years (1822, 1832, 1847–1848 in particular), burial registers may be fragmentary or overwhelmed. New Orleans newspapers published death notices that can substitute. Check *L'Abeille*, the *Louisiana Gazette*, and successor papers. *(Newspapers.com, subscription; LSU Louisiana Digital Library)*

7. **Use Spanish colonial *padrones* (censuses) for the pre-1803 generation.** If your ancestor appears in New Orleans in 1800–1810, their parents likely appear in the Spanish colonial censuses of the 1770s–1790s, which survive at the Louisiana State Archives and the Archivo General de Indias (Seville). The PARES digital portal (pares.mcu.es) provides some online access to Spanish colonial Louisiana records.

8. **For Anglo-American migrants arriving post-1803, check both Louisiana records and the states they came from.** Many post-Louisiana Purchase arrivals came from the Carolinas, Virginia, Maryland, Kentucky, and Tennessee. Documents may have been created in both jurisdictions.

9. **The Louisiana civil law system means that** ***tutorships*** **(guardianship) and** ***interdictions*** **generated court records that have no common-law equivalent.** These can reveal minor children's relationships and ages when no birth record exists. Search FamilySearch collection 2078341. *(Source: [Louisiana Genealogy — Parish System and Civil Law Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))*

10. **New Orleans was a major immigration port — check passenger lists from 1820 onward.** Pre-1820 arrivals are poorly documented, but from 1820 federal law required ship captains to list passengers. Ancestry and FamilySearch index these. If an ancestor arrived in New Orleans and later naturalized, the naturalization petition may name their birthplace and prior residence.

---

Consulting those wiki pages directly is recommended for additional depth.

The central answer to your question: **most New Orleans record losses from the 1788 and 1794 fires are compensable** because the Spanish colonial notarial system and the Catholic Church's dual-register practice created built-in redundancy. The survival map is:

| If this was destroyed… | Look here instead |
|---|---|
| Colonial parish church registers | Archdiocesan Archives (diocesan duplicate copies) |
| Civil vital records (pre-registration) | St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (collection 1612905); notarial succession acts (collection 2078341) |
| Burial records in epidemic years | New Orleans newspapers (death notices); notarial succession files |
| Pre-1803 census/population lists | Spanish *padrones* at Louisiana State Archives or Archivo General de Indias |
| Marriage records before 1837 | Church registers (collection 1612905) + notarial marriage contracts at Notarial Archives |
| Any transaction, will, or property act | New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (400 Royal St.) — 30M+ pages from 1734 |

# Locality Research Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Immigrant Arrivals, 1840s

**Place:** Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States
**Period covered:** 1840s (collections surveyed: c. 1820–1870)
**Focus:** Port-of-entry records and post-arrival immigrant tracing

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Boston (a city since 1630) sits in **Suffolk County**. No boundary changes during the 1840s affect record jurisdiction. In the 1840s Boston was one of the five principal U.S. ports of entry, receiving a surge of Irish famine refugees after 1845; by 1850 over a quarter of the city's residents were Irish-born. Immigrants settled primarily in the North End and Fort Hill.

**Two vital-records series coexist from 1841 onward:** Massachusetts town clerks were ordered by the General Court to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639**; **statewide** registration was added in **1841**. Do not assume "Massachusetts didn't require registration until 1841" — the town series predates that by two centuries. From 1841, search both the town series and the state series.

---

## 1. Port of Boston Customs Passenger Lists ⭐ First priority

**What is recorded:** 1840s customs-era lists (pre-1891) capture name, age, sex, occupation, and **country of origin only** — not a specific county, village, or parish within Ireland or elsewhere. Originals are held at **NARA–Waltham** (National Archives at Boston, 380 Trapelo Rd., Waltham, MA) in **Record Group 36**.

**On FamilySearch:**
- Collection **"Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891"** (ID 1784312) — reported: 1,234,567 records, 617,283 images. Also indexed on **Ancestry.com**.
- `volume_search` identified **1 digitized image volume** covering specifically 1840–1850:
  - Image group **003345210** — 389 images
  - **Only 3% name-indexed** — standard name search will miss nearly all entries
  - **Full-text searchable** — use FamilySearch's fulltext search as the primary access method; browse image-by-image as fallback
  *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Immigration — Port of Boston," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)*

---

## 2. Naturalization Records (Pre-1906) ⭐ Critical for origin details

Before 1906, any court of record could naturalize an immigrant. The process had two steps, both genealogically valuable:

- **Declaration of Intention ("first papers")** — filed shortly after arrival; frequently records birthplace, age, and date of arrival — far more specific than the passenger list
- **Petition for Naturalization ("second papers")** — filed after five years of residence

**Courts to search for Boston immigrants:**
| Court | Records Held At |
|---|---|
| Suffolk County Superior Court | Massachusetts Archives, Boston |
| Boston Municipal Court | Massachusetts Archives, Boston |
| Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas | Massachusetts Archives, Boston |
| U.S. Circuit / District Courts for Massachusetts | NARA–Waltham |

**Online access:** FamilySearch collection **"Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906"** (ID 1459213) — reported: 345,678 records, 172,839 images. Also on Ancestry. **NEHGS** (americanancestors.org) published printed indexes to many early Boston naturalization records.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Naturalization and Citizenship — Pre-1906 / Boston," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Naturalization_and_Citizenship#Pre-1906)*

---

## 3. *The Boston Pilot* — "Missing Persons" Column ⭐ Unique Irish origin source

The **Boston Pilot**, an Irish Catholic newspaper (est. 1829), published notices placed by immigrants searching for lost family members. These run **1831–1921** and frequently name the **specific Irish county, barony, or townland of origin** — filling exactly the gap left by 1840s passenger lists. This is often the only source that supplies sub-country origin data for pre-1891 arrivals.

**Database:** Digitized and searchable at **NEHGS** (americanancestors.org — subscription). Search here whenever a passenger list shows only "Ireland" as the origin.
*(Source: Wikipedia, "Boston," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)*

---

## 4. Church Records — Catholic and Protestant

Catholic parish registers are the primary source for Irish immigrant vital events (baptisms, marriages, burials). Key 1840s Boston parishes include **Cathedral of the Holy Cross** and **St. Patrick's**. The **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds these registers; many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.

**FamilySearch collection:** **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (ID 1921657) — reported: 987,654 records, 493,827 images. Covers Catholic and Protestant denominations. Partially name-indexed; browse-only portions exist for some parishes.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Massachusetts Church Records — Boston Area Churches," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)*

---

## 5. Town Vital Records and Statewide Registration

**FamilySearch collection:** **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (ID 2061550) — reported: 3,456,789 records, 1,728,394 images. Name-indexed and searchable. For immigrants arriving in the 1840s, vital records in this series will capture post-arrival events (births of children born in Boston, marriages, deaths) rather than the arrival itself.

---

## 6. Federal Census Records

- **1840 census** (taken June 1840): Names only the head of household; other members appear as age/sex tallies only — limited value for individual immigrants.
- **1850 census** ⭐: First federal census to name all household members. Records name, age, sex, **country of birth**, occupation, real estate value, and school attendance. The first reliable census snapshot for individual immigrant family members.
- **1860 census**: Same detail as 1850; also captures value of personal estate.
- **Mortality schedules (1850, 1860)**: List individuals who died in the year preceding the census enumeration — a useful source for early deaths after arrival.

All available on **Ancestry.com**, **FamilySearch**, and **MyHeritage**.

---

## 7. Massachusetts Alien Passenger Records (State Level)

Massachusetts law in the 1840s required tracking of arriving immigrants and provision of relief to destitute arrivals. The **Boston Commissioners of Alien Passengers** (later the Board of State Charities) maintained records of pauper and destitute immigrants. These are held at the **Massachusetts Archives**, Boston. This series is **physical only** — not known to be digitized or indexed online.

---

## 8. Probate Records

**FamilySearch collection:** **"Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (ID 1678901) — reported: 567,890 records, 283,945 images. Suffolk County probate originals are at the **Suffolk County Probate Court**, Boston. Useful for tracing property and family relationships after settlement.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **NARA–Waltham** (380 Trapelo Rd., Waltham, MA) | Customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal court naturalization records |
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Statewide vital records from 1841; Suffolk County court naturalization records; alien passenger records |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers (by appointment; partially on FamilySearch) |
| **NEHGS / americanancestors.org** | *Pilot* Missing Persons database; naturalization indexes; published vital record transcriptions |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Collections 1784312 (passenger lists), 1459213 (naturalizations), 1921657 (church records), 2061550 (town vitals), 1678901 (probate) — all free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists, census, naturalization records (subscription) |
| **Newspapers.com / GenealogyBank** | *Boston Pilot* and other period newspapers (subscription) |
| **archives.gov (NARA)** | Federal records finding aids and some online digitized collections |

---

## Digitization Level at a Glance

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status | Key Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850 (vol. 003345210) | **Full-text searchable; 3% name-indexed** | Must use fulltext search or browse all 389 images — standard name search misses nearly all entries |
| Massachusetts Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (coll. 1784312) | **Indexed + images** | Also on Ancestry |
| Massachusetts Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (coll. 1459213) | **Indexed + images** | Search all three court levels; originals at Mass. Archives & NARA-Waltham |
| Massachusetts Church Records, 1630–1920 (coll. 1921657) | **Indexed + images (partial)** | Browse-only portions exist; originals at Archdiocese of Boston |
| Massachusetts Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (coll. 2061550) | **Indexed + images** | Town series (from 1639) and state series (from 1841) both searchable |
| Massachusetts Probate Records, 1635–1991 (coll. 1678901) | **Indexed + images** | Suffolk County Probate Court holds originals |
| *Pilot* Missing Persons database | **Indexed** (NEHGS, subscription) | Only source with Irish parish/townland specificity for many 1840s arrivals |
| State alien/pauper registers | **Physical only** (Massachusetts Archives) | Not known to be digitized |

---

## Key Quirks for 1840s Boston Immigration Research

1. **1840s passenger lists record country of origin, not hometown.** "Ireland" is all you get. The naturalization declaration of intention and the *Pilot* Missing Persons database are the two places to look for anything more specific.

2. **Volume 003345210 (Port of Boston, 1840–1850) is only 3% name-indexed.** Standard FamilySearch name search will miss the overwhelming majority of entries. Use fulltext search first; browse all 389 images if that fails.

3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across multiple court levels.** Suffolk Superior Court, Boston Municipal Court, and federal courts all had jurisdiction. Search all three series — an immigrant might have filed at whichever court was convenient.

4. **The declaration of intention ("first papers") is usually more genealogically useful than the final certificate.** It records birthplace, age, and arrival date. File it even if the final naturalization is what you ultimately want.

5. **Massachusetts has two vital-records series running simultaneously from 1841.** The town series (required since 1639) and the statewide series (begun 1841) both exist for the 1840s. Search both.

6. **The 1840 federal census names only the household head.** For immigrants arriving before June 1840, the 1840 census gives you only the head of household by name. Wait for the 1850 census (first to name all members) for individual family members.

7. **The *Pilot* "Missing Persons" column is the bridge to Irish origins.** Running 1831–1921, it is searchable at NEHGS and routinely provides county or parish of origin in Ireland — information entirely absent from customs passenger lists before 1891.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

For a typical 1840s Boston immigrant:

1. **Passenger lists** (FamilySearch coll. 1784312 / vol. 003345210 via fulltext search / Ancestry) — establish the arrival
2. **Naturalization declaration of intention** (FamilySearch coll. 1459213 / NARA-Waltham / Mass. Archives) — extract birthplace and arrival date
3. ***Pilot* Missing Persons database** (NEHGS) — identify Irish county, barony, or townland
4. **1850 federal census** (Ancestry / FamilySearch) — household snapshot after settlement
5. **Catholic parish registers** (FamilySearch coll. 1921657 / Archdiocese of Boston) — post-arrival vital events
6. **Town vital records** (FamilySearch coll. 2061550) — corroborate civil registrations from 1841 onward

## 🗺️ Locality Research Guide
### Native American Families in Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) — Mid-1800s (c. 1830–1880)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Oklahoma during the mid-1800s was **Indian Territory** — not yet a U.S. state. The region was formally designated as Indian Territory under the **Indian Removal Act of 1830**, and the Five Civilized Tribes — **Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole** — were forcibly relocated there primarily in the 1830s–1840s (Trail of Tears). The territory was administered federally through the **Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)**, with each tribe maintaining its own sovereign government, laws, courts, and records.

A critical jurisdictional split applies to your research:
- **Indian Territory** (the eastern Five Nations' lands) and **Oklahoma Territory** (organized 1890 for the western portion) were legally distinct jurisdictions right up to joint statehood in **1907**. Pre-1907 records will be filed under one or the other — not under any county system.
- The Five Nations held their own tribal courts, citizenship rolls, and land records. There was **no county-based civil registration** during this period; tribal rolls are the primary substitute for vital records.

Wikipedia source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma

---

### Record Classes, Coverage & Access

#### 1. 🏛️ Tribal Rolls — **PRIORITY SOURCE**

Tribal enrollment records are the backbone of Native American genealogy for this period. They substitute for birth, marriage, and death records.

| Roll | Date | Tribe | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Various removal-era rolls | 1830s–1840s | All Five Tribes | Compiled during and just after Trail of Tears relocation |
| **Old Settler Cherokee Roll** | **1851** | Cherokee | Lists those who arrived in Indian Territory before 1839 |
| **Drennen Roll** | **1852** | Cherokee | Documents Cherokees relocated from the Southeast |
| Dawes Rolls | 1898–1914 | All Five Tribes | Post-period but contain birth years reaching into the mid-1800s; essential for identity confirmation |

**FamilySearch collection:** [Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) — 567,890 records, 283,945 images. **Indexed + images** (high access).

**Digitized volume:** Image Group `002298871` — *Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870*, 940 images, **99% name-indexed**, **full-text searchable**. Reachable via FamilySearch record search and full-text search. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))

**Physical repositories:**
- **National Archives — Fort Worth, TX** (primary): Dawes Rolls, enrollment jackets, allotment records
- **National Archives — Washington, D.C.**: Original BIA records, earlier removal-era rolls
- **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS), Oklahoma City**: Tribal records on microfilm, some digitized

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Dawes Rolls categorized citizens into separate schedules — *Citizens by Blood*, *Citizens by Intermarriage* (non-Native spouses), *Delaware Freedmen/Cherokee Freedmen*, and *Doubtful* cases. Each schedule must be searched separately; they are not combined in a single index.

---

#### 2. 📜 Treaties

Federal treaties with the Five Civilized Tribes are primary records for establishing who belonged to a tribe at a given time. Key mid-1800s treaties include the **1835 Treaty of New Echota** (Cherokee removal), **1855 treaties** (Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw), and **1866 Reconstruction Treaties** (which also addressed Freedmen citizenship).

**Where held:**
- **National Archives (Washington, D.C.)**: Original treaty documents
- **Library of Congress**: Digitized treaty texts online at https://www.loc.gov
- **Oklahoma Historical Society**: Treaty copies and related records
- [**NARA**](https://www.archives.gov) — Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs) holds the bulk of federal-tribal administrative correspondence tied to treaties

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** Annuity payment rolls (lists of tribal members who received payments under treaty provisions) are held within **NARA Record Group 75** and often name individuals not found on other rolls. These are the closest mid-1800s equivalent to a census for many families.

---

#### 3. 🏢 Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records

The BIA operated agencies within Indian Territory (e.g., Cherokee Agency, Choctaw Agency, Creek Agency). Agency records include:
- **Annuity payment rolls** (periodic, listing heads of household and family members)
- **Correspondence and letters** (naming individuals in disputes, land matters, citizenship claims)
- **School/education records** (boarding schools, mission schools)
- **Census and population counts**

**Repository:** NARA Record Group 75, held in part at Fort Worth and in part at Washington, D.C. Some records are on microfilm at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.

**Online access:** [NARA — archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov); [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com) has a growing Native American records collection.

---

#### 4. ✝️ Missionary and Church Records

Christian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward — **Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian** denominations kept registers of converts, baptisms, marriages, burials, and school enrollment.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) — 123,456 records, 61,728 images. **Indexed + images**.

([FamilySearch Wiki — Missionary Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records))

**Other access points:**
- **Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia)**: Manuscript mission records
- **American Baptist Historical Society**: Cherokee and other mission registers
- **OHS microfilm collection**: Various denomination records

---

#### 5. 🌍 Land Records

The Five Nations held lands communally under treaty rights — there was no individual land ownership by tribal members until allotment under the Dawes Act (1887–1898). Despite this, **pre-allotment improvements records**, **leases**, and **permits** granted to non-Indians document occupancy and family ties.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. **Indexed + images**.

Post-allotment: The **Dawes allotment packets** (at NARA Fort Worth) contain survey maps, deeds, and family statements that trace families into the late 1800s.

---

#### 6. 📋 Tribal Government Records (Internal)

Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintained its own government records:
- **Cherokee Nation**: Council acts, citizenship court records, district court records — held at the **Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah, OK)** and on microfilm at OHS
- **Choctaw/Chickasaw**: Council records, citizenship cases — held at tribal headquarters and OHS
- **Creek (Muscogee)**: Town records, council minutes — held at the **Muscogee (Creek) Nation Archives**
- **Seminole**: Records are sparser for this period; OHS holds what survives

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** The Five Nations each operated district courts with their own jurisdictions. Do not assume a single tribal archive — each nation's records are housed separately. Contact the tribal historic preservation officer (THPO) for access to non-digitized holdings.

---

#### 7. 🪖 Military Records

Many tribal members served in Civil War units organized along tribal lines (e.g., Cherokee Regiment, Choctaw Battalion). These records survive at:
- **NARA** (Compiled Military Service Records, pension files)
- [**Fold3**](https://www.fold3.com) — indexed Civil War pension and service records

The 1866 Reconstruction Treaties also generated post-war enrollment and loyalty oath records in NARA RG 75.

---

#### 8. 📰 Newspapers and Local Publications

Tribal newspapers are an underused source:
- **Cherokee Phoenix / Cherokee Advocate** (published 1828–1906, with gaps): Named individuals in notices, deaths, and civic affairs — held at OHS and the **University of Tulsa Special Collections**
- [**Newspapers.com**](https://www.newspapers.com) and [**ChroniclingAmerica (LOC)**](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) have partial digitized runs

---

#### 9. ⚰️ Cemetery and Burial Records

Many burials in Indian Territory were in **mission cemeteries** or tribal burial grounds, often poorly documented for the mid-1800s. Later memorialization efforts produced:
- [**Find A Grave**](https://www.findagrave.com): Partial coverage of Oklahoma/Indian Territory cemeteries
- **OHS cemetery surveys** (physical, some microfilmed)

---

### Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA Fort Worth** | Dawes Rolls, allotment records, Five Nations tribal records | In-person; many microfilmed/digitized |
| **NARA Washington D.C.** | RG 75 BIA records, treaties, early agency records | In-person; NARA catalog online |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Tribal records, newspapers, cemetery surveys, microfilm | In-person + online catalog |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indian Censuses & Rolls, Land Records, Mission Records collections | Free online |
| **Cherokee Nation Archives (Tahlequah)** | Internal tribal government records | Contact THPO |
| **Five Civilized Tribes Museum** | Artifact and document collections | In-person |
| **Univ. of Oklahoma Western History Collections** | Manuscript collections, agency records | In-person |
| **Fold3** | Military records, some BIA/Indian records | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls index, federal censuses | Subscription |

---

### Key Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **No county system in Indian Territory** — do not search by county before 1907. Search by tribe and agency instead.
2. **Identify the correct tribe first** — each nation's records are in separate archives. Knowing whether your ancestor was Cherokee vs. Choctaw determines the entire research path.
3. **Dawes Rolls categories must each be searched separately**: Citizens by Blood, Citizens by Intermarriage, Freedmen, and Doubtful — a name absent from one may appear in another.
4. **Annuity payment rolls in NARA RG 75** are often the closest mid-1800s equivalent to a census; don't overlook them.
5. **Freedmen (formerly enslaved by tribal members)** were enrolled on separate Dawes Roll schedules; they also appear in earlier BIA records and some missionary registers. Their genealogy overlaps both African American and Native American research strategies.
6. **Non-Native intermarried whites** required tribal permits and were enrolled separately — check for ancestors who may have married into a tribe.
7. **Oklahoma Territory (organized 1890) ≠ Indian Territory** — if your ancestor lived in the western portion, records shift to Oklahoma Territorial courts and NARA Kansas City rather than the Five Nations' records.
8. **Pre-removal records** for families originating in the Southeast (Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee) are equally important — start with those states' records to establish the family before relocation, then follow them into Indian Territory.

---

### Recommended Starting Points

1. **Determine tribal affiliation** (or likely affiliation) before doing anything else — use family tradition, oral history, or pre-removal state records.
2. Search [FamilySearch — Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) and Image Group `002298871` (Tribal Enrollment Cards, 1840–1870).
3. Pull the **Dawes Roll jacket** at NARA Fort Worth for any ancestor enrolled — the jacket often contains a family group sheet, birth affidavit, and correspondence naming parents and siblings.
4. Search NARA RG 75 at Fort Worth and D.C. for the relevant agency's **annuity rolls** for each decade.
5. Check [FamilySearch — Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) for baptisms and marriages in the target period.
6. Consult the tribal archive or THPO for non-digitized internal tribal government records.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania — Quaker (Society of Friends) Records (ca. 1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Colony/State formed:** Pennsylvania was granted to William Penn in 1681 and established as a haven for Quakers. It became the second state to ratify the U.S. Constitution in December 1787.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial and early national capital)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown (colonial); United States (post-1776)
- **Population during period:** No census data was returned by the population tool for this period. The first federal census (1790) counted Pennsylvania's population; pre-1790 tax records are the primary enumeration substitute.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, trade, milling, iron forging; Philadelphia was the largest city in colonial North America and a major Atlantic port.
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** English Quakers dominant in southeastern counties (Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, Delaware); German Lutherans and Reformed; Scotch-Irish Presbyterians in central and western areas; Welsh Quaker communities in Montgomery/Chester counties; Mennonites and Amish in Lancaster County.
- **Key historical events:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) — Quaker pacifism led to many disownments for military service; Wyoming Valley conflict (1778); rapid county formation across the state throughout the 1780s–1790s.

---

## Boundary Changes

The late 1700s saw intense county formation from the three original counties of 1682 (Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester). Quaker records follow the **monthly meeting**, not civil boundaries, but identifying which civil county applies matters for land, probate, and court records:

| County | Formed | From |
|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester | 1682 | Original proprietorship |
| Lancaster | 1729 | Chester |
| York | 1749 | Lancaster |
| Cumberland | 1750 | Lancaster |
| Berks | 1752 | Philadelphia, Chester, Lancaster |
| Northampton | 1752 | Bucks |
| Bedford | 1771 | Cumberland |
| Northumberland | 1772 | Lancaster, Cumberland, Berks, Bedford, Northampton |
| Westmoreland | 1773 | Bedford |
| Washington | 1781 | Westmoreland |
| Fayette | 1783 | Westmoreland |
| Franklin | 1784 | Cumberland |
| Montgomery | 1784 | Philadelphia |
| Dauphin | 1785 | Lancaster |
| Delaware | 1789 | Chester |
| Allegheny | 1788 | Washington, Westmoreland |

> **Quirk:** If an ancestor's record is not found under a county, search the **parent county** — it held all records before the daughter county was formed. Quaker meeting jurisdictions and civil county boundaries did not align; a family in Chester County might attend a Bucks County quarterly meeting.

---

## Available Record Types

### 🔵 Church / Meeting Records — **Primary source for this period**

Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906** ([Pennsylvania Vital Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)). For Quaker families in the late 1700s, **meeting records are the closest equivalent to civil registration**.

**Quaker meeting record types** ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)):

| Record Type | Content | Research Value |
|---|---|---|
| **Birth registers** | Name, date, parents' names | Equivalent to birth certificate |
| **Marriage records** | Date, names of both parties, witnesses (often 50–100 signatures) | Exceptionally detailed; witness lists identify community |
| **Death/burial records** | Name, date, sometimes age or cause | Equivalent to death certificate |
| **Certificates of removal** | Issued when a Friend transferred to a new meeting; names origin and destination meeting | Crucial for tracing migration between meetings and states |
| **Disownment proceedings** | Minutes recording why a member was disowned (military service, marrying outside the meeting, etc.) | Confirms identity; may cite parents, children, dates |
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Governance, membership, disciplinary proceedings | Background on the family's standing in community |
| **Quarterly and Yearly Meeting minutes** | Regional and statewide Quaker business | Certificates of removal passed through these levels |

**Meeting hierarchy** (records are created at every level):
- **Monthly meeting** → **Quarterly meeting** → **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** (PYM)
- The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (founded 1681) governed all Friends in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, and Maryland. Its minutes are the apex record set.

**Densest Quaker concentrations in Pennsylvania** ([Wikipedia — Quakers in Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania)):
- **Philadelphia County** — Arch Street, Race Street, Pine Street, and other city meetings
- **Chester County** — one of the earliest Quaker settlements; many colonial meetings
- **Bucks County** — Quaker stronghold from the 1680s
- **Delaware County** — split from Chester in 1789; Quaker meetings predated the county
- **Montgomery County** — Welsh Tract and other Welsh Quaker settlements

**Digitized on FamilySearch (volume search result):**
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** — 145 images (imageGroupNumber: 001188322)
  - ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be read image by image.

**Published abstracts — key finding aid:**
- **William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) — abstracts births, marriages, deaths, disownments, and removals from Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, North Carolina, Indiana, Ohio, and Virginia meetings ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)). This is the first place to look for any Pennsylvania Quaker family. Volume 2 covers Pennsylvania.

**Access:**
- **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) — largest collection of American Quaker records in the world; holds original monthly meeting registers, minutes, and removal certificates for most Pennsylvania meetings. Many records also microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Quaker & Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA) — second major repository; strong holdings for southeastern PA meetings.
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives** (Philadelphia, PA) — original PYM minutes and affiliated collections.

---

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration did not begin until **1906** for births and deaths; **no civil birth or death records exist** for the 1750–1800 period.
- **Marriage records:** Marriage licenses and bonds were kept at the **county level** from the colonial period. FamilySearch collections include:
  - *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* (collection 1571957) — 312,045 records — **indexed + images**
  - *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* (collection 1502909) — 198,765 records — **indexed; no images** (index only)
- **Critical note for Quakers:** Quakers did not obtain civil marriage licenses because they married under the care of the meeting. Do **not** expect to find Quaker marriages in civil marriage registers; the meeting record is the marriage record.

---

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** First enumeration in **1790** — heads of household only, with counts of free white males, females, and enslaved persons by age group. **No earlier federal census exists.**
- **Colonial/provincial enumerations:** No comprehensive colonial census survives for Pennsylvania.
- **Tax lists as census substitutes (pre-1790):**
  - County tax assessment lists (tax duplicates) survive from the **1690s** in some counties and are the primary enumeration substitute before 1790 ([Pennsylvania Land Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records)). They name male taxable inhabitants annually or triennially.
  - The 1693 Chester County tax list is one of the earliest surviving colonial tax records.
  - Many counties have nearly continuous tax series from the 1750s onward — essential for locating a family across years without census records.

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Types:** Wills, intestate administrations, inventories, guardianships, estate distributions
- **Where held:** County **Register of Wills** from county formation; earlier records trace back to Philadelphia, Bucks, or Chester County.
- **FamilySearch:** *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection 1999196) — 893,214 records — **indexed + images** — covers the full late 1700s.
- **Research value for Quaker families:** Probate inventories name children, sons-in-law, and creditors; wills often identify religious community connections. Quakers frequently mentioned meeting affiliation or left bequests to the meeting.

---

### Land Records

- **System:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state, not a federal public domain state)
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents (state Land Office); deeds (county recorder of deeds)
- **Date range:** Land Office records begin **1681** with William Penn's original grants.
- **Where held:**
  - **Pennsylvania State Archives / Land Office** (Harrisburg) — warrant books, survey books, patent books from 1681 onward
  - **County recorder of deeds** — deed books from county formation
- **Research value:** Quaker land transactions often clustered within the community; grantor/grantee deed indexes can link neighbors who were fellow meeting members.

---

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflict:** Revolutionary War, 1775–1783
- **Important Quaker caveat:** The Society of Friends held a **peace testimony**; many Pennsylvania Quakers refused military service. The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting formally disowned members who bore arms, paid militia fines in lieu of service, or accepted substitutes. Disownment records are therefore a significant military-related source for Quaker families — they confirm the family was still affiliated with the meeting at that time.
- **Military records that do exist:** Some Quakers served despite the peace testimony and left muster rolls, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA (Fold3 and Ancestry both index Revolutionary War pension files).
- **Oath of allegiance records** (1777–1778): Pennsylvania required loyalty oaths; refusals by Quakers are documented in court records and meeting minutes.

---

### Tax Records

- **Types:** County assessment lists, tax duplicates, provincial taxes
- **Date range:** From **1690s** in Chester County; most counties have surviving tax lists by the 1750s–1760s.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; many microfilmed and some digitized. County historical societies hold originals or transcripts.
- **Substitute value:** The single most important census substitute for the pre-1790 period. Annual or triennial lists name adult male taxable inhabitants with property values.

---

### Cemetery Records

- **Quaker burial grounds:** Most Quaker meetings maintained their own burial grounds, often adjacent to the meetinghouse. Markers were traditionally plain (or absent entirely in the 18th century).
- **Burial registers:** Monthly meetings kept burial records; these overlap with death registers.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have some Quaker burial ground entries, but coverage is uneven for 18th-century plain-marked graves.
- **Physical records:** Many Quaker meetinghouse burial registers survive at Friends Historical Library or local monthly meetings.

---

### Newspapers

- **Pennsylvania Gazette** (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) — the leading colonial-era paper; marriage notices, death notices, legal notices, runaway advertisements. Digitized on **Accessible Archives** (subscription) and partially on **Newspapers.com**.
- **Other Philadelphia papers:** Pennsylvania Journal, Pennsylvania Packet, Freeman's Journal — late 1700s; available on Readex Early American Newspapers (subscription, often accessible via university libraries).
- **Research value:** Quaker communities sometimes published marriage and death notices; legal notices (land sales, estate settlements) also appear.

---

### Immigration/Emigration Records

- **Relevant for:** Most Pennsylvania Quakers in the late 1700s were second or third generation; but for those immigrating from England, Wales, or Ireland, passenger records and removal certificates are both relevant.
- **Port of entry:** Philadelphia was the primary entry port.
- **Passenger lists:** Colonial-era lists are incomplete but some survive; Pennsylvania Archives (Series 2, Vol. 17) publishes lists of immigrants to Philadelphia.
- **Removal certificates:** When an English or Irish Friend emigrated to Pennsylvania, the sending meeting issued a **certificate of removal** addressed to the receiving Pennsylvania meeting — this is often the best documentation of immigrant origins.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Relevant Pennsylvania collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (col. 1999196); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (col. 1571957); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (col. 1502909); Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (browse-only, vol. 001188322) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | U.S. Federal Census (1790+); Pennsylvania tax lists; Revolutionary War records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Pennsylvania Gazette and other colonial-era papers | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Revolutionary War pensions, Continental Army records | Free (some) |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery records, burial transcriptions | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) | Original monthly meeting registers, minutes, removal certificates for most PA Quaker meetings; Hinshaw abstracts; PYM records | In-person; some materials on appointment; catalog at swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library |
| **Haverford College Quaker & Special Collections** (Haverford, PA) | Meeting records, Quaker history, southeastern PA meetings | In-person; catalog at haverford.edu/library/special |
| **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Archives** (Philadelphia, PA) | PYM minutes and affiliated records | Contact PYM directly at pym.org |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg, PA) | Land Office records, tax assessment lists, colonial court records, militia records | In-person and online request; phmc.pa.gov |
| **County Register of Wills** | Probate records from county formation dates | In-person / mail |
| **County Recorder of Deeds** | Deed books from county formation | In-person; some digitized on county websites |
| **Local historical societies** (Chester County, Bucks County, Philadelphia) | Transcribed tax lists, early records, published genealogies | In-person; some online finding aids |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following exist but are **not fully available in any online database**:
- Most **monthly meeting birth, marriage, and death registers** — FamilySearch has microfilmed many, but they are browse-only on film or in physical repositories; few are name-indexed online.
- **Certificates of removal** — almost entirely in physical repositories at Friends Historical Library and Haverford.
- **Quarterly meeting minutes** — largely physical.
- **County tax assessment lists** pre-1780 — many are on microfilm at the Pennsylvania State Archives but not digitized for name searching.
- **County deed books** for newly formed counties — available at the county courthouse and partially on microfilm; digitization is uneven.

---

## Known Record Losses

- No catastrophic statewide record losses are known for Pennsylvania civil records from this period.
- **Individual courthouse fires** affected some counties; check specific county histories before assuming a record doesn't exist.
- **Quaker records**: The Society of Friends was generally meticulous; most colonial-era Pennsylvania monthly meeting registers survive. However, some smaller or short-lived meetings may have gaps.
- **Revolutionary War disruption**: Some Philadelphia records were disrupted during the British occupation (1777–1778). Quaker meeting business continued during the occupation; meeting minutes note the period.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Hinshaw.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, Vol. 2 (Pennsylvania), is the single most efficient first step. If your ancestor appears in any Pennsylvania Quaker meeting between roughly 1680 and 1900, Hinshaw likely has an abstract. It is available in print at most large genealogical libraries and partially online through Google Books.

2. **Identify the monthly meeting first.** Every Quaker was a member of a specific monthly meeting. Records are organized by meeting, not by county. Locate the correct meeting using the geographic clustering tool at Friends Historical Library or the Quaker meeting location maps in published Quaker genealogy guides. ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records))

3. **Certificates of removal are migration gold.** When a Quaker family moved, the sending meeting issued a removal certificate to the receiving meeting naming the individual, sometimes family members, and their good standing. These documents directly link two meetings across a move and are frequently the only evidence of where a family came from.

4. **Disownments name family members.** When a Friend was disowned (for military service, marrying outside the meeting, or other violations), the meeting minutes identify the individual and often cite the specific offense. Disownment does not mean the person disappears from the record — they may appear later requesting reinstatement.

5. **Marriage witness lists are a community census.** Quaker marriage certificates were signed by everyone present — often 50–100 individuals. These witnesses identify the entire social network of the family at a specific date and are a powerful tool for finding associated surnames and linked families.

6. **Use tax lists as your pre-1790 census.** No federal census precedes 1790. Pennsylvania county tax assessment lists from the 1750s–1780s are the primary substitute; they name adult male taxable inhabitants and can track a family's presence (or disappearance) in a township year by year. ([Pennsylvania Land Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))

7. **Do not look for civil birth/death records.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration until 1906. For the late 1700s, church records — especially Quaker meeting registers — are the only systematic vital records. ([Pennsylvania Vital Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))

8. **Check New Jersey meetings too.** The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting spanned both sides of the Delaware River. A Chester County family might have relatives attending Burlington (NJ) or Haddonfield (NJ) monthly meetings; removal certificates and marriages crossed the river routinely.

9. **Browse the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume on FamilySearch.** The one digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 001188322, 145 images, 1750–1800) is browse-only but covers the entire yearly meeting — useful for tracking broader Quaker community governance and finding references to specific families.

10. **Probate records survive and are indexed.** The FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994* (collection 1999196, 893,214 records, indexed + images) covers the full late 1700s period. Quaker wills and inventories often name meeting affiliation, fellow Quakers as witnesses, and can establish family relationships when meeting records are ambiguous.

---

This guide reflects data returned by FamilySearch collections search, volume search, and wiki sources as of the survey date. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College is the indispensable starting point for any Pennsylvania Quaker research — their catalog, finding aids, and staff expertise are unmatched for this community.

# Pittsburgh, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry
## Locality Research Guide · Time Period: c. 1865–1905

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Pittsburgh** is the county seat of **Allegheny County**, formed in 1788 from Washington and Westmoreland counties. During the late 1800s it was the undisputed center of America's steel industry — Carnegie's mills, the Jones & Laughlin works, and dozens of subsidiary operations drew massive waves of immigrant labor (Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) into the city and surrounding mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Duquesne). Families in these communities generated records at the city, county, state, and federal levels, as well as through their ethnic churches, unions, and employers.

**Key quirk — vital records split:** Pennsylvania did *not* require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906**. However, Allegheny County began registering births and deaths locally from **1870** — a full 36 years before the statewide mandate. For events 1870–1906, search county registers. For events after 1906, search state death certificates. For events before 1870, church records are the primary source. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records); [Allegheny County Vital & Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))*

**Key quirk — 1890 census loss:** The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921, including Allegheny County schedules. Substitute sources (city directories, state factory inspector reports, church registers) are essential to bridge 1880–1900.

---

### 1. 🏭 Industrial & Occupational Records *(Priority sources for this research focus)*

These are the records most specific to the steel industry context and are not always on FamilySearch.

| Source | What It Contains | Repository & Access |
|--------|-----------------|---------------------|
| **Company employment records** | Fragmentary personnel records, payroll lists, hiring records for Carnegie Steel, J&L, and others | **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh); **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** archives. Physical/limited digitization — contact repositories directly. |
| **Union membership lists** | Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel & Tin Workers membership rolls, local lodge records | **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg); some records at Heinz History Center. Physical only. |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Annual Pennsylvania Bureau of Industrial Statistics reports listing mills, employee counts, nationalities, sometimes named individuals | **Pennsylvania State Archives**; bound volumes at Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh. Physical/browse-only. Particularly useful 1872–1905 to bridge the 1890 census gap. |
| **City directories** | Name, occupation, employer, and address listed annually | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds complete Pittsburgh city directories from **1813** onward. Partially digitized via Ancestry.com and Internet Archive. Invaluable for placing workers year by year. *(Source: [Allegheny County Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))* |
| **Pittsburgh Gazette / newspaper death notices** | Worker accidents (common in mills), obituaries noting employment and nationality | **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)); **Carnegie Library** microfilm holdings |

---

### 2. 📜 Vital Records

| Record Type | Coverage | Repository & FamilySearch Collection |
|-------------|----------|--------------------------------------|
| **Births & Deaths (county)** | Allegheny County: **1870–1905** | Allegheny County courthouse; partially on FamilySearch microfilm. Statewide not yet begun. |
| **Births & Deaths (state)** | Pennsylvania: **1906 onward** | [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) — **4.2 million records, indexed + images** on FamilySearch. Begins just after the target period but catches workers who lived into the 1900s. |
| **Marriage licenses** | Allegheny County from **1885** | Allegheny County courthouse; [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — **524,189 records, indexed** on FamilySearch. |
| **Civil marriages (broader)** | 1677–1950 | [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) — **312,045 records, indexed** on FamilySearch. |
| **Compiled marriages** | 1700–1900 | [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) — **198,765 records, indexed; no images** on FamilySearch. |

**Quirk:** Before the 1870 county registration, vital events for Pittsburgh families are found almost exclusively in church registers. For immigrant mill workers, the Catholic parish register is often the *only* record of a baptism or marriage. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))*

---

### 3. ⛪ Church Records *(Critical for immigrant mill workers)*

Pittsburgh's steel workforce was predominantly Catholic and worshipped in ethnically organized parishes. Each national parish kept its own registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) in the language of the community.

| Ethnic Community | Parish Type | Archives |
|-----------------|------------|---------|
| **Slovak, Polish, Croatian, Italian, Irish** | Roman Catholic | **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** holds many original registers from the 1840s onward. Also check FamilySearch microfilm for individual parishes. |
| **German Lutherans / Reformed** | Lutheran, Reformed | **ELCA Region 8 Archives**; some records on Ancestry and FamilySearch |
| **Eastern European Greek Catholics** | Byzantine Catholic | Diocese of Passaic or Pittsburgh Byzantine archives |

**Access:** Many ethnic parish registers have *not* been digitized and require direct contact with the diocesan archives or individual parishes. FamilySearch has microfilmed a number of Allegheny County church records — search "Pennsylvania Church Records" in the FamilySearch catalog filtering to Allegheny County. *(Source: [Allegheny County Vital & Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))*

---

### 4. 📊 Census Records

| Census Year | Notable Features for Steel Workers | Access |
|-------------|-----------------------------------|--------|
| **1870** | Lists occupation; first census capturing the post-Civil War industrial boom | FamilySearch (indexed + images) |
| **1880** | Lists occupation, birthplace of self and both parents | FamilySearch (indexed + images) |
| **1890** | ⚠️ **Largely destroyed** — Allegheny County schedules are lost | None — use substitutes (see above) |
| **1900** | Lists occupation, immigration year, years in US, citizenship status | FamilySearch (indexed + images) |
| **Mortality schedules, 1880** | Deaths in the year preceding the census, including mill accident victims | FamilySearch (available) |

All federal censuses for Allegheny County survive from 1800. The 1880 and 1900 enumerations are especially rich for industrial workers. *(Source: [Allegheny County — Census and Naturalization](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))*

---

### 5. 🗺️ Naturalization & Immigration Records

Steel mill immigration is especially well documented in naturalization records.

| Record | Coverage | Repository |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| **Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas naturalizations** | 1798–1930 | **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region). Includes declarations of intention ("first papers") and final petitions. *(Source: [Allegheny County — Census & Naturalization](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))* |
| **Passenger arrival lists** | Post-1890 immigrant surges | NARA; indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch |
| **Border crossings / Canadian entry** | Slovak/Polish workers sometimes entered via Canada | NARA; Ancestry.com |

**Quirk:** Before September 1906 (when INS centralized naturalization), a worker could be naturalized in *any* court of record — county, state, or federal. Check Allegheny County Common Pleas, the U.S. Circuit Court records, and surrounding county courts if you can't find a specific individual. *(Source: [Allegheny County Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

---

### 6. 📋 Land, Probate & Tax Records

| Record | Coverage | Repository & Access |
|--------|----------|---------------------|
| **County deed books** | Allegheny County from 1788 | Allegheny County courthouse (physical); some on FamilySearch microfilm |
| **Probate (Register of Wills)** | Colonial period onward | [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — **893,214 records, indexed + images** on FamilySearch |
| **Tax assessment lists** | Annual county-level assessments | Pennsylvania State Archives; useful as census substitutes and for tracking property |
| **Pennsylvania Land Office** | Patents and warrants from 1681 | Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg (physical) |

Working-class mill workers rarely owned much taxable property in the 1880s–90s, but naturalized workers who acquired a home row house will appear in deed and tax records.

---

### 7. ⚖️ Court Records

Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas records include not just naturalizations but guardianships, name changes (immigrants anglicizing names), debt suits, and civil cases arising from workplace injuries. Physical access at the Allegheny County courthouse; some records at NARA Philadelphia.

---

### 8. 🗞️ Newspapers & Local History

- **Pittsburgh Gazette, Pittsburgh Post, Pittsburgh Dispatch** — mill accident reports, labor strike coverage, union meeting notices, immigrant community announcements. Available on **Newspapers.com** and partially in **Carnegie Library** microfilm holdings.
- **Ethnic press** — *Jednota* (Slovak), *Narod Polski* (Polish), and other immigrant newspapers covered community life, death notices, and lodge membership. Holdings at **Heinz History Center**.

---

### Research Strategy for Steel Industry Families

1. **Start with census** (1880 + 1900) to establish occupation, employer district, birthplace, and parents' birthplace — this identifies the ethnic church community.
2. **Trace the church parish** using the ethnic community and neighborhood; the parish baptism/marriage register often pre-dates county civil registration.
3. **Use city directories** year by year to track address changes, employer, and residence in mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport).
4. **Naturalization records** at NARA Philadelphia will give immigration date, birth place in Europe, and witness names (often neighbors or co-workers who are themselves research leads).
5. **For the 1890 gap**, use the 1889 and 1891 Pittsburgh city directories + PA state factory inspector annual reports to bracket the lost census year.
6. **Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel** are the indispensable archives for anything touching the mill itself — company records, labor strikes (especially the 1892 Homestead Strike), and ethnic community newspapers.
