# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682 from the original Penn grant; Philadelphia City chartered 1701, occupying the core of the county. In 1793 the city proper was smaller than the county — surrounding townships (Northern Liberties, Southwark, Moyamensing, Kensington) were county territory outside city limits. The city and county did not become fully coextensive until the Consolidation Act of 1854.
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (city hall / County Court at Fifth and Chestnut Streets)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state-land state — metes and bounds land system)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793 (city and immediate suburbs), per [Wikipedia — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793). The first federal census (1790) documented the broader county and surrounding townships; the 1800 census captures the post-epidemic population.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port city; commerce, maritime trade, mercantile firms, artisan crafts, printing, and finance. Philadelphia was the U.S. capital in 1793.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (original settlers), Germans (large community by 1790s, many Lutheran and Reformed), Scots-Irish Presbyterians, Irish Catholics, Swedes (older colonial settlers along the Delaware), free Black Philadelphians (a significant and growing community, organized partly through the Free African Society and Mother Bethel AME Church, both active during the epidemic), and recent immigrants from the British Isles and France.
- **Religious denominations:** Quaker (Friends), Anglican/Episcopal, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei), German Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, Old St. Joseph's), Baptist, and African Methodist Episcopal. Each denomination kept its own registers.
- **Key historical event:** The yellow fever epidemic of August–November 1793 killed approximately 5,000 residents — roughly one-tenth of the population. Thousands more fled to surrounding counties. Mayor Matthew Clarkson, physician Benjamin Rush, and a Committee of citizens appointed to manage relief efforts left detailed documentary records. The epidemic generated a class of sources with no peacetime equivalent.

---

## Boundary changes

- Philadelphia County has existed since 1682 with stable outer boundaries for most of its history.
- **Critical distinction for 1793 research:** The incorporated City of Philadelphia occupied a much smaller footprint than the county. Epidemic victims living in Northern Liberties, Southwark, or other townships are documented in *county* records (Orphans' Court, county deed books), not city records. Know whether your ancestor lived inside or outside the city corporation before deciding which repository to target.
- The 1854 Consolidation Act merged city and county — records created after that date use the unified structure. Records from 1793 predate consolidation; maintain the city/county distinction throughout your research.

---

## Available record types

### ⚠️ Vital records (civil registration) — NONE for 1793

Pennsylvania **did not have statewide civil registration** for births, marriages, or deaths until **1906** (death certificates). The FamilySearch collection [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) (4.2 million records, indexed + images) begins more than a century after the epidemic and is irrelevant for 1793 research.

There are **no civil birth, death, or marriage records** for Philadelphia in 1793. Church records are the *only* vital records for this period.

---

### Church records — PRIMARY SOURCE for 1793 vital events

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the essential substitute for civil vital registration in 1793 Philadelphia. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ("Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)), the city's diverse religious communities each maintained registers, and many colonial and early national registers have been transcribed and published. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records.

Key congregations and their records:

| Congregation | Denomination | Records held |
|---|---|---|
| Christ Church | Anglican/Episcopal | Baptisms, marriages, burials — published and microfilmed |
| Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') | Swedish Lutheran | Baptisms, marriages, burials from 1697 — among oldest in the region |
| St. Mary's / Old St. Joseph's | Roman Catholic | Sacramental registers; older records may be in Latin |
| Friends (Quaker) Meeting Houses | Society of Friends | Births, marriages (recorded at monthly meeting), burials — exceptionally complete |
| German Lutheran congregations | German Lutheran | Records often in German; Zion and St. Michael's are primary |
| German Reformed | German Reformed | Records often in German |
| First Presbyterian | Presbyterian | Session minutes and burial records |
| St. George's / Mother Bethel AME | Methodist / AME | Records of the African American community; Mother Bethel founded 1794 |

**Digitization level:** Varies by congregation. FamilySearch has microfilmed many Philadelphia church registers; some are indexed, others browse-only or on film only. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine* contains published abstracts. Check FamilySearch.org by congregation name and also the [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) collection (198,765 records, indexed, no images) and [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (312,045 records, indexed + images) for marriage data spanning this period.

**Language warning:** German Lutheran and German Reformed registers from 1793 are likely written in German. Older Gloria Dei records may be in Swedish. Catholic registers may use Latin for sacramental formulas.

---

### Epidemic-specific records — UNIQUE to 1793 research

These sources have no peacetime equivalent and are the most targeted resources for documenting epidemic mortality:

**1. Mathew Carey's published account**
*A Short Account of the Malignant Fever, Lately Prevalent in Philadelphia* (1793, multiple editions) contains lists of the dead by name, neighborhood, and sometimes occupation. This is a searchable published document, digitized and freely available on **HathiTrust** and **Google Books**. Essential first stop for any surname search.

**2. Committee minutes and reports**
The Committee Appointed by the Citizens to Attend to and Alleviate the Sufferings of the Afflicted with the Malignant Fever maintained minutes documenting relief efforts, names of the sick and deceased, and disbursements to families. Manuscript originals are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)**. Per [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793) and the FamilySearch Wiki ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793)), these are key genealogical sources.

**3. Bush Hill hospital records**
Bush Hill (a mansion converted to an emergency hospital) treated hundreds of epidemic patients. Records of admissions, deaths, and survivors are among the documents held at the Philadelphia City Archives and HSP. These can identify individuals who were treated, survived, or died at the facility.

**4. Mayor Matthew Clarkson's records and Benjamin Rush's papers**
Rush documented patients and treatments extensively. His papers are held at the **American Philosophical Society** (Philadelphia). These are narrative sources but may name specific individuals and families.

---

### Census records

| Census | Year | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1790 Federal Census | 1790 (pre-epidemic) | Heads of household only; names family members only by count | Indexed + images — Ancestry, FamilySearch |
| 1800 Federal Census | 1800 (post-epidemic) | Heads of household with age groupings | Indexed + images — Ancestry, FamilySearch |

**Research strategy:** Compare the 1790 and 1800 censuses. A family present in 1790 that has disappeared, relocated, or changed in composition by 1800 may document epidemic mortality. Note that thousands fled to Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, and Bucks Counties — many may appear in 1800 having *not* returned. Pennsylvania did not conduct a separate state census for this period.

---

### Probate records — HIGH VALUE for epidemic deaths

The Philadelphia County Orphans' Court probated the estates of those who died during and after the epidemic. Victims who died intestate (without a will, very common in a sudden epidemic) had administration proceedings filed naming next of kin and heirs — often the most detailed family relationship evidence available.

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records, indexed + images. This collection covers the full epidemic period and is searchable by name.
- **Physical repository:** Original wills, inventories, and administration bonds are at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Research tip:** An estate administration in late 1793 or early 1794 for a Philadelphia decedent almost certainly reflects epidemic mortality. Check both testate (will) and intestate (administration) files.

---

### Land records

Pennsylvania is a **state-land state** using metes and bounds surveys. Philadelphia County deed books document land sales, mortgages, and estate distributions.

- **Date range:** Continuous from the 1680s through the present.
- **Epidemic relevance:** Estate land sales and partition deeds often followed epidemic deaths in 1793–1795, naming heirs and family members.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives (deed books, recorder of deeds); some abstracts and indexes at HSP and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Digitization level:** Pre-1800 Philadelphia deeds are largely **physical only** or available on **microfilm** at the Family History Library. FamilySearch does not appear to have an indexed deed collection for this period in the tool results.

---

### Tax records — substitute for missing census years

Philadelphia County maintained annual taxable inhabitant lists (assessors' records) that predate and supplement census records.

- **Types:** Real property assessments, personal property lists, occupiers lists.
- **Value:** Because they were created annually, they can show a family's presence *before* the 1793 epidemic (1791, 1792 assessments) and *absence* afterward (1794, 1795) — a powerful tool for documenting mortality and flight.
- **Where held:** Philadelphia City Archives; some transcribed volumes at HSP and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania.
- **Digitization level:** Largely **physical or microfilm only** for this period.

---

### Newspaper records — named lists of the dead

Philadelphia had multiple newspapers publishing throughout the epidemic:

- *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser* (est. 1791)
- *Federal Gazette* and *Philadelphia Daily Advertiser*
- *General Advertiser* (later *Aurora General Advertiser*)

These papers printed weekly and daily lists of the dead during the epidemic, death notices placed by families, notices of estate sales, and relief announcements — all naming individuals.

- **Where held:** **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** and **Library Company of Philadelphia** hold the most complete microfilm and original runs. Some issues are available on **GenealogyBank** (subscription) and **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free — though coverage of 1793 Philadelphia is partial). **Newspapers.com** also carries some Pennsylvania historical newspaper content.
- **Digitization level:** Partial. Not all 1793 issues are digitized or indexed; microfilm at HSP/Library Company is the most complete access point.

---

### Quaker (Friends) records — exceptionally complete

Quakers maintained meticulous vital records through their monthly meetings, recorded at the meeting level (not by individual congregation in the typical sense). These predate any civil registration and are among the best-documented genealogical sources in early Philadelphia.

- **Record types:** Births, marriages (certificates signed by all witnesses — typically 50–100 names), deaths, disownment records, removal certificates (documenting migration).
- **Where held:** **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (primary repository); **Haverford College Quaker Collection**; HSP. Many records are microfilmed by FamilySearch.
- **Published finding aids:** *Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (Vol. II covers Pennsylvania) — a major compiled abstract covering births, marriages, and deaths from Philadelphia area meetings.
- **Research note:** Quakers who intermarried with non-Quakers were often "disowned" — disownment records name the individual and explain the cause. These are valuable for tracing Quaker-adjacent families.

---

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) ended 10 years before the epidemic. Many 1793 Philadelphia residents were veterans.
- **Pension files:** Revolutionary War pension applications are at NARA; many are indexed and digitized on **Fold3** and **Ancestry**. These files often contain extensive family information including wives, children, and places of residence as of the 1790s–1820s.
- **Militia records:** Pennsylvania militia records from this period are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Record Group 19). Not comprehensively digitized.
- **1793 context:** No major military conflict was underway in 1793; military records are background context rather than epidemic-specific sources.

---

### Immigration records

Philadelphia was one of the busiest ports of entry in the early republic. Many 1793 residents were immigrants or children of immigrants.

- **Pre-1820 passenger lists:** Sparse and incomplete. Some published lists cover German arrivals in the 1700s–1780s; others exist for Irish and British arrivals. The **Pennsylvania German Society** has published many German ship lists.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906, naturalization could be filed in any court. Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas naturalization records are at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and partially on FamilySearch microfilm. Some 1790s declarations of intention exist.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal records); HSP and the Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (published abstracts); Philadelphia City Archives (court records).

---

### Cemetery records

- **Major burial grounds:** Christ Church Burial Ground, Gloria Dei churchyard, St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery, Friends burial grounds (multiple meetings), Ronaldson's Cemetery (one of the first nonsectarian cemeteries, est. 1827 — post-epidemic but relevant for later family members), and many individual congregation graveyards.
- **Epidemic burials:** The 1793 epidemic overwhelmed normal burial capacity. Some victims were buried quickly in churchyards; others in hastily expanded grounds.
- **Online coverage:** **FindAGrave** has transcriptions for major Philadelphia cemeteries, though coverage of pre-1800 stones is uneven. Many 1793-era stones have deteriorated.
- **Physical records:** Sexton registers and vestry burial records are the most reliable; held at individual churches or their denominational archives.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Relevant collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) (893K records, indexed + images); [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (312K records, indexed + images); [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (198K records, indexed, no images); many church record microfilms | Free |
| **HathiTrust / Google Books** | Mathew Carey's *Short Account* (1793) — digitized, full text searchable | Free |
| **Ancestry** | 1790 and 1800 Federal Census (indexed + images); some Pennsylvania church and probate records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War pension files (many 1793 Philadelphia veterans) | Subscription |
| **GenealogyBank** | Historical Philadelphia newspapers including 1793 issues | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America** (loc.gov) | Some early Philadelphia newspaper runs | Free |
| **FindAGrave** | Philadelphia cemetery transcriptions | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** (Philadelphia, PA) | Committee of 1793 minutes, Bush Hill records, city administrative records, deed books, tax assessments, Orphans' Court records, naturalization records | In-person; some records requestable by mail |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** (Philadelphia, PA) | Largest manuscript collection for Philadelphia and Pennsylvania; church records, newspapers, family papers, Rush papers, published indexes | In-person; some digitized items online |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Early printed books including Carey's account; colonial and early national Philadelphia | In-person |
| **American Philosophical Society** | Benjamin Rush papers; manuscript accounts of the epidemic | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **Presbyterian Historical Society** (Philadelphia, PA) | Presbyterian church records across Pennsylvania | In-person; some microfilm |
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA) | Quaker meeting records for all Philadelphia-area meetings | In-person; Hinshaw abstracts widely available |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg, PA) | State-level records, Revolutionary War militia, land warrants | In-person; some records online via PA PowerPort |
| **Family History Library / FamilySearch Centers** | Microfilm of many Philadelphia church, probate, and court records | Free at FHL or FamilySearch Centers worldwide |

---

## Records NOT online

The following records exist for 1793 Philadelphia but are **not** fully available in any online database:

- **Tax assessment lists** (1791–1795) — Physical at Philadelphia City Archives; partial microfilm at FHL
- **Bush Hill hospital admission/death records** — Manuscript at Philadelphia City Archives / HSP; not digitized
- **Committee of 1793 manuscript minutes** — At HSP and Philadelphia City Archives; not digitized
- **Pre-1800 Philadelphia deed books** — Physical at Philadelphia City Archives; microfilm at FHL
- **Most congregation-level burial registers** — Held by individual churches or denominational archives; some microfilmed but not indexed
- **Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas minute books** — At Philadelphia City Archives; not comprehensively digitized

---

## Known record losses

No major courthouse fire destroyed Philadelphia County records (unlike many Pennsylvania counties). The principal losses for 1793 research are:

- **Epidemic disruption:** The epidemic itself interrupted normal record-keeping from August–November 1793. Some church registers show gaps in entries during the height of the epidemic, likely because clergy also fled or died.
- **Deterioration of early church records:** Some 18th-century registers have suffered physical deterioration. Transcribed and published versions may be the only accessible form.
- **Incomplete newspaper runs:** Not every 1793 Philadelphia newspaper issue survives; some are missing from institutional collections.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with Mathew Carey's published list.** His *Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793) names the dead and is freely digitized on HathiTrust — it is the closest thing to a death register for the epidemic. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

2. **No civil death records exist for 1793.** Pennsylvania statewide registration began in 1906. Do not search for a death certificate — none was issued. Church burial records are the only vital registration for this event. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))

3. **Cross the 1790 and 1800 federal censuses.** The epidemic killed ~10% of the population. Compare household compositions across both censuses to detect mortality and displacement. Families present in 1790 who vanished by 1800 may have died or permanently relocated.

4. **Search surrounding counties for refugees.** Thousands fled Philadelphia during August–November 1793 — to Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, and Bucks Counties, and as far as New Jersey. If you lose a family in Philadelphia records around this time, check those neighboring jurisdictions for any record of their presence during the epidemic months. They may have generated church, tax, or court records there before returning (or not returning).

5. **Check probate for intestate estates opened in late 1793 or early 1794.** Many epidemic victims died suddenly without writing wills. Administration proceedings in the Philadelphia County Orphans' Court name next of kin and are available in [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) on FamilySearch (indexed + images).

6. **Philadelphia City vs. Philadelphia County matters before 1854.** Know where your ancestor lived — inside the city corporation or in a surrounding township. City administrative records are at the Philadelphia City Archives; county records are there too but accessed through different record series. After the 1854 Consolidation Act this distinction disappears; before it, it is essential.

7. **Quaker researchers: use Hinshaw.** *Hinshaw's Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, Volume II, abstracts births, marriages, and deaths from Philadelphia-area Friends meetings. It is indexed and widely available in genealogical libraries — far more accessible than the original manuscript registers.

8. **German-community records require German-language ability.** Zion and St. Michael's Lutheran congregations and the German Reformed congregation kept registers in German through the 18th century. Plan for translation or seek published English abstracts.

9. **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GenSocPA) is a key resource.** Their compiled indexes, published abstracts in the *Pennsylvania Genealogical Magazine*, and library holdings (accessible through HSP) cover Philadelphia church and court records systematically. Check their holdings before visiting physical repositories.

10. **For Black Philadelphians:** The Free African Society (founded 1787) and the early AME church community kept records. The epidemic is notable because the Black community provided many of the nurses and caregivers — documented in Absalom Jones and Richard Allen's *A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People* (1794), freely available digitized. This pamphlet names community members and their epidemic roles.

## 🔥 Locality Research Guide: Chicago / Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire Families (c. 1850–1890)

### Jurisdictional Context

Cook County was formed in **1831** and has always contained Chicago. The **Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871** is the defining genealogical event for this jurisdiction: it destroyed the **Cook County Courthouse**, wiping out deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls accumulated before that date. Approximately 300 people died and 100,000 were left homeless. The fire created a hard documentary break — pre-1871 records largely do not survive in local repositories, and researchers must pivot to substitute sources (below). Post-1871 Cook County records survive in good volume.

> **Sources:** Wikipedia — *Great Chicago Fire* (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire); FamilySearch Wiki — *Cook County, Illinois Genealogy* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy)

---

### ⚠️ Critical Quirks for Fire-Affected Research

1. **Pre-1871 local records are almost entirely destroyed.** Do not assume deed books, court files, or vital registers survive at the county level before the fire. They do not.
2. **The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived** — original schedules were held in Washington, D.C., not Chicago. This is your single most important pre-fire population source.
3. **The Burnt Record Act (1872)** required property owners to re-register their deeds. These reconstructed records are the primary substitute for pre-fire property ownership.
4. **Church records are uneven.** Some parish registers burned with their churches; others were held off-site or by denominational archives and survived. Always check both the local parish and its central archive.
5. **Illinois statewide vital registration began in 1877** (births and deaths). Pre-1877 vital events in Cook County depend on county-level registration (largely destroyed by the fire) or church records. For events 1871–1876, check Cook County civil registers and church records together.
6. **FamilySearch collections for Cook County begin at 1871** — the fire year — reflecting what survived.

---

### Record Types, Availability & Access

#### 🔴 Pre-Fire Substitute Sources (for events before Oct. 8, 1871)

|---|---|---|---|
| **1870 Federal Census** | Households in Chicago as of June 1870 | FamilySearch / Ancestry | Indexed online — priority source |
| **1860 & 1850 Federal Census** | Earlier households | FamilySearch / Ancestry | Indexed online |
| **1865 Illinois State Census** | Illinois population mid-decade | Illinois State Archives | Partially available; check IRAD |
| **City Directories (1840s–1871)** | Names, addresses, occupations | **Newberry Library**, Chicago | Physical + some digitized |
| **Insurance Records** | Pre-fire property & business ownership | **Chicago History Museum** (Chicago Title & Trust collection) | Physical repository |
| **Pre-fire Reconstructed Court Records** | Probate, deeds (partial copies) | FamilySearch — vol. **009982110** (1865–1871, 38 images) | **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, no full-text; must be examined image by image |
| **Federal Land Patents** | Original land grants | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Indexed online |

#### 🟡 Fire-Era Records (1871–1875)

| Source | What It Covers | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Post-fire Property Re-recordings** | Deed reconstructions under the Burnt Record Act | FamilySearch — vol. **009982111** (1871–1880, 112 images) | **Partially indexed** — 41% name-searchable; remainder browse-only; no full-text |
| **Relief Lists** | Names of families who received disaster aid | Chicago History Museum; Newberry Library | Physical; some published lists exist |
| **Newspapers** | Fire victim lists, missing persons notices, survivor accounts | Newspapers.com; Newberry Library | Keyword-searchable online |

| Chicago Church Records | 285,000 | 1833–1925 | [1803978](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803978) |

> Note: The church records collection spans 1833, but surviving pre-fire entries will be limited to parishes whose registers escaped the fire.

#### Additional Record Classes

**Census & Population**
- Federal censuses: 1880, 1900, 1910, 1920, 1930 — fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry
- Illinois state censuses (1865, 1885) — check Illinois State Archives / IRAD

**Military Records** (Civil War era, highly relevant for 1871 fire survivors)
- Service records and pension files at **NARA** and **Fold3** (fold3.com)
- Many Chicago men served in Illinois regiments; pension files name wives and children — valuable when vital records are destroyed

**Immigration & Naturalization**
- Chicago was a major immigrant destination (German, Irish, Scandinavian, Polish communities)
- Passenger arrival lists at NARA / Ancestry
- Pre-1906 naturalizations scattered across Cook County Circuit Court and federal courts — many original files were burned; look for declarations of intention filed in other counties or states before arrival in Chicago

**Cemetery Records**
- Find A Grave (findagrave.com) — Chicago-area cemeteries
- Many pre-fire burials documented by cemetery registers that survived independently of the courthouse

**Newspapers**
- *Chicago Tribune* and other papers reported fire victim lists and "lost persons" notices — Newspapers.com and ProQuest Historical Newspapers
- The Newberry Library holds a strong Chicago newspaper collection

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to Fire Research | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | Post-1871 vital records, church records, census, reconstructed court/property volumes | Free online |
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories 1840s+, maps, manuscripts, newspapers | In-person; some digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title & Trust insurance records, photographs, personal papers, relief records | In-person research library |
| **IRAD — Northeastern Illinois University** | Illinois Regional Archives Depository — Cook County records post-1871 | In-person; inquire in advance |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) | In-person; appointment required |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records (births, marriages, deaths) from 1871 onward | In-person or mail request |
| **Illinois State Archives** (Springfield) | State-level records, land records, territorial period | In-person and online finding aids |
| **NARA — Great Lakes Region** (Chicago) | Federal court records, naturalization, military | In-person |

### Research Strategy for Fire-Affected Families

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — it predates the fire and places the family in Chicago with neighbors, ages, and birthplaces. It survived because originals were in Washington.
2. **Search Cook County post-fire vital records (1871+)** on FamilySearch — even if your target event was destroyed, siblings' births or parents' deaths in the 1870s–1890s survive and anchor the family.
3. **Check church records** — especially Catholic (Bernardin Archives) and German Lutheran/Reformed parishes, which often kept duplicate registers off-site.
4. **Use the Chicago History Museum's insurance/title records** for pre-fire property ownership, which can establish residence, economic status, and neighbors.
5. **Search newspapers** for fire-era missing persons, survivor lists, and rebuilding notices (Newspapers.com).
6. **Pivot to military pension files** (NARA/Fold3) for Civil War veterans in the household — pension files often contain the most detailed family genealogical information of the era.
7. **Check city directories at the Newberry Library** before and after 1871 to track a family's disappearance, relocation, or return.

# 📜 Louisiana — French Colonial Period (c. 1699–1803): Locality Research Guide

## Jurisdictional Context

The 1700s in Louisiana span **two colonial regimes**, and that split directly determines which language your records are in and where they are held:

| Period | Regime | Record Language | Primary Archives |
|--------|--------|-----------------|-----------------|
| 1699–1762 | French Louisiana (*La Louisiane*) | French | Louisiana Historical Center; Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (France) |
| 1762/1769–1800 | Spanish Louisiana | Spanish | Louisiana Historical Center; Archivo General de Indias (Spain) |

**Key dates (from Wikipedia, *French Louisiana*):**
- New Orleans founded 1718 by Bienville
- France ceded territory **west** of the Mississippi to Spain via the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762); Spain took actual possession in **1769**
- France ceded territory **east** of the Mississippi to Britain (1763 Treaty of Paris); Spain later recovered much of it (1779–1780)
- Spain secretly retroceded Louisiana to France (1800); U.S. acquired it via the Louisiana Purchase (1803)

⚠️ **Critical quirk:** A family straddling 1762 will have records in **two languages under two governments**. If you don't know which side of the Mississippi your ancestors lived on, check both the French-period and Spanish-period record sets.

---

## Record Types, Access, and Repositories

### 1. 🏛️ Catholic Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
**This is the primary vital-record substitute for the entire colonial period.** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana. The *Code Noir* required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, making these registers a critical source for African-descended families as well.

- **St. Louis Cathedral (New Orleans)** holds registers from **1720**. *(wiki_search result: "Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (collection ID 1612905) — **987,654 records; 493,827 images**. Date range begins squarely in the French colonial period. Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905
- Records are in **French** (pre-1762) and **Spanish** (post-1762); some later registers are bilingual. You must be able to read the original language or work with a translation.
- Physical originals: **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans (partially digitized). *(wiki_search result)*
- Rural parishes (Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Attakapas, Opelousas): each mission or post kept its own registers — check the originating parish, not just New Orleans.

### 2. ⚖️ Superior Council Records (*Conseil Supérieur*)
The colony's governing body produced **land grants (concessions), court proceedings, contracts, and estate inventories** — the closest equivalent to civil and probate court records.

- Held at the **Louisiana Historical Center**, partially digitized. *(wiki_search result, same source URL)*
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (collection ID 2078341) — **456,789 records; 228,394 images**. The date range begins in 1756, within the French colonial period. Access: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341
- For Spanish-period proceedings (post-1769), the governing body was reorganized as the *Cabildo*; those records are also held at the Louisiana Historical Center.

### 3. 📋 New Orleans Notarial Archives
**The oldest continuous notarial office in North America.** Holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements (*contrats de mariage*), and property transactions from the **1730s** onward. *(wiki_search result: "Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)*

- Public access available at the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center**.
- Records are in French (pre-1762) and Spanish (post-1762), with some in both.
- Marriage contracts (*contrats de mariage*) routinely name parents of both spouses — a genealogically rich source often overlooked.

### 4. 🌾 Land Grants and Concessions
French *concessions* and Spanish land grants followed civil-law traditions — **not** English common law — and are documented in:

- **American State Papers: Public Lands** series (widely available online and in research libraries)
- **Louisiana State Land Office** (Baton Rouge) *(wiki_search result, same source URL)*
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France: holds French administrative correspondence and **census rolls** (*recensements*) for the colony — these list settlers, their households, and landholdings *(wiki_search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)*
- For Spanish-period land claims: **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain

### 5. 🌐 Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) — France
ANOM in Aix-en-Provence is a **top-tier repository for French colonial Louisiana** that many researchers overlook:

- Holds administrative correspondence, **colonial census rolls**, military rosters, ship passenger lists, and governor's correspondence
- Many of the census rolls (*recensements*) from 1699–1762 name heads of household with family members, servants, and enslaved people
- Some records have been published and indexed by Louisiana genealogical societies; a portion are accessible via ANOM's online portal (portail-anom.culture.gouv.fr)

### 6. 🗺️ Census and Population Records
There was no federal census during the colonial period. Substitutes:

- **Colonial census rolls** at ANOM (France) — periodic military/civilian musters, 1699–1762
- **Spanish colonial censuses** in Louisiana records and at the Archivo General de Indias — post-1769
- The first U.S. federal census covering Louisiana was **1810** (Louisiana became a state in 1812), though the 1800 census covered parts of the Mississippi Territory; the **1820 census** is the first full enumeration as a state

### 7. 🪖 Military Records
Louisiana was a garrison colony; military service records are valuable:

- **ANOM (France)**: French colonial troop rosters and muster rolls, 1699–1762
- **Archivo General de Indias (Spain)**: Spanish militia and regular army records, 1769–1800
- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/): U.S.-era military records; minimal colonial-period coverage *(external_links_search result)*

### 8. ⛏️ Slave Trade and Enslaved-Person Records
- The **Code Noir** (1724 Louisiana version) required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons — they appear in sacramental registers, often with the enslaver's name as sponsor
- Estate inventories in the Superior Council records name enslaved individuals and their ages
- The **Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database** (slavevoyages.org) documents ships arriving in Louisiana from West Africa and the Caribbean

### 9. 📰 Newspapers and Published Sources
- *La Gazette de la Louisiane* (Spanish period): earliest Louisiana newspaper; Louisiana State University holdings
- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — limited colonial-era coverage; more useful post-1803 *(external_links_search result)*

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|------------|--------------|--------|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Superior Council records, sacramental registers, Cabildo records, Spanish-period documents | In-person; partial digitization |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s: wills, contracts, marriage settlements | In-person; some online |
| **ANOM, Aix-en-Provence (France)** | French colonial censuses, administrative correspondence, military rosters | In-person + partial online portal |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Spain)** | Spanish colonial records, 1769–1800 | In-person; partial Pares digitization |
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984 | Free online |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Post-1803 U.S. records; some territorial-period material | In-person + online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge)** | State and some territorial-era records | In-person |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Colonial land grants, American State Papers | In-person |

---

## FamilySearch Collections With Colonial-Period Coverage

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|------------|----|-----------|---------|--------|--------------|
| Louisiana, Church Records | 1612905 | 1718–1925 | 987,654 | 493,827 | Indexed + images |
| Louisiana, Probate Records | 1756–1984 | 2078341 | 1756–1984 | 456,789 | 228,394 | Indexed + images |

*Note: Record and image counts are as reported by collections_search. Collections beginning after 1800 (Parish Marriages 1837–1957; Statewide Death Index 1819–1964) are not listed here as they fall outside the French colonial period.*

---

## Key Quirks and Gotchas

1. **Language barrier is real.** French-period records (pre-1762) are in 18th-century French; Spanish-period records (1762–1800) are in Spanish. Budget for translation assistance or learn the record forms in both languages.

2. **No civil registration during the colonial period.** Catholic sacramental registers *are* the vital records for this era. Do not expect birth, marriage, or death certificates — they did not exist.

3. **The 1762 split is geographic.** The French cession divided the colony at the Mississippi River. Which government's records apply to your ancestor depends on *which bank* they lived on — west-bank families fall under Spain from 1769; east-bank families may have British-era records (1763–1779) before Spanish takeover. Research both if location is uncertain.

4. **"Parish" is an administrative unit, not just a church.** Louisiana uses parishes (not counties) as its primary civil division — a legacy of French and Spanish Catholic administration. Church parish boundaries and civil parish boundaries sometimes differ; early records may be filed under the originating *post* (Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Mobile, etc.).

5. **ANOM is essential and often skipped.** Most North American researchers don't think to look to France for Louisiana colonial records, but the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence holds colonial census rolls and administrative records that are irreplaceable for this period.

6. **Enslaved ancestors in sacramental registers.** The Code Noir's baptism requirement means enslaved persons appear in Catholic registers by first name, often with the enslaver's name noted. Estate inventories add age and sometimes origin.

7. **New Orleans Notarial Archives from the 1730s** are genealogically rich — marriage contracts name parents of both spouses and were culturally standard in civil-law Louisiana, making them far more useful than in common-law states.

---

## Suggested Research Order for French Colonial Ancestors

1. **Start with FamilySearch** — *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (free, indexed, covers the full French period)
2. **Check the New Orleans Notarial Archives** for marriage contracts, wills, and property acts
3. **Louisiana Historical Center** for Superior Council and Cabildo records
4. **ANOM (France)** for colonial censuses and administrative correspondence — especially if your ancestor was a soldier, official, or early settler
5. **American State Papers / Louisiana State Land Office** for land grant documentation
6. **Archivo General de Indias (Spain)** if research extends into the Spanish period (post-1769)

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Region (c. 1870–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Region:** Pennsylvania's coal districts span two distinct geographic zones:
  - **Anthracite (NE Pennsylvania):** Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, and Northumberland counties — the heart of the "Coal Region" ([Wikipedia: Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region))
  - **Bituminous (SW Pennsylvania):** Allegheny, Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, and Greene counties
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (state since 1787)
- **Economy:** Anthracite and bituminous coal extraction, colliery operations, company towns. Mining companies maintained employment records, payroll ledgers, and accident reports ([Wikipedia: Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region))
- **Ethnic composition:** Early waves from Ireland, Wales, and Germany; from the 1880s onward, large-scale immigration from Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, and Ukraine. Each group formed its own ethnic parish ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **Religious denominations:** Irish Catholic, Welsh Congregational, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, Slovak Catholic/Lutheran, Italian Catholic, German Lutheran/Reformed, Welsh Baptist — ethnic parish registers are the primary vital-record source for this period
- **Key events:** Molly Maguires trials (1870s–1880s, Schuylkill County); founding of the United Mine Workers of America (UMWA, 1890); major labor strikes; industrial expansion via Philadelphia & Reading and Delaware, Lackawanna & Western railroads

---

## Boundary changes

- **Lackawanna County** was carved from **Luzerne County** on **August 13, 1878**. Records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before that date are in Luzerne County, not Lackawanna. Search Luzerne County first for any events before 1878 in that area.
- **Carbon County** was formed in 1843 from Monroe and Northampton counties. Records before 1843 for the Mauch Chunk (Jim Thorpe) area are in those parent counties.
- **Schuylkill County** was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties. Pre-1811 events fall under those parents.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Statewide registration start:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906** — meaning nearly the entire target period (1870–1900) is not covered by civil registration at the state level ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)).
- **Exceptions:** Philadelphia County registered births and deaths from **1860**; Allegheny County from **1870** — both before the 1906 state mandate.
- **Marriage records:** Kept at the **county level** from the colonial period onward — marriage licenses and bonds are at each county courthouse.
- **FamilySearch collections (overlapping target period):**
  | Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
  | [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | Indexed + images |
  | [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | 0 | **Index only — no images** |
  | [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) | 1906–1968 | 4,218,763 | 4,218,763 | Indexed + images *(post-target period, but captures deaths of people who lived through the 1870–1900 era, including birthplace and parents)* |

- **Gap:** For births and deaths in the coal counties 1870–1906, **church records are the primary and often only source.** Do not assume civil registration exists for this window.

### Church records

Church registers are the **essential foundation** for vital-event research in this period. Each ethnic community organized its own parish, and those registers often contain more complete family data than any civil record.

- **Denominations present:** Irish Catholic, Polish Catholic, Lithuanian Catholic, Slovak Catholic/Lutheran, Italian Catholic, Welsh Congregational/Baptist, German Lutheran/Reformed, English Methodist
- **Record types:** Baptisms (with parents' names and godparents), marriages (with witnesses, sometimes villages of origin in the homeland), burials, confirmations (a separate dated event, years after baptism)
- **Language note:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and some German Catholic parish registers are in Latin or the heritage language — researchers must be prepared to read those originals
- **Where held:** Parish offices, diocesan archives (Diocese of Scranton, Diocese of Allentown, Diocese of Harrisburg, Diocese of Pittsburgh), and FamilySearch microfilm holdings. The Historical Society of Schuylkill County holds local church records ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Access:** Varies by parish — some are microfilmed by FamilySearch, others are physical-only at the parish or diocesan archive

### Census records

- **Federal censuses available for the target period:**
  | Year | Coverage | Notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1870 | All coal counties | Lists occupation; **indexed + images** on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
  | 1880 | All coal counties | Lists occupation, birthplace of parents; **indexed + images** |
  | 1890 | **Mostly destroyed** | Fire at Washington DC Commerce Building, 1921; minimal fragments survive |
  | 1900 | All coal counties | Lists birthplace, immigration year, years in US, naturalization status; **indexed + images** |
- **1890 substitute sources:** City/town directories, tax assessment lists, Pennsylvania Miners' and Farmers' directories, state and local schedules where they survive
- **No Pennsylvania state census** was conducted during this period

### Occupational and mining records ⚑ *Distinctive to this region*

These records are unique to coal-mining localities and often the richest source for tracing individual miners:

| Volume | County | Dates | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards (IGN 002240015) | Schuylkill | 1870–1900 | 410 | **Indexed + images; full-text searchable** (95% indexed) |
| Mine Accident Reports (IGN 002240016) | Luzerne | 1870–1895 | 287 | **Browse-only** — must be viewed image by image; 0% name-indexed |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers (IGN 002240017) | Lackawanna | 1878–1900 | 199 | **Browse-only** — must be viewed image by image; 0% name-indexed |

- FamilySearch's `volume_search` returned 23 total volumes for Pennsylvania 1870–1900; the three above are the first page. Additional volumes likely cover other county record types — worth browsing the full set.
- **Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870):** Published annually by the state; list every fatal accident with the miner's name, age, nationality, and cause of death. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). These are physical and/or microfilm — not fully digitized or name-indexed online ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining))
- **UMWA Records (from 1890):** Membership rolls and grievance files from the United Mine Workers of America. Contact the UMWA archives for access.
- **Company records** (pay ledgers, employment cards not yet digitized): Fragmentarily held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records, 446,607 images — **indexed + images**
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships held at each county's **Register of Wills** (courthouse) from county formation onward ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Land and Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **Court records:** Include naturalizations (pre-1906 — see Immigration below), guardianships, name changes, and civil/criminal cases. County court minute books name ordinary people never party to a suit — road supervisors, relief recipients, witnesses.

### Land records

- **System:** Metes-and-bounds; Pennsylvania is a state-land state
- **Pennsylvania Land Office** (Harrisburg): Warrant, survey, and patent records from William Penn's grants (1681) onward ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **County deeds:** At each county Recorder of Deeds from county formation
- **Company-owned housing:** Many coal-region miners lived in company-owned patches and patches — they may appear in company housing ledgers rather than deed records
- **Tax records:** County assessment lists and tax duplicates survive from colonial era in some counties; serve as census substitutes

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) predates the target period but produced pension files active through 1900s; Spanish-American War (1898) is within period
- **Civil War draft records:** Schuylkill and Luzerne counties had significant draft enrollment; Irish miners were notably involved in draft resistance (1862–1864)
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pension files); [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) for indexed military records online; Pennsylvania State Archives for state militia/adjutant general records

### Immigration and naturalization records

Naturalization is **critical** for coal-region families — the majority of miners in this period were foreign-born.

- **Pre-1906:** Naturalization could be filed in any court of record — county Courts of Common Pleas, state courts, or federal courts. No centralized index exists for this period.
- **Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906):** Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))
- **Arrival ports:** Most coal-region immigrants entered through **Philadelphia** and **New York** (Ellis Island records begin 1892; Castle Garden covers 1820–1892), then traveled inland by rail
- **1900 census:** Lists immigration year and years in U.S. — use this to target specific passenger lists
- **Access:** NARA holds passenger lists; Ancestry.com and FamilySearch have indexed collections; Fold3 for military naturalization records ([NARA](https://www.archives.gov/))

### Cemetery records

- **Online:** [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many coal-region cemeteries with headstone photos and some burial data
- **Types:** Catholic parish cemeteries (most ethnic miners), public/municipal cemeteries, fraternal order plots (Ancient Order of Hibernians, Slovak Jednota, etc.)
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at parish offices and cemetery offices — not universally digitized

### Newspaper records

- **Key papers:** *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville/Schuylkill County, from 1825), *Scranton Tribune*, *Wilkes-Barre Times*, various ethnic-language papers (Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak)
- **Content:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports, naturalization announcements, legal notices, labor-action coverage
- **Access:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription); state library microfilm; local historical societies. The *Miners' Journal* is particularly valuable for accident and death notices.

### Tax records

- **County assessment lists** and tax duplicates are held at county archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives
- **Value as 1890 substitute:** With the 1890 census mostly destroyed, county tax lists for 1889–1891 are the best substitute for locating a family in that gap year

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections / tools for this region | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) | County marriages, probate records, mine employment cards (Schuylkill), mine accident reports (Luzerne), payroll ledgers (Lackawanna), 1870–1900 censuses | Free |
| [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | U.S. Federal Censuses (1870, 1880, 1900), passenger lists, city directories | Subscription |
| [FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records and headstone photos | Free |
| [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) | Historical newspapers including *Miners' Journal* | Subscription |
| [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| [NARA (archives.gov)](https://www.archives.gov/) | Passenger arrival manifests, naturalization records, federal court records | Free (some digitized, some in-person) |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports (from 1870), Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906), state records, company records | In-person; some microfilm via ILL |
| County courthouses (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland) | Deeds, probate, court minutes, marriage licenses | In-person or mail request |
| Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) | Local church records, mining company records, newspapers, photographs | In-person |
| Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton / Lackawanna County) | Mining community records, ethnic community collections | In-person |
| Diocese of Scranton Archives | Catholic parish registers for Lackawanna and Luzerne counties | In-person or written request |
| Diocese of Allentown Archives | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill and Carbon counties | In-person or written request |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (1870–1900):** Annual state publications naming every fatal accident. Physical at Pennsylvania State Archives; not name-indexed online.
- **Most ethnic parish registers:** Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian church registers are largely at parish offices or diocesan archives, not digitized. Some FamilySearch microfilm exists for select parishes.
- **UMWA membership rolls (1890 onward):** Not digitized; contact UMWA archives.
- **Mining company employment ledgers** beyond the three digitized FamilySearch volumes: Fragmentarily held at Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies.
- **County naturalization records** outside Schuylkill County: Generally physical at county courthouses or state archives.

---

## Known record losses

- **1890 Federal Census:** Approximately 99% destroyed in a 1921 fire in Washington, D.C. — substitute with 1889–1891 tax lists, city directories, and church records.
- **No statewide birth/death registration before 1906:** This is a policy gap, not a record loss — researchers must pivot to church records for the entire 1870–1905 window.
- No major courthouse-fire losses are documented in the FamilySearch Wiki results for the key coal counties in this period, but individual parish and company record losses from flooding, fire, or neglect are common and should be assumed possible.

---

## Research tips

1. **Church records first for vital events.** Since Pennsylvania had no statewide birth or death registration until 1906, ethnic parish registers are your primary source for 1870–1905 events. Identify the specific ethnic parish your family attended — an Irish miner and a Polish miner in the same town belonged to entirely different parishes ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)).

2. **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are in Luzerne County.** Any event in the Scranton/Carbondale area before August 13, 1878 was recorded in Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for those years.

3. **Use the 1900 census strategically.** It lists immigration year and years in the United States, letting you pinpoint the approximate arrival window for passenger list searches. Citizenship status columns can also tell you whether to look for a naturalization record.

4. **Mine Inspector Reports are an underused resource.** Published annually from 1870, they name every fatality in Pennsylvania mines with age, nationality, and cause of death — extremely valuable for families where a miner died on the job. At the Pennsylvania State Archives ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)).

5. **Naturalization records are scattered pre-1906.** Before the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization centralized records in September 1906, any court of record could naturalize. Check county Courts of Common Pleas, state courts, and federal courts. Schuylkill County records are confirmed at the Pennsylvania State Archives; for other counties, contact the courthouse directly ([FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)).

6. **For the 1890 gap:** Use 1889–1891 county tax assessment lists (at county archives and Pennsylvania State Archives), city directories (many coal towns had them), and church registers from that year.

7. **Ethnic newspapers:** Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and other language papers were published in the coal region and contain obituaries, marriage notices, and community news not in English-language papers — check local historical societies and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project.

8. **FAN club (Family, Associates, Neighbors):** Chain migration means mining families from the same Old World village often settled together. Tracking neighbors and associates in the same mining patch can break through brick walls and confirm identities across records.

9. **The Miners' Journal (Pottsville)** is the region's paper of record from 1825 — invaluable for Schuylkill County accident reports, obituaries, and legal notices throughout the late 1800s. Available on microfilm at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and in part on Newspapers.com.

10. **Coal company records beyond what's digitized:** Contact the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies for employment ledgers, blacklists, and company-town store records (truck system) that name individual miners and their families.

# Massachusetts Early Colonial Period (ca. 1620–1700)
## Locality Research Guide

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Two **separate colonial governments** generated records for this period — always identify which one applies to your ancestor before searching:

| Colony | Years Active | Core Territory | Key Towns |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620–1691 | Southeastern MA (present Plymouth, Bristol, Barnstable counties) | Plymouth, Duxbury, Scituate, Barnstable |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628–1691 | Boston area north and west | Boston, Salem, Cambridge, Charlestown, Watertown, Roxbury |
| **Province of Massachusetts Bay** | 1691 onward | Both merged by royal charter | — |

Governor John Winthrop led the **Great Migration of approximately 20,000 settlers** into Massachusetts Bay Colony between 1630 and 1640 ([Wikipedia: Massachusetts Bay Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony)).

**County formation:** Massachusetts Bay Colony established four counties in 1643 — **Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Norfolk**. Before 1643, court and land records were kept at the colony level. Plymouth Colony created its own counties (Plymouth, Bristol, Barnstable) around 1685.

---

### Critical Quirks

> ⚠️ **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691) records are published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records.** Search both sets for southeastern Massachusetts families — they will not cross-appear.

> ⚠️ **Town-level vital registration was mandated in 1639; statewide registration did not begin until 1841.** The 1600s period relies on town clerk records and church registers, not a state system. Citing "Massachusetts didn't require registration until 1841" for this era is wrong — registration existed at town level from 1639.

> ⚠️ **No federal census exists until 1790.** Substitutes for the 1600s include town tax lists, colonial militia musters, freeman lists, and church membership rolls.

> ⚠️ **Counties before 1643 did not exist in Massachusetts Bay.** Pre-1643 records (deeds, court proceedings) were kept at the colony level — look to the Massachusetts Archives, not county courthouses, for those years.

---

### Record Types, Availability & Access

#### 1. 🟢 Town Vital Records (1639+) — Indexed on FamilySearch
- **Coverage:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded by town clerks. The General Court mandated this in **1639** — making Massachusetts one of the earliest jurisdictions in North America to require civil vital registration at the town level. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Genealogy – Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* — **name-indexed and searchable**
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550
- **Published abstracts:** The multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series (Tanner-Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for **over 200 Massachusetts towns** — widely held by libraries and often available before you need to examine originals. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Gap to know:** Very small or newly-formed 1600s towns may have incomplete indexing — browse images for completeness.

---

#### 2. 🟢 Church Records (1630+) — Indexed on FamilySearch
- **Coverage:** Congregational (Puritan) church registers are **central to early Massachusetts genealogy** — the established church kept membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and records of disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments). These often name family relationships not found in town records. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Church Records – Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* — **name-indexed and searchable**
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657
- **Published transcripts:** Many early church records appear in *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* publications and local historical society volumes. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Note:** Not all church registers have been digitized — check NEHGS manuscript holdings for unpublished registers.

---

#### 3. 🟢 Probate Records (1635+) — Indexed on FamilySearch
- **Coverage:** Wills, estate inventories, and letters of administration. County probate courts began in **1635** (Massachusetts Bay Colony). Plymouth Colony maintained its own parallel probate system through 1691. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* — **name-indexed and searchable**
  👉 https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901
- **Note:** Pre-1643 probate may be filed under colony-level court records at the Massachusetts Archives rather than individual county courts.

---

#### 4. 🟡 Land and Deed Records (1630s+) — Access varies; largely microfilm or physical
- **Coverage:** Deeds, land grants, and property transfers. County registries of deeds were established from the **1630s**. Town proprietors' records (original grants of town land to settlers) also survive for many early towns and can establish a family's presence in a community. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **No FamilySearch indexed collection** was returned by the collections search for this record type and period — this is a digitization gap.
- **Access:** County registries of deeds (at each county courthouse); Massachusetts Archives for colony-level land records; some deed books microfilmed by FamilySearch and browsable.

---

#### 5. 🟡 Colony and Court Records (1620s+) — Physical; some microfilmed
- **Coverage:** The **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) holds the original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records from the **1620s onward**, including General Court (legislature/supreme court) acts, county Courts of Quarter Sessions, and Courts of Common Pleas. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Plymouth Colony Records:** Published and indexed separately in the multi-volume *Plymouth Colony Records* series — widely available in research libraries. This covers 1620–1691 and is the primary resource for Plymouth-area families. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Access:** Massachusetts Archives, 220 Morrissey Blvd., Boston — in-person or written request; some holdings on FamilySearch microfilm.

---

#### 6. 🟡 Tax Lists, Militia Musters, and Freeman Lists — Physical; some published
- **Coverage:** No census existed in the 1600s. The closest substitutes are colonial **tax (rate) lists**, **militia muster rolls**, and **lists of freemen** (adult male church members entitled to vote in colony elections). These establish a person's presence in a town and approximate date of arrival.
- **Access:** Massachusetts Archives; published in Massachusetts Historical Society, NEHGS, and local historical society volumes.

---

#### 7. 🟡 Immigration Records (ca. 1620–1643) — Published compilations; no 1600s passenger list on FamilySearch
- **Coverage:** 17th-century passenger lists are highly **incomplete** — few survive, and ships' manifests were not systematically kept for most sailings.
- **Premier resource:** The **Great Migration Study Series** (NEHGS) documents every known settler arriving in New England **1620–1643** with all surviving sources cited for each family. This is the essential starting point for any ancestor in this window. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Other published resources:** John Camden Hotten's *Original Lists of Persons of Quality* (1874); Charles Banks' *Planters of the Commonwealth* (1930).
- **⚠️ Note:** The FamilySearch collection *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (id: 1784312) is entirely post-1700 and does **not** apply to this period — do not confuse it with colonial-era immigration records.
- **Access:** NEHGS (Boston) in person; online via **AmericanAncestors.org** (subscription).

---

#### 8. 🟡 Military Records — Published; physical at Massachusetts Archives and NARA
- **Coverage:** **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** is the major military event of this period. Colonial militia records and muster rolls survive at the Massachusetts Archives and have been partially published. Earlier colonial militia records also exist for the Pequot War (1636–1637) and other actions.
- **External resource:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) hosts some military records, though 1600s coverage is limited.

---

#### 9. 🟡 Cemetery Records — Physical; partially indexed online
- **Coverage:** Many early Puritan burying grounds survive in Massachusetts towns. Gravestone inscriptions give death dates and often family relationships.
- **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) has indexed thousands of Massachusetts colonial-era gravestones — coverage varies by town. Browse-only for unindexed cemeteries.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings for This Period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Colony court records, governor's correspondence, colony laws, tax lists, militia muster rolls — from the 1620s | In-person or written request; some on FamilySearch microfilm |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** (Boston) | Largest genealogical library in New England; Great Migration Study Series; manuscript church and town records; published genealogies | In-person; online via [AmericanAncestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org/) (subscription) |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (id 2061550); Church Records 1630–1920 (id 1921657); Probate Records 1635–1991 (id 1678901) | Free online |
| **County Registries of Deeds** (by county) | Deed books from 1630s | County courthouse; some microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| **Pilgrim Hall Museum** (Plymouth) | Plymouth Colony documentation; Mayflower passenger records | In-person; [pilgrimhall.org](https://www.pilgrimhall.org/) |
| **American Antiquarian Society** (Worcester) | Colonial publications; early newspapers | In-person; [americanantiquarian.org](https://www.americanantiquarian.org/) |
| **Massachusetts Historical Society** (Boston) | Manuscript collections; Winthrop papers; colonial correspondence | In-person; [masshist.org](https://www.masshist.org/) |
| **NARA (National Archives)** | Federal records (limited pre-1790 content); some colonial-era militia records | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |

---

### Research Strategy for Early Massachusetts Families

1. **Determine the colony first.** Plymouth or Bay Colony? This controls which published record series and archives apply.
2. **Start with the Great Migration Study Series** if the ancestor arrived 1620–1643 — it is the most authoritative compiled source and cites every surviving record per family.
3. **Search by town, not county.** Vital records are at the town level; deeds and probate are at the county level. Identifying the specific town is the prerequisite to efficient searching.
4. **Mine published transcripts before going to originals.** The Tanner-Corbin series, *Plymouth Colony Records*, and many published church records mean transcripts exist for many early families — check those first.
5. **Church membership records are essential.** For Puritans, church membership was legally and socially significant. Disciplinary records name witnesses and family members; membership lists establish presence in a town.
6. **Cross-border awareness.** Families near the Connecticut, Rhode Island, or Plymouth Colony/Bay Colony boundary may have generated records in multiple jurisdictions — consult Connecticut and Rhode Island colonial records if the family was near those borders.

---

### Coverage Gaps Noted

- The FamilySearch Wiki place pages for Massachusetts did not return Massachusetts-specific content in this environment — consult the wiki directly at **https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy** for the full online overview.
- `volume_search` (browse-only digitized volumes) was not available in this environment — additional unindexed FamilySearch image volumes may exist for Massachusetts beyond the three indexed collections surfaced above.
- No population data was returned for 1620–1700 — historical estimates suggest Massachusetts Bay Colony grew from ~2,000 settlers in 1630 to roughly 50,000–70,000 colonists by 1700.

The combination of the three FamilySearch indexed collections (town vitals, church records, probate), the Great Migration Study Series at NEHGS, and the Massachusetts Archives gives you a genuinely deep record base for Puritan-era families.
