# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory (1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Period covered:** April 22, 1889 (Land Run) through early statehood; Oklahoma achieved statehood November 16, 1907
- **Dual jurisdictions (1890–1907):** Oklahoma Territory (organized May 2, 1890, under the Organic Act; capital: Guthrie) and Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole — with separate tribal governments, courts, and schools) coexisted as *separate* jurisdictions across the same geographic area until merger at statehood
- **Pre-territory (1889):** The "Unassigned Lands" opened by the April 22, 1889 Land Run were not yet formally organized; no county or territorial government existed until the Organic Act of 1890
- **County formation:** Oklahoma Territory originally had 7 counties in 1890; additional land runs (1891 Sac & Fox; 1892 Cheyenne-Arapaho; 1893 Cherokee Strip; 1895 Kickapoo) added more territory and counties. By statehood in 1907, Oklahoma had 77 counties — records begin at the date each county was organized, not 1889
- **Population:** No population data returned by the tool for this period; the 1900 federal census enumerated Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory separately; the 1910 census is the first full state enumeration
- **Economy:** Primarily agricultural (wheat, cotton), cattle ranching, and nascent oil industry; railroad expansion drove settlement
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers (many from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas); Five Civilized Tribes and their freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members); smaller groups including Buffalo Soldiers and African American "Exoduster" communities
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (Unassigned Lands); subsequent openings 1891–1895; Dawes Commission allotments 1898–1914; statehood 1907

---

## Boundary changes and jurisdictional quirks

This is the most complex aspect of Oklahoma research — **which jurisdiction a family's records fall under depends on exactly where they lived**:

- **Oklahoma Territory vs. Indian Territory (1890–1907):** These were legally distinct jurisdictions. A settler living in the opened Unassigned Lands (future Oklahoma and Logan counties, etc.) was in Oklahoma Territory. A person — Native or non-Native — living in the unrelinquished tribal lands (eastern Oklahoma) was in Indian Territory, under tribal or federal court jurisdiction, not territorial court jurisdiction. Check historical county maps before assuming which jurisdiction applies.
- **Indian Territory had no standard county system before 1907.** Tribal nations divided their lands into districts with their own courts. Records generated there are tribal or federal (U.S. courts in Indian Territory were established at Muskogee under the Curtis Act of 1898), not Oklahoma Territory county records.
- **After statehood (November 16, 1907):** All records consolidated under the state's 77 counties. Records created before statehood remain in the jurisdictional series where they were created (territorial, tribal, or federal court).
- **The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed** (fire, 1921) — but Oklahoma Territory's own 1890 territorial census survived and is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society. This is one of the few surviving 1890 enumerations anywhere in the country.

---

## Available record types

### Land records ⭐ *The premier source for Land Run families*

- **Homestead entry files** are the single most important record class for 1889 Land Run settlers. Each file contains the original application, affidavits of settlement and cultivation, witness testimony, and the final certificate — often naming family members, ages, origin states, and length of residence. Files may also include contest files when a claim was challenged.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), specifically the **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** (the regional branch for Oklahoma). The Bureau of Land Management's [General Land Office Records site](https://glorecords.blm.gov) provides free online access to land patents; full case files require a records request to NARA Fort Worth.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — **234,567 records, 117,283 images** — **indexed + images** ([collection 1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)). Covers the territorial period through statehood.
- **Digitization level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch for the collection above; original homestead case files at NARA Fort Worth are **physical only** and require a records request
- **Tax records:** County-level property tax rolls begin with county organization (1890 for original 7 counties); held at county courthouses and Oklahoma State Archives — useful substitute for census years and for tracking settlement

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Birth and death registration:** No Oklahoma Territory law required statewide registration of births or deaths. Statewide registration began only after statehood, effective **October 1, 1908** (Oklahoma State Department of Health). Pre-1908 births and deaths must be documented through church records, cemetery records, funeral home records, or federal schedules.
- **Marriage records:** Marriage records begin with each county's organization, starting 1890 for the original Oklahoma Territory counties; Indian Territory marriages were recorded by tribal governments or U.S. courts before 1907. County marriage records are held at **county courthouses**.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* — **456,789 records, 228,394 images** — **indexed + images** ([collection 2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789))
- **Statehood-era vital records (post-1908):** Oklahoma State Department of Health holds original certificates; some are available through Ancestry.com and the Oklahoma Historical Society

### Indian censuses, rolls, and tribal records ⭐ *Essential for Native ancestry and Indian Territory residents*

- **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The Dawes Commission enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes and their freedmen for individual land allotments. The final rolls (approved 1906–1914) are the definitive index of tribal citizenship at allotment. These are fully indexed and widely available.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — **567,890 records, 283,945 images** — **indexed + images** ([collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432))
- **Ancestry.com** holds a digitized indexed collection of Dawes Rolls (subscription required)
- **NARA (National Archives at Fort Worth)** holds the original Dawes enrollment jackets, which contain supporting documentation — testimony, photographs, and rejected applications — far beyond what the rolls themselves show. These are not fully digitized.
- **Earlier tribal censuses (1851–1890s):** Individual tribes conducted censuses. FamilySearch's collection above covers these. Tribal records (Cherokee National Records, Choctaw tribal records, etc.) are held by individual tribal nations and the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Enrollment cards:** Each person enrolled on the Dawes Rolls has a corresponding enrollment card at NARA, with family groupings and often birth dates and places.
- **Freedmen rolls:** Formerly enslaved people of tribal members were enrolled separately on Freedmen rolls — critical for African American families with Indian Territory connections.

### Census records

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|--------|----------|-------|
| 1890 federal | Largely destroyed | Oklahoma Territory's 1890 territorial census **survived** — at Oklahoma Historical Society and partially digitized |
| 1900 federal | Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory enumerated separately | Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| 1910 federal | First state-wide enumeration | Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| 1907 Oklahoma Statehood Census | County-level head-of-household enumeration | Taken at statehood; partially digitized; at Oklahoma Historical Society |
| School censuses (territorial) | Annual county-level enumeration of school-age children | At Oklahoma State Archives and Oklahoma Historical Society |
| Territorial census (1890) | Oklahoma Territory only | Rare surviving 1890 enumeration; Oklahoma Historical Society |

### Church records

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — **123,456 records, 61,728 images** — **indexed + images** ([collection 1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321))
- **Denominations present:** Baptist (especially among tribal nations, with long mission history), Methodist, Presbyterian (active in Indian Territory missions), Catholic, and various Protestant denominations that followed settlers. The Five Civilized Tribes had established mission churches from the 1820s–1830s.
- **Mission church records predate civil registration by decades** and are often the only source for tribal members' vital events before the Dawes Commission
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society, tribal archives (Cherokee Nation Archives at Tahlequah; Choctaw Nation; Creek Nation), and individual denominational archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed many mission records.
- **Language note:** Some early mission records for tribal communities are in tribal languages (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek/Muskogee). Most post-1870 records are in English.

### Probate and court records

- **Oklahoma Territory:** District courts (established 1890) handled civil, criminal, probate, and naturalization. Records are at county courthouses, Oklahoma State Archives, and NARA Fort Worth. The wiki confirms these are held at the Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma Historical Society, and National Archives at Fort Worth ([Oklahoma Territory Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory_Records)).
- **Indian Territory:** U.S. courts at Muskogee (established under the Curtis Act of 1898) handled cases involving non-citizens of tribal nations; tribal courts handled intra-tribal matters. Records are at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Pre-statehood probate:** Territorial district court probate files are at county courthouses or Oklahoma State Archives. Tribal estates were handled separately under tribal law.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record; after September 27, 1906, only federal courts. Oklahoma Territory district courts are a prime source. Look also at U.S. courts in Indian Territory.

### Military records

- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Oklahoma Territory furnished troops. Muster rolls and service records at NARA, digitized on Fold3.
- **Civil War connections:** Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans (Union or Confederate). Their pension files at NARA are rich biographical sources — search by veteran's name at Fold3 or Ancestry.
- **Indian Wars:** Buffalo Soldiers (African American cavalry) were stationed in Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory. Records at NARA.
- **Veterans' schedules:** 1890 Veterans/Widows schedule (a separate enumeration taken alongside the 1890 census) partially survived and covers Oklahoma Territory — search at Ancestry or FamilySearch.
- **Access:** Military service records and pension files are at **NARA** (Washington, D.C., and Fort Worth); Fold3 is the primary online repository (subscription).

### Newspapers

- **Territorial newspapers** began immediately after the 1889 Land Run — the *Oklahoma City Times* and *Guthrie Daily Leader* both launched in April 1889. Many county seats had papers by the early 1890s.
- **Content value:** Obituaries (often very detailed for community founders), marriage notices, legal notices (land contests, probate, sheriff sales), and local news naming settlers
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society has an extensive newspaper collection; Newspapers.com has digitized Oklahoma territorial newspapers (subscription); the Oklahoma Digital Newspaper Program (ODNP) offers some free access at <https://gateway.okhistory.org>
- **Key tip:** Legal notice columns in territorial papers frequently name parties to land contests, naturalization filings, and estate proceedings — a rich supplement to courthouse records.

### Cemetery records

- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has extensive Oklahoma coverage including many pioneer cemeteries established post-1889; free access
- **BillionGraves** ([billiongraves.com](https://www.billiongraves.com)) has additional indexed Oklahoma grave photos
- **Oklahoma Cemetery Survey:** Oklahoma Historical Society maintains a statewide cemetery survey
- **Tribal cemeteries** (especially Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) are documented by tribal historic preservation offices and partially indexed at FindAGrave

### Immigration and naturalization

- **Most 1889 Land Run settlers came overland from neighboring states** (Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas) — not by sea — so passenger lists are rarely the entry point. Focus on naturalization records and origin-state records instead.
- **Naturalizations in territorial district courts** are the primary source; these are at county courthouses and Oklahoma State Archives. Post-1906 naturalizations are federal records at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Declarations of intention** ("first papers") frequently predate the Land Run — many settlers filed in Kansas or Missouri before moving; search those states' court records too.
- **Immigrant communities:** German-Russian Mennonites, Czech settlers, and others formed ethnic communities. Their church records (often in German or Czech) are at denominational archives and the Oklahoma Historical Society.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for Oklahoma 1889–1910 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Early Land Records 1834–1907 (234,567 records); Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959 (567,890 records); County Marriages 1890–1995 (456,789 records); Mission & Church Records 1820–1965 (123,456 records) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls; 1900 & 1910 federal census; Oklahoma vital records; newspapers | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military service records, pension files, Spanish-American War | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Oklahoma cemetery records, pioneer graves | Free |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical Oklahoma territorial newspapers | Subscription |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents — free, searchable by name | Free |
| **Oklahoma Gateway** (gateway.okhistory.org) | Oklahoma Digital Newspaper Program; some OHS digitized collections | Free |
| **NARA Online** (archives.gov) | Catalog and some digitized records; Dawes enrollment case files | Free catalog; some digitized |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** | Homestead case files; U.S. court records for Indian Territory; Dawes enrollment jackets; territorial district court records; military records | In-person or written request; some via Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS), Oklahoma City** | 1890 territorial census; 1907 statehood census; newspapers; county histories; photographs; OHS Research Center open to public | In-person; some collections digitized online at gateway.okhistory.org |
| **Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City** | Territorial government records; county tax rolls; school censuses; post-1908 vital records; naturalization records | In-person; contact for copies |
| **County courthouses (77 counties)** | Marriage records (from county organization date); deed books; probate files; district court records | In-person; some counties have mail/email request options |
| **Tribal archives** (Cherokee Nation Archives, Tahlequah; Choctaw Nation, Durant; Creek Nation, Okmulgee; etc.) | Tribal census records; citizenship records; tribal court records; church records | Contact individual tribe; access policies vary |
| **National Archives, Washington D.C.** | Military service records; pension files; post-1906 naturalization | Online request via archives.gov; Fold3 for military |

---

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist but have no significant online presence and require visiting or writing to the repository:

- **Original homestead case files** (the full application packet beyond the patent): NARA Fort Worth — physical request required
- **Dawes enrollment jackets** (the supporting documentation behind each Dawes Roll entry): NARA Fort Worth — physical request required
- **County-level school censuses** (annual enumeration of school-age children): Oklahoma State Archives — physical/written request
- **County tax rolls** for early territorial counties: Oklahoma State Archives and county courthouses
- **U.S. court records for Indian Territory** (Muskogee Division and other divisions): NARA Fort Worth
- **Tribal court records** (pre-statehood intra-tribal proceedings): Individual tribal archives — contact required
- **Funeral home records**: Individual businesses; no centralized index; some held by OHS
- **Early church records** not microfilmed by FamilySearch: Denominational archives and individual congregations

---

## Known record losses

- **1890 federal census:** The bulk of the 1890 federal census was destroyed in a Commerce Department fire in 1921. **Exception:** Oklahoma Territory's 1890 territorial census survived and is at the Oklahoma Historical Society — a critical substitute.
- **Early courthouse losses:** Several Oklahoma county courthouses suffered fires or other losses in the early territorial period, before systematic record preservation. Check OHS and Oklahoma State Archives for transcriptions or microfilmed backups before assuming records are gone.
- **Indian Territory pre-Curtis Act records:** The Curtis Act (1898) began federalizing Indian Territory governance; records from purely tribal courts before that date are less systematically preserved and held by individual tribal archives with varying access.

---

## Research tips

1. **Determine jurisdiction first — always.** Was your ancestor in Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory between 1890 and 1907? This single determination controls which court created records, which archives hold them, and which census schedules to search. Historical county maps at the Oklahoma Historical Society and at David Rumsey Map Collection can help pin a location to the correct jurisdiction.

2. **Homestead entry files are the foundation.** For any Land Run settler, the homestead case file at NARA Fort Worth is almost always more informative than the patent alone. It names witnesses (often neighbors and relatives), states where the claimant moved from, and documents the family's presence on the land. Contest files — when a claim was disputed — can be especially rich.

3. **The 1890 Oklahoma territorial census fills the federal gap.** Since the 1890 federal census is gone, this territorial enumeration at the Oklahoma Historical Society is essential for placing families immediately after the Land Run. It covers Oklahoma Territory only (not Indian Territory).

4. **County organization dates matter enormously.** Records begin only when a county was formally organized. The original 7 counties (1890) have records dating to that year; counties carved out of later land runs don't have courthouse records until their own organization dates. Check the OHS county history pages for formation dates.

5. **Search for Dawes Rolls even for non-Native families.** Non-Indian intermarried citizens (whites or freedmen married into tribal nations) were enrolled on the Dawes Rolls alongside tribal members and also received allotments. If a family lived in Indian Territory, check the rolls regardless of perceived ancestry.

6. **Naturalization records straddle jurisdictions.** Pre-1906 naturalizations filed in Oklahoma Territory district courts are at county courthouses or state archives. Settlers who naturalized in Kansas or Missouri before moving to Oklahoma may have "second papers" (petitions for citizenship) in Oklahoma Territory courts and "first papers" (declarations of intention) in their prior state.

7. **Oklahoma newspapers are underused.** The territorial press was prolific and often published detailed land contest notices, probate legal notices, and family-level news. The Oklahoma Historical Society's newspaper collection and the Oklahoma Digital Newspaper Program (gateway.okhistory.org) are starting points; Newspapers.com fills in additional titles.

8. **African American families: search Freedmen rolls separately.** Formerly enslaved people of the Five Civilized Tribes and their descendants were enrolled on separate Freedmen rolls by the Dawes Commission. These are indexed and available at FamilySearch and Ancestry alongside the main tribal rolls. African American "Boomer" settler families (not Freedmen) are in Oklahoma Territory records alongside other settlers.

9. **Church records bridge the vital-registration gap.** With no statewide birth or death registration before 1908, mission church baptismal and burial registers — especially Baptist and Methodist mission records held at OHS and indexed in FamilySearch's *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records* collection — are often the only pre-1908 vital record substitute.

10. **FamilySearch wiki has an Oklahoma Territory Records article** at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory_Records) — start there for a record-type overview confirmed by the wiki search. The four standard wiki place pages for Oklahoma returned only generic content and should not be taken as Oklahoma-specific guidance.

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1780–1820 (Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdictional Context

Alabama in 1800 did not yet exist as a jurisdiction. The territory passed through several governing authorities in rapid succession, and **which jurisdiction applies depends on both the date and the location within Alabama**:

| Period | Governing Authority | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French Louisiana | Mobile established 1702 |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | Mobile District |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish West Florida | Mobile District; Spain held Mobile until 1813 |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory (U.S.) | Covered all present-day Alabama + Mississippi |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory (U.S.) | Carved from eastern Mississippi Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Statehood December 14, 1819 |

**A critical geographic split:** The Mobile coastal area and the interior uplands were under *different* sovereign authorities simultaneously around 1800. American settlers moving into the Tombigbee and Tennessee river valleys (interior Alabama) were in the Mississippi Territory after 1798, but the Mobile Bay settlement remained under Spanish control until 1813. If your family was near Mobile, their records are European colonial in nature; if they were in the interior, look to territorial American records. **Do not assume a single record trail — determine which part of Alabama your family inhabited.**

**County formation was extremely rapid.** Washington County (organized 1800) initially covered nearly all of present-day Alabama. Later counties were carved from it:
- **Madison County** — 1808 (Tennessee Valley / Huntsville area)
- **Baldwin County** — 1809 (south Alabama)
- **Mobile County** — 1812 (Mobile Bay area, after U.S. seized it from Spain)

To find territorial-era court, probate, and land records, you must first determine which county your location fell under *at the time of the event*, then search that county's records — or its parent if it hadn't yet been formed. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties)*

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. Census and Census Substitutes

**Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, 1816):** The Mississippi Territory government took periodic enumerations of its settlers. These cover inhabitants of present-day Alabama during the territorial era. They are held physically at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery**, and the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson**. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*

**Federal census (1810):** The first federal decennial census to enumerate the Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory. Alabama residents appear under Mississippi Territory. This is name-indexed and searchable.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* (collection 2016756) — **287,634 records, index only, no images.** This is the earliest FamilySearch name-indexed entry point for the region and covers 1810 forward. Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756

⚠️ **Digitization status — browsable volumes:** FamilySearch's `volume_search` returned **zero results** for Alabama in the 1780–1820 window. There are no browsable image volumes for this period on FamilySearch. The territorial census manuscripts themselves have not been digitized to FamilySearch; consult ADAH and MDAH directly or their microfilm holdings.

---

### 2. Land Records

This is the **single richest record class** for pre-statehood Alabama, and some of it is genuinely online and browsable.

**Federal land sales:** Congress opened the St. Stephens Land Office (for southern Alabama) and the Huntsville Land Office (for the Tennessee Valley) beginning in 1803. These offices issued the first American land patents in the region. Entry files are in **NARA Record Group 49**. The patents themselves are fully searchable and browsable by name and place on:

> 🌐 **BLM General Land Office Records** — https://glorecords.blm.gov
> *Name-indexed and image-accessible; download original patent images for free.*

**Spanish land grants (Mobile area, 1780–1813):** Spain issued grants in the Mobile District. These records are held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress**. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

**British grants (Mobile area, 1763–1780):** Held at the **UK National Archives, Kew**.

**French grants (Mobile area, 1702–1763):** Held at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence**, with some on microfilm at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**.

**County deed books:** After county formation, local land transfers were recorded at the county courthouse. Washington County deed books begin around 1800. These are the most likely physical-only source for private land sales in the interior.

---

### 3. Church Records

No statewide civil vital registration existed in Alabama during this period — civil registration at the statewide level did not begin until the late 19th century. **Church records are the primary vital record source** for births, marriages, and deaths before and through statehood.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (collection 1986396) — **156,789 records indexed; 78,394 images.** This is the earliest FamilySearch collection with images touching the target period (from 1803). Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396

**Access level:** Indexed + images (searchable by name; images viewable).

**Mobile area Catholic records:** The Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Mobile maintained sacramental registers under French, British, and Spanish administration. These are among the oldest continuous parish records in the present-day United States. Originals and microfilm copies are at the **Mobile Municipal Archives** and the **Diocese of Mobile Archives**. Some transcriptions have been published.

**Protestant records (interior Alabama):** Methodist and Baptist circuit riders began entering the interior in the early territorial period. These records are scattered among individual church histories, denominational archives, and local historical societies. Coverage is sparse for the 1800–1810 window.

---

### 4. Marriage Records

**FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* (collection 1598408) — **612,345 records; 306,172 images.** Begins 1809, the earliest formal county-level marriage registrations in what became Alabama. Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408

**Access level:** Indexed + images.

⚠️ Marriage bonds and licenses before formal county record-keeping (pre-1809) were not systematically recorded. For the 1800–1808 window, church registers are the main substitute.

---

### 5. Probate Records

**FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* (collection 1537764) — **438,210 records; 219,105 images.** Begins 1809 (earliest county probate activity). Access at: https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764

**Access level:** Indexed + images.

For the pre-1809 territorial period, probate would have been handled by the territorial court. These records — if they survive — are at ADAH or the original county courthouses.

---

### 6. Tax Lists and Militia Rolls

The territorial government assessed taxes and organized militia, generating lists of free male inhabitants. These function as census substitutes for years without a formal enumeration.

- **Territorial militia rolls and tax lists (c. 1800–1817):** Held at ADAH. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*
- Published abstracts exist for some lists — check ADAH's online catalog and publications by the Alabama Genealogical Society.
- **FamilySearch volume_search returned zero results** for these record types in the 1780–1820 window; no browsable images of territorial tax/militia lists are currently on FamilySearch.

---

### 7. Court Records

The territorial superior court and, after county formation, county courts generated minutes, order books, case files, naturalizations, and guardianship records.

- **Washington County court records (from 1800):** Original courthouse in St. Stephens (first territorial capital).
- **Territorial superior court records:** At ADAH.
- These records are **not on FamilySearch** for this period (volume_search = 0). Physical access via ADAH or county courthouses.

---

### 8. Military Records

**War of 1812 and Creek War (1813–1814):** These conflicts produced militia service records and pension files for many Alabama-area men. Many received **bounty land warrants** redeemable in the new federal land offices.

- **Pension and bounty land warrant files:** NARA; also searchable on Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com) and Ancestry.
- **Territorial militia records:** ADAH.
- **1812 pension index:** Searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

### 9. Colonial Records (Mobile Area, Pre-1798)

For families with roots in the Mobile coastal settlement before American control, a parallel European colonial paper trail exists:

| Record Type | Location |
|---|---|
| Spanish censuses, church registers, land grants (1780–1813) | Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress |
| French colonial records (1702–1763) | Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| British colonial records (1763–1780) | UK National Archives, Kew |

*(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

⚠️ These are largely **physical or microfilm only** — not on FamilySearch. Many are in French or Spanish. Published abstracts and transcriptions by local historians (e.g., Peter Hamilton's *Colonial Mobile*) can help navigate them.

---

### 10. Newspapers

The *Mobile Centinel* (established 1811) is among the earliest Alabama newspapers, followed by papers in Huntsville from 1812. For the very earliest period (1800–1810), no Alabama newspaper survives in usable form. Check **Newspapers.com** and the **Library of Congress Chronicling America** (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) for what exists.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery | Territorial censuses, militia rolls, tax lists, territorial court records, county records | In-person; growing online catalog |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives and History (MDAH)**, Jackson | Mississippi Territory records predating the 1817 split | In-person; some digital |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal land entry files (RG 49), military pensions, 1810 federal census | In-person; Fold3/Ancestry for many series |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from St. Stephens & Huntsville offices | **Free, online, name-indexed, image-accessible** |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm of French colonial records; local city records | In-person |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville | Spanish colonial records of Mobile District | In-person; some digitized via PARES portal |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence | French colonial records | In-person; partial online via Mémoire des hommes |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections from 1803/1809+; 0 browsable volumes for 1780–1820 | Free online |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status | Browsable Without Index? |
|---|---|---|
| Territorial censuses (1801–1816) | Not on FamilySearch | No — ADAH/MDAH physical |
| Federal land patents (from 1803) | Not on FS; **BLM GLO** has full images | **Yes — BLM GLO is fully browsable** |
| Church records (from 1803) | Indexed + images (FS collection 1986396) | Yes, via index |
| County marriages (from 1809) | Indexed + images (FS collection 1598408) | Yes, via index |
| Probate records (from 1809) | Indexed + images (FS collection 1537764) | Yes, via index |
| Census substitutes index (from 1810) | Index only — no images | No |
| Tax lists / militia rolls | Not on FamilySearch | No — ADAH physical |
| Spanish colonial records | Not on FamilySearch | Partially via PARES (Spain) |
| French colonial records | Not on FamilySearch | Partially via ANOM portal |

---

## Critical Quirks for Researchers

1. **Search under Mississippi Territory, not Alabama**, for records created before 1817 — filing labels, indexes, and microfilm rolls often use the territorial name.
2. **County boundary changes are essential to navigate.** Washington County (1800) is the parent for most interior Alabama records until 1808–1812. If a record can't be found in a later county, search its parent.
3. **The Mobile area is a completely different research trail** from the interior. Mobile families before 1813 generated Spanish, French, and British colonial records, not American territorial ones. Search both trails if your family was anywhere near the coast.
4. **No statewide civil vital registration** existed during this period. Church registers are the primary (often only) source for births, marriages, and deaths.
5. **FamilySearch has no browsable image volumes for Alabama in the 1780–1820 window** (volume_search returned 0). The territorial-era manuscripts — censuses, court records, tax lists — are at ADAH in physical or microfilm form. The BLM GLO site is the one major online source with *browsable* images for this era.
6. **The 1810 federal census** is the first federal enumeration covering the Alabama portion of Mississippi Territory and the earliest name-indexed federal census for the region.
7. **Bounty land warrants** issued after the Creek War (1813–1814) and War of 1812 brought a large wave of new settlers to Alabama 1815–1819, making federal land records at BLM GLO especially dense for those years.

---

## Bottom Line for Your Search

For Alabama families around 1800, **before any Alabama record infrastructure existed**, your best starting points — roughly in order of online availability — are:

1. **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) — free, browsable, name-indexed land patents from the St. Stephens and Huntsville offices from 1803 onward
2. **FamilySearch collection 1986396** — Church Records, 1803–1950, indexed with images
3. **FamilySearch collection 2016756** — Compiled Census & Substitutes Index, 1810–1890, name-indexed (no images, but links to source documents)
4. **ADAH directly** (https://www.archives.alabama.gov) — territorial censuses 1801/1805/1808/1810/1816, militia and tax lists, territorial court records
5. **NARA / Fold3** — military pensions, War of 1812 service records, federal land entry files (RG 49)
6. **Mobile Municipal Archives / ANOM / Archivo General de Indias** — if your family was in the Mobile coastal area under European colonial rule

# 🪨 Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide
**Counties:** Schuylkill · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Carbon · Northumberland
**Period:** 1860–1890 | **Focus:** Irish immigrant ancestors, coal mining records

---

## 1. Jurisdictional Context & Critical Boundary Quirks

Understanding the county-formation history is essential before you search — records will be filed under different county names depending on the event date.

| County | Formed | Parent(s) | Key Quirk |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Northumberland** | 1772 | Lancaster, Bedford, Northampton, Cumberland, Berks | One of PA's original counties; records continuous from colonial era |
| **Luzerne** | 1786 | Northumberland | Holds all pre-1878 records for present-day Lackawanna County |
| **Schuylkill** | 1811 | Berks + Northampton | Southern anthracite field; the heart of Irish mining settlements |
| **Carbon** | 1843 | Monroe + Northampton | Search Monroe and Northampton for any pre-1843 events |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | Luzerne | ⚠️ All events before 1878 in present-day Lackawanna (Scranton, Carbondale) are in **Luzerne County** records — search Luzerne first |

> **The most important quirk in this region:** Lackawanna County did not exist until 1878. If your Irish ancestor was in Scranton or Carbondale before that date, every court record, naturalization, deed, and marriage was filed in Luzerne County. This is a constant source of missed finds.

**Schuylkill County population growth** (driven by anthracite coal):
- 1860: **89,510** | 1870: **116,428** | 1880: **129,974**
- Tool note: *"Rapid growth driven by anthracite coal mining. Large immigrant population (Irish, Welsh, German, later Eastern European) from 1840s onward."*

---

## 2. ⭐ Specialized Coal-Region Indexes (FamilySearch Wiki)

The FamilySearch Wiki page **[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)** identifies three specialized indexes unique to the anthracite field that you will not find through standard county searches:

### Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
- Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field
- Drawn from company **payroll books** that survived a 1903 records consolidation
- Each entry records: **occupation** (loader, breaker boy, mule driver), **wage rate**, and **parish of origin** where stated
- Critical for Irish ancestors: the "parish of origin" field can directly link a miner to his Irish townland or parish — information rarely captured anywhere else
- ⚠️ Per the wiki: distinguish payroll-derived indexes (name-indexed, genealogically direct) from mine-inspection and accident reports (organized by colliery, not by person)

### Catholic Parish Survival — Diocese Split
- Most coal-region Catholic parishes were established **1840–1870** to serve Irish and Eastern European communities
- **Before 1868:** Baptismal registers held by the **Diocese of Harrisburg**
- **After 1868:** Registers held by the **Diocese of Scranton** (when it was created from Harrisburg)
- ⚠️ An Irish ancestor baptized in 1865 vs. 1875 in the same Scranton parish will have their register in *different* dioceses — always check both if straddling 1868

### Triennial State Tax Assessments, from 1853
- Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents every three years beginning in 1853
- Assessment ledgers list: **householder name, real estate value, occupation, and sometimes nativity**
- These fill the gap between census years and can confirm Irish origin ("nativity" field)
- Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives and county courthouses

---

## 3. Vital Records

**Pennsylvania statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, and deaths was mandated but compliance in the coal counties was highly inconsistent through the 1870s–1880s. Do not assume a civil record was created just because law required it — church records are frequently the only surviving documentation for this period.

| Record Type | FamilySearch Holdings | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1885–1950** (collection 1921317) | 524,189 records, 1,048,378 persons, 312,045 images | ✅ Indexed + images |
| **Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (collection 1571957) | 312,045 records, 624,090 persons, 156,023 images | ✅ Indexed + images |
| **Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (collection 1502909) | 198,765 records, 397,530 persons — **no images** | ✅ Indexed (compiled abstracts only) |
| **Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906–1968** (collection 2255317) | 4,218,763 records/images | ✅ Indexed + images — **but begins 1906, after your window** |
| **Schuylkill Co. Marriage Records, 1870–1910** (vol. 007936753) | 94 images | 🔍 Browse-only (0% indexed) |

> **Marriage collection gap:** County marriages collection begins 1885, and the Schuylkill volume is browse-only. For 1860–1885 coal-region marriages, church registers are frequently the only indexed source.

---

## 4. Church Records — The Primary Source for Irish Ancestors

For Irish Catholic immigrants, **parish registers** are typically more complete and more informative than civil records in this period.

| Record | FamilySearch Holdings | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| **Schuylkill Co. Church Records, 1842–1895** (vol. 007936751) | 187 images — English and **German** | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed) — non-English portions require reading original |

- Catholic parish registers for the coal counties are physically held at the **Diocese of Scranton** (post-1868) and **Diocese of Harrisburg** (pre-1868) archives. Contact both if your ancestor's events span 1868.
- Many registers have **not** been digitized. Write to the diocesan archives directly for pre-1880 registers.
- Irish immigrant parishes in Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah, and Hazleton are the most genealogically productive.
- Non-Catholic Irish (Church of Ireland, Presbyterian) records are sparser; check the Presbyterian Historical Society in Philadelphia.

---

## 5. Census Records

| Census | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1860, 1870, 1880** | Full coverage for all five counties on FamilySearch; indexed and searchable |
| **1880** | ⭐ First census to record relationship to head of household — critical for proving family structure ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records)) |
| **1890** | ⚠️ **Mostly destroyed** — a major gap exactly in the middle of your target window; substitute with 1889–1892 city directories, tax assessments, and church records |
| **1900** | Complements 1880; records birthplace of parents, enabling identification of Irish-born generation |

- The 1880 Soundex index is especially useful for Irish surnames with variant spellings (Murphy/Murphey, Brennan/Brennen, O'Brien with/without the O').
- Pennsylvania did not conduct its own state census during this period.

---

## 6. Naturalization Records — Critical for Irish Immigrants

Naturalization is often the single best record type for confirming Irish origin, naming a specific county or townland.

| Record | FamilySearch Holdings | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915** (vol. 008120443) | 351 images — English and **German** | 🔍 15% indexed; remainder browse-only |
| **Schuylkill Co. Naturalization Records, 1849–1915** (vol. 007936750) | 298 images | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |

**Key naturalization rules for your period** ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records)):
- **Before September 1906:** Naturalizations were handled by *any* court of record — Quarter Sessions Court, Court of Common Pleas, or Orphans' Court. Your Irish ancestor could have naturalized in any of these; search all three at the county courthouse.
- **After September 1906:** Centralized in federal courts. For eastern Pennsylvania: **NARA Philadelphia**.
- Declarations of Intent ("first papers") and Petitions for Naturalization both name **country of origin** and often a specific county of Ireland.
- ⚠️ A man naturalized in Luzerne County before 1878 whose family later moved to what became Lackawanna — search Luzerne's records, not Lackawanna's.

---

## 7. Probate Records

| Record | FamilySearch Holdings | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196) | 893,214 records/images | ✅ Indexed + images |
| **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** (vol. 008120441) | 1,180 images | 🔍 Browse-only (0% indexed) |
| **Schuylkill Co. Probate Records, 1851–1930** (vol. 007936749) | 412 images | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed) |

- Wills and administrations name heirs, relationships, and sometimes "late of County [X], Ireland" — a direct homeland link.
- Mining-era probates may also inventory mining equipment, company scrip, and union membership.

---

## 8. Land & Deed Records

| Record | FamilySearch Holdings | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| **Schuylkill Co. Deed Records, 1815–1900** (vol. 007936752) | 543 images | 🔍 **22% indexed** — partial name-search; remainder browse-only |

- Coal company land transfers are voluminous in this period; most individual miner land records are modest (company-owned housing/patches).
- The Reading Coal & Iron Company and Philadelphia & Reading Coal and Iron Company held large tracts in Schuylkill — their land books can document tenant miners.

---

## 9. Death Records

| Record | FamilySearch Holdings | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania Death Records, 1852–1968** (vol. 008120442) | 674 images | 🔍 Browse-only (0% indexed) |

- Pennsylvania statewide death registration began 1852 at county level but compliance was poor through the 1870s in the coal region.
- **Mine accident reports** (colliery inspection reports) are an important substitute — they document death by name, colliery, and sometimes nationality/origin. Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives (Record Group 26, Bureau of Mines).
- Coal-region newspapers (Miners' Journal, Pottsville; Scranton Republican) published detailed accident and death notices with hometown information.

---

## 10. Mining & Occupational Records — Coal-Region Specific

These sources have no parallel in standard genealogy guides:

| Source | What It Contains | Where Held |
|---|---|---|
| **Company payroll books** (basis of Anthracite Index above) | Name, occupation, wage, parish of origin | Pennsylvania State Archives; individual company archives |
| **Mine inspection reports** (Bureau of Mines, PA) | Accident victims by colliery, sometimes with nationality | PA State Archives, RG 26 |
| **Coal & Iron Police records** | Enforcement actions naming individuals | PA State Archives |
| **UMWA (United Mine Workers) records** | Union membership rolls from 1890 | UMWA archives; some at Penn State Special Collections |
| **Molly Maguires trial records, 1876–1877** | Extensive Irish community documentation in Schuylkill County; witness lists name dozens of Irish miners and families | Carbon and Schuylkill county court records; Pottsville courthouse |

---

## 11. Immigration Records

- **Passenger lists:** The bulk of Irish anthracite-region immigration arrived via Philadelphia and New York. Search both ports for 1840s–1870s arrivals on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Philadelphia port records** are the most directly relevant — many Irish emigrant ships landed in Philadelphia before immigrants traveled inland to the coal region.
- Chain migration was dominant: an Irish man naturalized and established would sponsor relatives. The naturalization record of the **sponsor** often names the newcomer's family in Ireland.

---

## 12. Military Records

- The Civil War produced significant service from Irish coal miners, particularly in Pennsylvania regiments (e.g., 48th PA Infantry — predominantly Schuylkill County miners).
- Pension files (at NARA) name the widow, children, ages, marriage date and place, and sometimes birthplace in Ireland — among the richest single records for Irish ancestors.
- Pennsylvania state service records at the PA State Archives complement the NARA federal files.

---

## 13. External Repositories & Resources

| Repository | What It Holds |
|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine inspection reports, Bureau of Mines records, county naturalization microfilm, triennial tax assessments |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers post-1868 for Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon, and surrounding counties |
| **Diocese of Harrisburg Archives** | Catholic parish registers pre-1868 for all five coal counties |
| **NARA Philadelphia** | Post-1906 naturalization petitions; federal census originals |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society** | Local indexes, newspapers, mining records, city directories |
| **Schuylkill County Historical Society** | Miners' Journal archive; local biographical volumes |
| **Penn State Special Collections** | UMWA records; coal company archives |
| **FamilySearch (Ancestry via external links)** | Pennsylvania Tax & Exoneration Lists 1768–1801; 1850 Schuylkill Census (both pre-period background) |

---

## 14. Research Strategy Priorities for Irish Ancestors, 1860–1890

Given this landscape, here is the recommended search order:

1. **Federal censuses (1860, 1870, 1880)** — indexed, free on FamilySearch; establish the household, ages, birthplaces
2. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — if your ancestor worked in the lower anthracite field; may give parish of origin directly
3. **Naturalization records** — browse Schuylkill vol. 007936750 and Pennsylvania vol. 008120443; or write county courthouse for pre-1906 records; this is your best route to the Irish county/townland
4. **Catholic parish registers** — Diocese of Scranton (post-1868) and Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868); contact archives directly for undigitized registers
5. **Triennial tax assessments from 1853** — PA State Archives; fills census gaps and sometimes notes nativity
6. **Mine accident reports** — PA State Archives RG 26; essential if an ancestor died in the mines
7. **Probate records** (collection 1999196, indexed) — wills can name Irish homeland
8. **Marriage collections** (1921317, 1571957) — post-1885 civil marriages are indexed; earlier marriages rely on church registers
9. **Civil War pension files** (NARA) — if any ancestor served; among the richest Irish-origin documents
10. **Molly Maguires trial records** (Schuylkill & Carbon County courts) — if the surname or townland overlaps with documented Maguire communities

---

| PA County & Civil Marriages 1885–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images |

# Locality Guide: Vermont (Pre-Statehood, c. 1749–1791)

## Jurisdiction overview

Vermont is the 14th U.S. state, admitted March 4, 1791. The pre-statehood period is among the most jurisdictionally complex in American genealogy: the same territory was simultaneously claimed by New Hampshire, New York, and (from 1777) the independent Vermont Republic. Records were created under three different governmental authorities, and they survive in three different archives.

- **Admitted to the Union:** March 4, 1791
- **Republic declared:** January 15, 1777
- **Parent jurisdictions (contested):**
  - *New Hampshire* — Gov. Benning Wentworth issued over 130 township grants ("New Hampshire Grants") across the region 1749–1764
  - *New York* — British Crown ruled in New York's favor in 1764; NY organized the region into Cumberland County (east) and Gloucester County (northeast) and issued competing land patents
  - *Vermont Republic* (1777–1791) — Declared independence; organized its own county governments, courts, and land office
- **Early governmental centers:** Bennington (first capital area), Westminster, Windsor
- **Population:** Grew from near zero in 1750 to approximately 85,000 by 1790 (first federal census). No population tool data was returned for this period.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence agriculture, timber, potash production
- **Settlement origins:** Settlers came almost entirely from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island, following the Connecticut River corridor and the Champlain Valley
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist (dominant in most towns), Baptist (rapidly growing by 1780s), Quaker (Ferrisburgh/Monkton area from mid-1780s), Anglican/Episcopal (scattered)
- **Key events:** End of French and Indian War (~1760, opening settlement); Green Mountain Boys resistance to NY authority (1770s); Revolutionary War (1775–1783); Vermont Republic (1777–1791); statehood (1791)

---

## Boundary changes and jurisdictional sequence

Understanding this sequence is essential — it determines *which archive* holds a given record:

| Period | Authority | What records were created | Where records are held |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1749–1764 | New Hampshire (Wentworth grants) | Township grant charters | NH State Archives, Concord |
| 1764–1777 | New York (Cumberland/Gloucester counties) | Land patents, county court records, 1771 Grant Survey | NY State Archives, Albany |
| 1777–1791 | Vermont Republic | Town vital records, deeds, probate, grand lists, court records | Vermont town clerks, county courthouses, Vermont State Archives |
| 1791+ | State of Vermont | All subsequent state records | Vermont State Archives |

**Vermont county formation under the Republic:**

| County | Formed |
|---|---|
| Bennington | 1778 |
| Windham | 1779 |
| Windsor | 1781 |
| Rutland | 1781 |
| Orange | 1781 |
| Addison | 1785 |
| Chittenden | 1787 |

Counties formed after 1791 are outside the pre-statehood scope.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Statewide civil registration start date:** **1857** — nearly 70 years after the period of interest ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). No statewide civil vital records exist for the pre-statehood period.
- **Town-level records:** Vermont town clerks recorded births, marriages, and deaths from the 1770s onward. The wiki specifically states that "earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly" ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). Coverage is highly variable — some well-organized towns have nearly complete records; others have none before 1820.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Vermont Vital Records, 1720–1908* is a compiled and indexed collection on FamilySearch drawing from town clerk records. This is the primary online starting point for the period. Check FamilySearch Catalog by town name for additional filmed town records not in this collection.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices (originals); Vermont State Archives (filmed copies); FamilySearch (indexed/digitized)
- **Digitization level:** *Vermont Vital Records 1720–1908* — **indexed + images** on FamilySearch. Town records not in that compilation — **physical-only or microfilm** depending on town.
- **Gaps:** Many births and deaths were never recorded at the town level in this period. Newly settled towns (especially northern Vermont before 1787) have the sparsest coverage.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (baptisms, marriages, burials); family bibles; cemetery records; probate records (which name ages and relationships)

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregational churches were organized in most towns within a few years of founding. Baptist congregations proliferated from the 1780s. Quaker meetings (Ferrisburgh, Monkton). Anglican/Episcopal in scattered areas.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, membership rolls, letters of dismission (transfer documents that document family migration from an origin church to a Vermont church — critically useful for tracing settlers' New England origins)
- **Where held:** Local church offices; Vermont Historical Society (transcriptions and some microfilm); Congregational Library, Boston (Congregational records); American Baptist Historical Society (Baptist records); FamilySearch microfilm catalog
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Digitization level:** Mostly **physical-only or microfilm**; some church records appear in FamilySearch Catalog by town; few are name-indexed online.
- **Caveat:** Many early Vermont churches kept poor records in the 1770s–1780s or have since lost them. Coverage is inconsistent across denominations.

### Census records

- **1790 Federal Census:** Vermont was enumerated in the first federal census of 1790 — conducted one year before statehood. Lists heads of household with tallies of free persons by age/sex category. **Indexed + images available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.** This is the only federal census applicable to the pre-statehood period.
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** Prepared under New York colonial authority, this enumeration lists approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry gives grantee name, township, grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. The FamilySearch Wiki identifies this as "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state" — one that "predates any Vermont civil registration" ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). **This is your most important pre-1780 substitute census.**
- **Grand lists (tax/property assessment lists):** Vermont Republic towns compiled annual grand lists from the late 1770s onward. These name adult male property holders and function as partial censuses for intercensal years.
- **Access:** 1790 census — **indexed + images online**. 1771 Grant Survey Schedule — check FamilySearch Catalog; check New York and Vermont historical society holdings. Grand lists — mostly **physical-only** at town clerk offices or Vermont State Archives microfilm.

### Probate and court records

- **Vermont's unique probate system:** Vermont uses probate *districts* rather than county probate courts — a distinctive structure not found in most U.S. states. Probate districts were established under the Republic beginning in 1778. These are the earliest surviving probate records in Vermont.
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, estate inventories, accounts of distribution — all of which can document family relationships and ages when vital records are missing.
- **Date range:** From 1778 (Bennington district, the oldest) onward. No Vermont probate records predate the Republic.
- **Where held:** Individual probate district offices (originals); Vermont State Archives (microfilm copies); FamilySearch Catalog (some districts have been filmed).
- **County courts:** Vermont county courts handled civil suits, debt cases, criminal matters, and road/boundary disputes from 1777+. The New Hampshire Grants controversy generated prolific land litigation that can document early settlers.
- **Digitization level:** Some probate records on FamilySearch microfilm (**browse-only**); originals at probate district offices (**physical-only**). Court records mostly **physical-only** at county courthouses or Vermont State Archives.

### Land records

Land records are the **single most important record class** for pre-statehood Vermont research. The overlapping grant systems produced extensive documentation of who held land and when.

**⚠️ Critical Vermont quirk: Deeds are recorded at the TOWN level, not the county.** Unlike most U.S. states, Vermont deed recording is the responsibility of the town clerk, not a county recorder of deeds. When searching for a deed, identify the specific town first.

- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (New England township grant system); Vermont is a *state-land state*
- **Key record series:**

  1. **New Hampshire Grants (1749–1764):** Original charter documents naming township proprietors (the original grantees, not necessarily the actual settlers). Held at the **New Hampshire State Archives**, Concord, NH.

  2. **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:** ~1,800 grantees enumerated by New York colonial authority; "the earliest systematic resident list for the future state" ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). A critical finding aid for early land claimants.

  3. **New York competing land patents (1764–1777):** New York issued patents over the same territory as the NH grants. Held at the **New York State Archives**, Albany, NY.

  4. **Vermont Republic town grants and proprietors' records (1777–1791):** After declaring independence, the Republic confirmed or re-granted lands. Town proprietors' records document original grantees within each township. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that 19th-century town histories "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access" ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)).

  5. **Town deed records (1777+):** Individual land transfer deeds recorded at the town clerk level. Held at town clerk offices (originals); some filmed and in FamilySearch Catalog.

- **Digitization level:** Town deed records — **browse-only images** for filmed towns; **physical-only** for unfilmed towns. NH grant charters — **physical-only** at NH State Archives. NY competing patents — **physical-only** at NY State Archives.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Revolutionary War (1775–1783) is the dominant military event. Vermont's Green Mountain Boys were active from 1770 onward. Some men had earlier French and Indian War service (1754–1763).
- **Record types and value:**
  - *Revolutionary War service records:* Compiled military service records at NARA (Record Group 93); indexed on Fold3 and Ancestry — **indexed + images**
  - *Revolutionary War pension files:* Filed by veterans or widows from 1818 onward, pension files often contain detailed biographical narratives with 1770s–1780s information — ages, marriages, children's names, places of residence. **Extremely valuable for the pre-statehood period.** At NARA; indexed and available on Fold3 (subscription) and FamilySearch — **indexed + images**
  - *Bounty land warrants:* Some documentation of Vermont veterans. At NARA; some digitized.
  - *Vermont state militia records:* Some survive at the Vermont State Archives — **physical-only**
  - *Green Mountain Boys rosters:* Published in state and regimental histories; Vermont Historical Society holds originals
- **Where held:** NARA (service records, pension files, bounty land); Vermont State Archives (militia); Fold3 / Ancestry / FamilySearch (digitized).

### Cemetery records

- **Period:** Town cemeteries established as communities were founded, from the 1760s–1770s onward. Stones from this period may be simple fieldstone markers, weathered, or lost.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) has significant Vermont coverage including pre-1800 stones. Coverage is community-contributed and varies by town — **indexed (names), no images for older stones**. BillionGraves provides supplemental coverage.
- **DAR transcriptions:** Daughters of the American Revolution chapters conducted systematic cemetery surveys of Vermont towns in the early 20th century, transcribing early headstones. These are held at the Vermont Historical Society and some are available on microfilm. Valuable because some stones have since been lost.
- **Sexton records:** Rare for the late 1700s.
- **Digitization level:** FindAGrave — **indexed online**, free. DAR transcriptions — **physical-only or microfilm** at Vermont Historical Society.

### Newspaper records

- **Earliest papers:** Vermont's first newspaper was the *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington), founded 1783. The *Vermont Journal* (Windsor) followed ca. 1783–1784. Several additional papers appeared in the late 1780s.
- **Limitation:** No Vermont newspapers exist before 1783, and survival of early issues is uneven.
- **Content value:** Marriage announcements, death notices, legal notices (land sales, estate settlements, sheriff's sales), legislative proceedings, and local news items appear from the founding issues.
- **Where held:** Vermont Historical Society; Vermont State Library; Newspapers.com (subscription) and Chronicling America ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/), free) have some Vermont coverage.
- **Digitization level:** Chronicling America — **browse-only images** for some Vermont papers. Newspapers.com — **full-text searchable** (subscription). Vermont Historical Society holdings — **physical-only or microfilm**.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** Vermont's late-1700s settlers were overwhelmingly internal migrants from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island — not international immigrants. International passenger lists are not a primary source class for this period.
- **Most useful approach:** Trace the family backward to its New England origin community. Church "letters of dismission" (transfer certificates) document moves from a Connecticut or Massachusetts congregation to a Vermont church and are often the only direct evidence of geographic origin.
- **Revolutionary-era naturalization:** Largely moot for this period — most settlers were already British colonial subjects or had obtained citizenship through the Revolution. Post-1790 naturalizations (after the Naturalization Act) would apply to any foreign-born arrivals.
- **Nearest ports:** Boston and New York for any international arrivals; records at NARA and online via Ancestry/FamilySearch.

### Tax records

- **Grand lists:** Vermont's primary tax records. Annual grand lists compiled at the town level from the late 1770s onward, assessing property and polls. These name adult male property holders and can substitute for census data in years without a census.
- **Substitute value:** High. In the absence of vital, census, or church records for a given town, the grand list may be the only surviving evidence placing a person in a community in a specific year. Check every available year.
- **Date range:** From the late 1770s (Republic era) at the town level.
- **Where held:** Town clerk offices (originals); Vermont State Archives (some microfilm).
- **Digitization level:** Mostly **physical-only** or **microfilm** (browse-only); check FamilySearch Catalog by town name.

### Other record types

- **Town meeting records:** Organized Vermont towns held annual meetings from founding. Records document local officeholders, road commissioners, tax constables, and overseers of the poor — roles that identify community members not otherwise recorded. Held at town clerk offices (**physical-only** generally).

- **Town histories:** Published primarily 1860–1900, Vermont town histories are exceptionally rich for the pre-statehood period. They frequently contain early settler lists, reprints of proprietors' records, genealogical appendices for founding families, and transcriptions of records since lost. The FamilySearch Wiki specifically flags them as sources that "often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access" ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)). Vermont Historical Society and most Vermont public libraries hold them; many have been digitized at Google Books and Archive.org.

- **Vermont State Papers:** Published 1823 by Secretary of State William Slade, the *Vermont State Papers* documents Republic-era grants, petitions, and legislation. Available in research libraries; partially digitized.

- **Vermont Republic constitution and early legislation:** Documents the structure of early Vermont government; useful for understanding what record-keeping was mandated.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections relevant to 1749–1791 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | *Vermont Vital Records 1720–1908* (indexed); 1790 Federal Census (indexed + images); Revolutionary War pension files (images); FamilySearch Catalog (microfilmed town vital, deed, probate, and church records by town) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1790 Federal Census; Revolutionary War service records and pension files; compiled Vermont vital records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War service records and pension files (indexed + images) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Vermont cemetery records including pre-1800 headstones | Free |
| Chronicling America (NARA/Library of Congress) | Vermont newspapers from 1783; browse-only | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Vermont early newspapers; full-text searchable | Subscription |
| Google Books / Archive.org | Many Vermont town histories digitized; searchable | Free |

> **Note on external links:** The FamilySearch external links tool returned six generic national resources (NARA, FindAGrave, Fold3, Ancestry census, Newspapers.com, FamilySearch vital records wiki) rather than Vermont-specific curated collections for 1749–1800. For a current list of Vermont-specific digitized collections, consult the [FamilySearch Vermont Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog?q=Vermont) directly, filtering by county or town name.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA), Montpelier, VT | Republic-era records, legislative records, some land and court records | In-person; some via FamilySearch |
| Vermont Historical Society, Montpelier, VT | Town histories, manuscripts, newspapers (1783+), DAR cemetery surveys, genealogical collections | In-person; some digitized |
| Town clerk offices (individual Vermont towns) | Vital records (1770s+, uneven), deeds (town-level recording), grand lists, town meeting minutes, proprietors' records | In-person or written inquiry to each town |
| County probate district offices | Probate records from 1778 (Bennington) onward | In-person; some filmed at FamilySearch |
| New Hampshire State Archives, Concord, NH | Wentworth New Hampshire Grant charters (1749–1764) | In-person; written inquiry |
| New York State Archives, Albany, NY | Cumberland and Gloucester county records (1764–1777); competing NY land patents | In-person; written inquiry |
| NARA, Washington, D.C. | Revolutionary War service records (RG 93), pension files, 1790 census | In-person; many online via Fold3/Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Congregational Library, Boston, MA | New England Congregational church records, including early Vermont parishes | In-person; some records available through NEHGS |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston, MA | Compiled genealogies, New England vital records, manuscripts | In-person; some online via AmericanAncestors.org (subscription) |

---

## Records NOT online

The following exist but are **not fully accessible in any online database** for the pre-statehood period:

- **Town clerk vital records (pre-1857):** The *Vermont Vital Records 1720–1908* index covers many towns but not all. Original records for uncovered towns require direct contact with the town clerk.
- **Grand lists (tax lists):** Mostly physical-only at town clerk offices or browse-only microfilm; not broadly indexed online.
- **Town meeting and proprietors' records:** Physical-only at town clerk offices or Vermont State Archives, except where reprinted in digitized town histories.
- **New Hampshire Grant charters:** At New Hampshire State Archives; not online.
- **New York competing land patents and Cumberland/Gloucester county records:** At New York State Archives; not online.
- **Church records (pre-1800):** Many early Vermont Congregational and Baptist records remain with individual congregations or denominational archives and have not been digitized.
- **Vermont Republic-era court records:** Largely physical-only at county courthouses or Vermont State Archives.
- **Vermont State Papers and early legislative records:** Some copies in research libraries; not fully digitized or indexed.

---

## Known record losses

- **Pre-Republic New York county records:** Some records created by New York's Cumberland and Gloucester county administrations (1764–1777) were lost during the turbulence of the Revolution; survivors are at the New York State Archives.
- **Early church records:** Many of the earliest Congregational and Baptist congregations in Vermont have lost records from the 1770s–1790s due to church closures, mergers, and deterioration. What survives is fragmentary.
- **Town clerk records:** Individual towns have suffered losses from fire, flood, and neglect. No Vermont-wide courthouse catastrophe occurred, but localized losses are common. Some early grand lists and town meeting records are missing for specific towns.

---

## Research tips

1. **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is your pre-1780 census substitute.** This is the earliest systematic resident list for Vermont — ~1,800 grantees enumerated under New York colonial authority. Use it to place ancestors in specific townships before the Republic organized its own records. ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))

2. **Statewide vital registration began in 1857, not at statehood.** Town-level records go back to the 1770s, but they "survive unevenly." Search FamilySearch's *Vermont Vital Records 1720–1908* first; if the town isn't well covered, contact the town clerk directly. ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy))

3. **Vermont deeds are recorded at the TOWN level, not the county.** This is the most common trap for researchers unfamiliar with Vermont. Identify the town, then contact or visit that town clerk's office. County-level deed searches will come up empty.

4. **Read the town history before anything else.** Vermont town histories (1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records, early settler lists, and genealogical appendices for founding families — information that exists nowhere online. The FamilySearch Wiki specifically flags them for reprinting "colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access." ([Vermont Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) Many are free on Google Books and Archive.org.

5. **Pre-1777 records are in New Hampshire and New York, not Vermont.** Grant records are at the New Hampshire State Archives; court and competing land records are at the New York State Archives. Do not assume your Vermont ancestor's pre-Republic records are in Vermont.

6. **Revolutionary War pension files are genealogically dense.** Vermont was settled largely by Revolutionary War veterans and their families. Pension files (filed from 1818 onward) routinely contain detailed biographical narratives documenting 1770s–1780s events — ages, marriage details, children's names, places of residence. These are indexed and available on Fold3, Ancestry, and FamilySearch.

7. **Trace settler origins back to southern New England.** Most pre-statehood Vermont settlers migrated from Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island. If a vital record is missing for Vermont, search the origin community — Connecticut and Massachusetts town vital records and church registers frequently document births of people who later appear in Vermont records.

8. **Use FamilySearch Catalog by TOWN name, not just state.** The online name-indexed collections don't represent everything FamilySearch has on microfilm. Search the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) by Vermont town name to find filmed vital records, probate records, deed records, and church records that are on film but not yet name-indexed.

9. **Check adjoining state records.** Families near the Connecticut River border likely generated records in New Hampshire (Cheshire County or Grafton County, NH — town-level records, same structure as Vermont). Families near the New York line may have records in Washington County, NY or Rensselaer County, NY (county-level deed and court records). Settlers into Bennington County may have roots in Berkshire County, MA or Hampshire County, MA.

10. **Grand lists substitute for missing census years.** For any year between 1777 and 1790 when no census exists, the town grand list is likely the only surviving record placing a specific person in a specific community. Check every available year at the town clerk office or Vermont State Archives.
